body_text:
## What happens

`DROP TABLE t` on a WAL table that still has a pending `ALTER TABLE t SET TYPE WAL` request does not stick. After the next restart the table is registered again, is visible in the catalogue, and returns the rows it held when it was dropped.

```java
execute("create table zombie (x long, ts timestamp) timestamp(ts) partition by DAY WAL");
execute("insert into zombie values (1, '2022-02-24T00:00:00.000000Z')");
drainWalQueue();

execute("alter table zombie set type bypass wal");   // writes _convert
execute("alter table zombie set type wal");          // overwrites _convert: walEnabled=true
execute("drop table zombie");                        // dir survives: WAL apply has not purged it yet
assertNull(engine.getTableTokenIfExists("zombie"));  // gone, as expected

engine.releaseInactive();
engine.load();                                       // simulated restart

assertNull(engine.getTableTokenIfExists("zombie"));  // FAILS: the table is back
// select * from zombie -> 1, 2022-02-24T00:00:00.000000Z
```

The resurrection is durable, not an in-memory artifact: the reload writes the token back into `tables.d` and forces a compaction, so every later boot sees an ordinary live table with no trace of the drop.

Variants, same harness:

| pending `_convert` | outcome after restart |
| --- | --- |
| none | stays dropped |
| `set type bypass wal` (WAL -> non-WAL) | stays dropped, guarded |
| `set type wal` (-> WAL) | **resurrected, with data** |

The window is not narrow. Dropping a WAL table only marks the table and schedules the directory for deletion by WAL apply / `WalPurgeJob`. Any instance where WAL apply is disabled, suspended, backlogged, or that exits before the purge completes keeps the directory, and with it the `_convert` file.

Reproduced on master `dbf0a87b51`; the same code is on current master.

## Why

`core/src/main/java/io/questdb/cairo/TableConverter.java`

1. The "nothing to do" pre-check resolves the existing token with `tableNameRegistry.getTableTokenByDirName(dirName)`, which returns `null` for a dropped table (`AbstractTableNameRegistry.getTableTokenByDirName`). A dropped table therefore never matches "already has the expected type" and always falls through to conversion — being dropped makes conversion *more* likely, not less.
2. The `walEnabled == true` branch has no dropped-table check. It re-registers the table with the sequencer (`tableSequencerAPI.registerTable`, which recreates `txn_seq` and wipes the `DROP_TABLE_STRUCTURE_VERSION` marker), resets the metadata version, and appends the token to `convertedTables`.
3. `tableNameRegistry.reload(convertedTables)` republishes it as live (`TableNameRegistryStore`: `dirNameToTableTokenMap.put(dirName, ReverseTableMapItem.of(token))`) and forces registry compaction.

The mirror branch does carry the guard — `!tableNameRegistry.isWalTableDropped(dirName)` — added in #5295 ("fix table type conversion leading to table drop if db restarts midway"). That fix covered WAL -> non-WAL only; the non-WAL -> WAL branch has been unguarded since.

## Second route, same class of bug

`TableNameRegistryStore.reloadFromRootDirectory()` registers every table directory that is not already in the reverse map. Normally a dropped table occupies that key as `ReverseTableMapItem.ofDropped(...)` and the scan skips it, but when the maps are cleared (`clearRegistryToReloadFromFileSystem()`, reached from a duplicate dir-to-name mapping) or when `tables.d` is lost, the scan re-registers the dropped directory as live. The code says so itself:

> the registry is the pointer store every name resolves through, and the directory-scan fallback cannot tell a dropped-but-unpurged table from a live one, so dropped tables come back.

The on-disk evidence of the drop is available in both cases: `SequencerMetadata.dropTable()` writes and fsyncs `DROP_TABLE_STRUCTURE_VERSION` into `txn_seq/_meta`, and `TableNameRegistryStore.checkWalTableInPendingDropState()` already reads exactly that. It is currently consulted only from `resolveTableNameConflict()`, i.e. only when two directories claim the same logical name.

## Suggested fix

1. `TableConverter`, WAL branch: refuse the conversion when the directory is dropped, mirroring the non-WAL branch.

```java
if (walEnabled) {
    if (tableNameRegistry.isWalTableDropped(dirName)) {
        LOG.info().$("table will not be converted to WAL, table is dropped [dirName=").$(dirNameSink).I$();
        continue;   // leave _convert in place; the purge removes the whole dir
    }
    ...
}
```

2. `TableNameRegistryStore.reloadFromRootDirectory()`: for a WAL directory, consult `checkWalTableInPendingDropState()` before registering it as live, and register it as `ofDropped(...)` when the sequencer metadata says the table was dropped.

3. Regression tests: the three variants in the table above, plus a registry-rebuild variant that clears `tables.d` and asserts the dropped directory does not come back.

## Impact

A table an operator deleted becomes readable again after a restart. For a deletion made to satisfy a data-removal request, that is a compliance problem rather than only a correctness one. The resurrected table also carries a reset metadata version and a freshly seeded sequencer, so it re-enters the catalogue with a different lineage than it had.

`DROP TABLE t` on a WAL table that still has a pending `ALTER TABLE t SET TYPE WAL` request does not stick. After the next restart the table is registered again, is visible in the catalogue, and returns the rows it held when it was dropped.

```java
execute("create table zombie (x long, ts timestamp) timestamp(ts) partition by DAY WAL");
execute("insert into zombie values (1, '2022-02-24T00:00:00.000000Z')");
drainWalQueue();

execute("alter table zombie set type bypass wal");   // writes _convert
execute("alter table zombie set type wal");          // overwrites _convert: walEnabled=true
execute("drop table zombie");                        // dir survives: WAL apply has not purged it yet
assertNull(engine.getTableTokenIfExists("zombie"));  // gone, as expected

engine.releaseInactive();
engine.load();                                       // simulated restart

assertNull(engine.getTableTokenIfExists("zombie"));  // FAILS: the table is back
// select * from zombie -> 1, 2022-02-24T00:00:00.000000Z
```

The resurrection is durable, not an in-memory artifact: the reload writes the token back into `tables.d` and forces a compaction, so every later boot sees an ordinary live table with no trace of the drop.

Variants, same harness:

| pending `_convert` | outcome after restart |
| --- | --- |
| none | stays dropped |
| `set type bypass wal` (WAL -> non-WAL) | stays dropped, guarded |
| `set type wal` (-> WAL) | **resurrected, with data** |

The window is not narrow. Dropping a WAL table only marks the table and schedules the directory for deletion by WAL apply / `WalPurgeJob`. Any instance where WAL apply is disabled, suspended, backlogged, or that exits before the purge completes keeps the directory, and with it the `_convert` file.

Reproduced on master `dbf0a87b51`; the same code is on current master.

## Why

`core/src/main/java/io/questdb/cairo/TableConverter.java`

1. The "nothing to do" pre-check resolves the existing token with `tableNameRegistry.getTableTokenByDirName(dirName)`, which returns `null` for a dropped table (`AbstractTableNameRegistry.getTableTokenByDirName`). A dropped table therefore never matches "already has the expected type" and always falls through to conversion — being dropped makes conversion *more* likely, not less.
2. The `walEnabled == true` branch has no dropped-table check. It re-registers the table with the sequencer (`tableSequencerAPI.registerTable`, which recreates `txn_seq` and wipes the `DROP_TABLE_STRUCTURE_VERSION` marker), resets the metadata version, and appends the token to `convertedTables`.
3. `tableNameRegistry.reload(convertedTables)` republishes it as live (`TableNameRegistryStore`: `dirNameToTableTokenMap.put(dirName, ReverseTableMapItem.of(token))`) and forces registry compaction.

The mirror branch does carry the guard — `!tableNameRegistry.isWalTableDropped(dirName)` — added in #5295 ("fix table type conversion leading to table drop if db restarts midway"). That fix covered WAL -> non-WAL only; the non-WAL -> WAL branch has been unguarded since.

## Second route, same class of bug

`TableNameRegistryStore.reloadFromRootDirectory()` registers every table directory that is not already in the reverse map. Normally a dropped table occupies that key as `ReverseTableMapItem.ofDropped(...)` and the scan skips it, but when the maps are cleared (`clearRegistryToReloadFromFileSystem()`, reached from a duplicate dir-to-name mapping) or when `tables.d` is lost, the scan re-registers the dropped directory as live. The code says so itself:

> the registry is the pointer store every name resolves through, and the directory-scan fallback cannot tell a dropped-but-unpurged table from a live one, so dropped tables come back.

The on-disk evidence of the drop is available in both cases: `SequencerMetadata.dropTable()` writes and fsyncs `DROP_TABLE_STRUCTURE_VERSION` into `txn_seq/_meta`, and `TableNameRegistryStore.checkWalTableInPendingDropState()` already reads exactly that. It is currently consulted only from `resolveTableNameConflict()`, i.e. only when two directories claim the same logical name.

## Suggested fix

1. `TableConverter`, WAL branch: refuse the conversion when the directory is dropped, mirroring the non-WAL branch.

```java
if (walEnabled) {
    if (tableNameRegistry.isWalTableDropped(dirName)) {
        LOG.info().$("table will not be converted to WAL, table is dropped [dirName=").$(dirNameSink).I$();
        continue;   // leave _convert in place; the purge removes the whole dir
    }
    ...
}
```

2. `TableNameRegistryStore.reloadFromRootDirectory()`: for a WAL directory, consult `checkWalTableInPendingDropState()` before registering it as live, and register it as `ofDropped(...)` when the sequencer metadata says the table was dropped.

3. Regression tests: the three variants in the table above, plus a registry-rebuild variant that clears `tables.d` and asserts the dropped directory does not come back.

## Impact

A table an operator deleted becomes readable again after a restart. For a deletion made to satisfy a data-removal request, that is a compliance problem rather than only a correctness one. The resurrected table also carries a reset metadata version and a freshly seeded sequencer, so it re-enters the catalogue with a different lineage than it had.

body_text:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?

When working with many tables, the flat list in the Schema Explorer becomes
hard to navigate. There is currently no way to organize tables into logical
groups (except naming) , which makes managing large numbers of tables difficult and cluttered.

### Describe the solution you'd like.

A GUI-only organizational feature in the Web Console Schema Explorer that allows users to:

- Create named groups (e.g., "Schema1", "Schema2") in the Schema Explorer
- Assign existing tables to these groups
- Tables remain globally unique in the database . no backend or storage changes required
- Groups are persisted as a UI preference only

Example view in the Schema Explorer:

Schema1
  ├── Table1
  ├── Table2
  └── Table3

Schema2
  ├── Table4
  ├── Table5
  └── Table6

This would build on the existing tree-view and folder structure already
present in the Schema Explorer, which already groups objects into categories
like Tables, Materialized views, Views, and Live views.

### Describe alternatives you've considered.

Using table name prefixes (e.g., schema1_table1) — this works but is not
elegant.

A full SQL schema implementation (like PostgreSQL schemas) was also
considered, but this would require significant backend and storage changes.
The GUI-only approach solves the organizational problem without any breaking
changes to the query engine or SQL compatibility.

### Full Name:

Adrien Cassagnes

### Affiliation:

Quantitative researcher

### Additional context

This is intentionally scoped as a GUI-only feature to keep the implementation
lightweight:

- No impact on the query engine, storage format, or wire protocol
- No breaking changes to SQL or existing workflows
- The Schema Explorer already has a rich tree-view with expandable folders,
  making this a natural extension of existing UI patterns

body_text:
### Summary

Under `cairo.commit.mode=nosync` (the default) or `async`, an OS crash or power loss can leave a WAL
table's `_txn` with an applied seqTxn greater than the `maxTxn` recorded in its sequencer's
`txn_seq/_txnlog`. After restart, the sequencer hands out seqTxns that the table has already
applied. `ApplyWal2TableJob` starts from the table's applied seqTxn and never visits them, so those
new, acknowledged commits are never applied. Once the table catches up, `WalPurgeJob` treats their
WAL segments as fully applied and deletes them. Nothing is logged and the table is not suspended.

Losing un-synced commits at crash time is expected under nosync/async. This issue is about commits
made after a successful restart. They are lost without any further crash.

### Mechanism

- The sequencer header (`_txnlog`, `MAX_TXN_OFFSET_64`) and the table `_txn` are separate mmapped
  files. Under NOSYNC nothing is msynced. Under ASYNC, `msync(MS_ASYNC)` is a no-op on Linux. Kernel
  writeback can therefore persist the table's `_txn` (applied seqTxn A) while the `_txnlog` page on
  disk still says maxTxn M, with M < A.
- On open, `TableSequencerImpl` trusts the `_txnlog` header (`TableTransactionLogV1/V2.open`). No
  code compares it with the table's applied seqTxn, at open or at startup:
  - `CheckWalTransactionsJob` and `SeqTxnTracker` react only to `writerTxn < seqTxn`.
  - `wal_tables()` only displays both values.
  - `TableSequencerAPI.resumeTable` only moves the table forward.
  - The #7105 open-path reconciliation (`openOrRecoverMetadata` /
    `reconcileMetadataWithCommittedLog`) covers only the sequencer `_meta`. It treats the log header
    as the authority and never consults the table.
- The next commits get seqTxns M+1..A. `ApplyWal2TableJob.applyOutstandingWalTransactions` opens the
  txn-log cursor at the writer's applied seqTxn A, so it skips them. The first commit it applies is
  A+1.
- The applied seqTxn is `seqTxn + lagTxnCount` from `_txn` (`TableWriter.getAppliedSeqTxn`), not the
  bare `seqTxn`. Any detection must use it.

### Second consequence with the V2 (partitioned) txn log (from code reading, not reproduced)

`WalPurgeJob.fetchSequencerPairs` computes the current sequencer part from the table's seqTxn, and
`WalPurgeJob.Logic.run` deletes every part below it. If A has crossed a part boundary past the
header's part, the purge deletes the part that the sequencer still appends to.

Example with part size 16, M=15, A=17: the current part is computed as 1, so part 0 is deleted.
Part 0 holds records 1..15 and the slot for 16.

- The open sequencer keeps writing into the unlinked inode.
- The next open recreates an empty part, reads `maxStructureVersion = 0`, and the #7105 reconcile
  rebuilds the sequencer schema from `_meta.0`.

### Reproduction (test-level, simulating the crash image)

1. Run `CREATE TABLE t (x INT, ts TIMESTAMP) TIMESTAMP(ts) PARTITION BY DAY WAL`. Insert x=1..5 as
   five separate transactions and wait for apply (table seqTxn = 5).
2. Stop the engine. Rewrite the `txn_seq/_txnlog` header maxTxn from 5 to 3, and zero records 4..5.
   This models a `_txnlog` page last written back when maxTxn was 3.
3. Start the engine. `wal_tables()` reports writerTxn=5, sequencerTxn=3, suspended=false.
4. Insert x=6, 7, 8 as three transactions. `wal_transactions('t')` shows they receive seqTxns 4, 5
   and 6.
5. After apply, `wal_tables()` reports writerTxn=6, sequencerTxn=6, suspended=false.
   `SELECT x FROM t` returns 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 8. After WAL purge, the segment that held x=6 and x=7
   is deleted.

Reproduced with both the V1 txn-log format and the partitioned V2 format (part size 16), both with a
simulated restart and with a fresh engine.

### Expected

Acknowledged post-restart commits must not be silently discarded. The engine should either:

- refuse to hand out seqTxns at or below the table's applied seqTxn, or
- detect the condition at startup and suspend the table with a clear error.

Only the sequencer open path runs before any seqTxn is handed out. Every `nextTxn`,
`nextStructureTxn` and `getCursor` call goes through `TableSequencerAPI.getTableSequencerEntry`,
which runs the sequencer constructor. A check in `CheckWalTransactionsJob` races early commits. A
check at apply time alone can miss the gap: once post-restart commits push the header back up to A,
the state looks consistent.

One possible design, from an analysis done during the review of #6939:

- **Roll forward when the tail is intact.** On sequencer open, read records M+1..A read-only. If each
  one is structurally valid, advance the header to A and msync it. Checks: walId, structure version
  continuity, segment fields, a commit timestamp not earlier than the table-create timestamp, and a
  final structure version equal to the `_txn` column structure version. This restores the exact
  pre-crash log without inventing history or changing the file format. It covers the common case
  where only the header page was lost.
- **Otherwise, fence.** Refuse `nextTxn` / `nextStructureTxn` with an explicit error, suspend the
  table, keep `WalPurgeJob` from deleting the head part, and re-check at apply time. Recovery is then
  `ALTER TABLE ... SUSPEND WAL` followed by `ALTER TABLE ... REBASE WAL`, with
  `cairo.wal.apply.suspended.write.denied=true`. REBASE WAL refuses live views, so a fenced
  live-view table can only be dropped and recreated.

Writing placeholder records for M+1..A would keep the table writable, but it has costs:

- It invents log history and makes a walId-0 record legal on disk.
- Materialized views and live views skip records with walId <= 0, so they would silently miss that
  range.
- Replication consumers would see records that never existed on the primary.

### Related observations

- `TableTransactionLog.endMetadataChangeEntry` calls `fullSync()` before bumping the header maxTxn
  and never syncs the bump itself, in every commit mode. For V1, `fullSync` syncs the whole
  `_txnlog`, including the record. For V2, `fullSync` syncs only the header file, not the part file.
  A crash right after an ALTER is applied can therefore leave the table one metadata txn ahead even
  in SYNC mode.
  - In a test simulation this led to the sequencer rebuilding `_meta` without the new column, a
    skipped commit, and a suspended table ("could not open, file does not exist: .../wal2/0/y.d").
  - The #7105 reconcile rolls the sequencer schema back below the table's, so new WalWriters get the
    old schema.
  - PR #7411 adds these syncs, but that PR's recovery covers only tables enrolled in its new adaptive
    commit mode. The legacy modes stay as they are.
- `TableTransactionLogV2` never msyncs its part files (`sync0` syncs only the `_txnlog` header),
  including under SYNC. A lost record under a durable header makes apply hit walId 0 and suspend.
  That failure is loud, not silent.
- Checkpoint restore does not produce this state. `TableSnapshotRestore.processWalSequencerMetadata`
  only lowers the header, to a sequencer `lastTxn` captured after the table seqTxn. WAL conversion
  does not produce it either: `TableConverter` resets `_txn` seqTxn and lag before `registerTable`.
  A detection check should not false-positive on either path.
- Until a fix lands, `wal_tables()` showing writerTxn > sequencerTxn right after startup is a usable
  detection signal. A table that has already suffered the skip cannot be detected afterwards: once
  post-restart commits push the header to A or beyond, the state looks healthy.

### Scope

- No live views or materialized views are needed, and it affects the default commit mode.
- No recent change introduced it that I could find in git history. The apply cursor's contiguity
  check dates to the original WAL commit.
- Current master does not address it: the sequencer, txn-log, apply, and check-transactions code is
  identical between master and the #6939 branch.

`IODispatcherTest#testMaxConnections` failed on `windows-other-2` in [build 273988](https://dev.azure.com/questdb/questdb/_build/results?buildId=273988&view=logs&jobId=9aaa2a58-5dbe-5038-846a-39207b716d0c) (2026-09-28, PR #7650). It was the only failure out of 96,954 tests, and every other job in the build passed. PR #7650 changes join and symbol-translation code and adds one Cairo config property. It does not touch `IODispatcher`, `Net`, `HttpConnectionContext` or anything else under `cutlass/` or `network/`.

```
java.lang.AssertionError: Timed out waiting for dispatcher to stop listening
  at IODispatcherTest.testMaxConnections0(IODispatcherTest.java:8335)
  at IODispatcherTest.lambda$testMaxConnections$0(IODispatcherTest.java:5209)
  at TestUtils.assertMemoryLeak(TestUtils.java:949)
  at IODispatcherTest.testMaxConnections(IODispatcherTest.java:5136)
  Suppressed: java.lang.AssertionError: expected: cached file descriptors: 4, expected OS file descriptors: 2, list: ...
      actual: cached file descriptors: 404, OS file descriptors: 402, list: ...
    at TestUtils$LeakCheck.close(TestUtils.java:3315)
```

### What the test does

The test runs 10 iterations of `testMaxConnections0()` against a dispatcher configured with `getLimit() == 400`. Each iteration:

1. connects 400 sockets
2. waits up to 30 s for `dispatcher.isListening()` to turn false, meaning the dispatcher reached the limit and unregistered its listener
3. sends a request on each socket and reads a response
4. closes socket 0 and waits up to 30 s for the dispatcher to register the listener again
5. closes the remaining 399 sockets

Line 8335 is the wait in step 2. After the test connected 400 sockets, the dispatcher did not report 400 active connections within 30 s. The first iteration passed that wait, so the failure happened in a later iteration.

### What the log shows

- In the first iteration, the test connected 400 sockets between 14:22:36.196 and 14:22:36.393. The dispatcher hit the limit at 14:22:36.411962 (`max connection limit reached, unregistered listener [... connectionCount=400, limit=400 ...]`).
- The test thread logged `Sending request via socket #56` at 14:22:36.448867. The next record in the JVM log is at 14:22:46.257213, 10 s later. The Azure agent's timestamps show the same gap: a record the JVM wrote at 14:22:36.19 carries an agent timestamp of 14:22:46.277. The JVM, or at least its stdout pipe, appears to have stalled for about 10 s on the hosted Windows VM.
- After the stall, the log contains 267 pairs of `max connection limit reached` / `below maximum connection limit` records as the dispatcher cycled through connections. The last listener event is `below maximum connection limit, registered listener [connCount=399]` at 14:23:21.390448, just before the test failed.
- The log is missing records. It has only 400 `Connecting socket` lines and 64 `Sending request` lines, but the failure in a later iteration means the first iteration completed all 400 sends. For example, `Sending request via socket #0` shows up again at 14:22:46.289 with no `Connecting socket` lines before it. Because of the gaps, the log doesn't show which iteration failed or why the dispatcher stayed below 400 connections.

### History

- #1775 (2022, closed) reported this test flaking on Windows CI with a different symptom: `could not connect, errno=10061` in `TestUtils.assertConnect`.
- I checked the failed runs among the last 150 builds of the macwin pipeline (definition 46). This is the only one where `testMaxConnections` failed, so the flake is rare.

### Test hygiene problems

These don't cause the flake, but they make a failure harder to read:

1. `testMaxConnections0()` connects its 400 sockets outside the `try/finally`, and the `finally` only frees the request buffer. Any assertion failure during an iteration leaks the open sockets. That leak is the suppressed `LeakCheck` failure above (404 cached FDs instead of 4), and it gets reported alongside the real failure.
2. The step 4 wait, where the dispatcher should start listening again, reuses the message "Timed out waiting for dispatcher to stop listening". Only the line number tells the two waits apart.

body_text:
### Summary

`NumericException.instance()` (core/src/main/java/io/questdb/std/NumericException.java) contains:

```java
// This is to have correct stack trace in local debugging with -ea option
assert (ex = new NumericException()) != null;
```

The comment treats `-ea` as a local-debugging flag, but the production launchers enable it:

- `core/src/main/bin/questdb.sh:360` (`-ea -Dnoebug`)
- `core/docker-entrypoint.sh:124` (`-ea -Dnoebug ...`)

In both deployments, every throw of `NumericException.instance()` allocates a new Throwable and fills in its stack trace. Many hot paths use throw/catch for normal control flow. For example, the quiet casts `Numbers.parseIntQuiet`, `parseLongQuiet` and `parseDoubleQuiet` back `'abc'::int` and similar casts, and the numeric column-type converters also rely on it. On these paths each invalid value costs about 1 KB of garbage and a stack walk. This breaks the zero-GC guarantee on the query path.

### Measurement

A standalone probe on `core/target/classes` called `Numbers.parseIntQuiet("abc")` 2M times per round and took the best of 5 rounds:

| JVM flags | time/call | allocated/call |
|-----------|-----------|----------------|
| `-ea`     | 970 ns    | 1024 B         |
| (none)    | 28 ns     | 0 B            |

The probe's stack is shallow. Inside a query the stack is deeper, so the cost per row is higher.

### Impact

Any query or conversion that casts many unparseable text values to a numeric type (INT, LONG, DOUBLE, etc.) runs about 35x slower than it should on Linux/macOS/Docker installs and puts heavy pressure on the GC. The Windows service does not pass `-ea` and is not affected.

### Possible directions

- Keep the per-throw allocation for tests only. For example, gate it on a system property that test runs set, instead of on `-ea`. Or drop `-ea` from the production launchers. This needs a check that nothing else relies on assertions in production.
- Alternatively, give the hot quiet parsers non-throwing internal forms (tri-state or sentinel return), so they never reach `NumericException.instance()`.

### Location

- `core/src/main/java/io/questdb/std/NumericException.java:49`
- `core/src/main/bin/questdb.sh:360`, `core/docker-entrypoint.sh:124` (launchers passing `-ea`)

Found while reviewing PR #7680 (branch `vi_pgwire_deallocate`). That PR's text-to-BOOLEAN casts
hit the same cost and were switched to a non-throwing parse in commit 96a8b07bce. The other
quiet numeric casts still pay it on master.

### Summary

`NumericException.instance()` (core/src/main/java/io/questdb/std/NumericException.java) contains:

```java
// This is to have correct stack trace in local debugging with -ea option
assert (ex = new NumericException()) != null;
```

The comment treats `-ea` as a local-debugging flag, but the production launchers enable it:

- `core/src/main/bin/questdb.sh:360` (`-ea -Dnoebug`)
- `core/docker-entrypoint.sh:124` (`-ea -Dnoebug ...`)

In both deployments, every throw of `NumericException.instance()` allocates a new Throwable and fills in its stack trace. Many hot paths use throw/catch for normal control flow. For example, the quiet casts `Numbers.parseIntQuiet`, `parseLongQuiet` and `parseDoubleQuiet` back `'abc'::int` and similar casts, and the numeric column-type converters also rely on it. On these paths each invalid value costs about 1 KB of garbage and a stack walk. This breaks the zero-GC guarantee on the query path.

### Measurement

A standalone probe on `core/target/classes` called `Numbers.parseIntQuiet("abc")` 2M times per round and took the best of 5 rounds:

| JVM flags | time/call | allocated/call |
|-----------|-----------|----------------|
| `-ea`     | 970 ns    | 1024 B         |
| (none)    | 28 ns     | 0 B            |

The probe's stack is shallow. Inside a query the stack is deeper, so the cost per row is higher.

### Impact

Any query or conversion that casts many unparseable text values to a numeric type (INT, LONG, DOUBLE, etc.) runs about 35x slower than it should on Linux/macOS/Docker installs and puts heavy pressure on the GC. The Windows service does not pass `-ea` and is not affected.

### Possible directions

- Keep the per-throw allocation for tests only. For example, gate it on a system property that test runs set, instead of on `-ea`. Or drop `-ea` from the production launchers. This needs a check that nothing else relies on assertions in production.
- Alternatively, give the hot quiet parsers non-throwing internal forms (tri-state or sentinel return), so they never reach `NumericException.instance()`.

### Location

- `core/src/main/java/io/questdb/std/NumericException.java:49`
- `core/src/main/bin/questdb.sh:360`, `core/docker-entrypoint.sh:124` (launchers passing `-ea`)

Found while reviewing PR #7680 (branch `vi_pgwire_deallocate`). That PR's text-to-BOOLEAN casts
hit the same cost and were switched to a non-throwing parse in commit 96a8b07bce. The other
quiet numeric casts still pay it on master.

### Summary

`CREATE VIEW v AS (SELECT x FROM t WHERE x = $1)` succeeds. The view stores its text with `$1`
in it. Every later statement that reads the view compiles that text with the reader's own bind
variables. So `$1` in the view is silently the reader's first parameter.

PostgreSQL rejects the same DDL with `there is no parameter $1`.

### Reproduction (PostgreSQL wire protocol)

```
Q "CREATE TABLE t AS (SELECT x FROM long_sequence(3))"
Q "CREATE VIEW v2 AS (SELECT x FROM t WHERE x = $1)"      -> C[OK]
P '' "SELECT x FROM v2"      (no parameter types)
B '' ''                      (no values)
E '' 0
S                            -> E[bind message supplies 0 parameters, but prepared statement requires 1]
P '' "SELECT x FROM v2"
B '' '' '2'
E '' 0
S                            -> D(2) C[SELECT 1]
```

`CREATE VIEW v AS (SELECT x, $1 AS y FROM t)` also succeeds, and `SELECT x, y FROM v` then needs one
value.

### Impact

- A reader's statement text has no `$n`, but the statement still needs a value, and the
  ParameterDescription reports a parameter the client never wrote.
- A reader whose statement has its own `$1` binds the same value into the view's filter. For
  example, `SELECT x FROM v2 WHERE x > $1` uses one value for both conditions. The query then
  returns rows that differ from the rows the author meant.
- Any client can create such a view. The problem shows up only when someone reads the view.

### Expected

`CREATE VIEW` (and `ALTER VIEW` / `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW`, if they have the same gap)
rejects a definition that contains an indexed (`$n`) or named (`:name`) bind variable. The error
position points at the bind variable.

### Notes

This is not new in the PG wire Deallocate PR (#7680). That PR's Bind parameter-count check makes
it visible. At the PR base, `copyParameterValuesToBindVariableService()` defined `$1` and left it
NULL when the Bind sent no value, so `SELECT x FROM v2` should return no rows and no error (read
from the base code, not run).

### Location

- `core/src/main/java/io/questdb/griffin/SqlCompilerImpl.java:5031` `executeCreateView()`; the view
  definition is built in `core/src/main/java/io/questdb/griffin/engine/ops/CreateViewOperationBuilderImpl.java`.
  Neither the PR base (e756069d95) nor the PR head has a check that rejects bind variables in a view
  definition.

### Suggested fix

Reject indexed (`$n`) and named (`:name`) bind variables while compiling a CREATE VIEW (and ALTER VIEW)
definition, with the error position at the first bind variable, as PostgreSQL does.

body_text:
A LATERAL sub-query fails to compile when all of the following hold:

- its body joins two tables,
- it has GROUP BY,
- its WHERE correlates to the outer row with an equality on the joined (not the first) table and also has a non-equality correlation.

The join type inside the body does not matter (INNER and LEFT both fail). Each part on its own works: the same query without the join, without the non-equality conjunct, or with the equality on the first table returns rows.

Reproduced on master 641aa5fee5.

```sql
CREATE TABLE o (ok INT, k INT, v INT);
INSERT INTO o VALUES (1, 10, 1), (2, 20, 2), (3, 30, 2);
CREATE TABLE t (ts TIMESTAMP, id INT, v INT) TIMESTAMP(ts);
INSERT INTO t VALUES ('2024-01-01T00:00:01', 1, 1), ('2024-01-01T00:00:03', 2, 2), ('2024-01-01T00:00:05', 3, 3);
CREATE TABLE p (ts TIMESTAMP, id INT, k INT) TIMESTAMP(ts);
INSERT INTO p VALUES ('2024-01-01T00:00:00', 1, 10), ('2024-01-01T00:00:02', 2, 20), ('2024-01-01T00:00:04', 2, 30), ('2024-01-01T00:00:06', 3, 10);

SELECT o.ok, s.id, s.c
FROM o JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT t.id, count(*) c
    FROM t JOIN p ON t.id = p.id
    WHERE p.k = o.k AND t.v <= o.v
    GROUP BY t.id
) s
ORDER BY 1, 2;
```

Actual: `[0] Invalid column: p.__qdb_outer_ref__0_k` (the error position is 0, not the offending token).

Expected:

```
ok  id  c
1   1   1
2   2   1
3   2   1
```

Variants:

- `t LEFT JOIN p` instead of `t JOIN p`: same error.
- Drop `AND t.v <= o.v`: returns the correct rows.
- Single table (`FROM p WHERE p.k = o.k AND p.id <= o.v GROUP BY p.id`): returns the correct rows.

The rewritten column name `p.__qdb_outer_ref__0_k` suggests that the LATERAL rewrite (`LateralJoinRewriter`) qualifies the outer-ref column with the joined table's alias when it rewrites the GROUP BY layer.

A LATERAL sub-query fails to compile when its body joins two tables, has `ORDER BY ... LIMIT`, and its WHERE correlates to the outer row with an equality on the joined (not the first) table. The join type does not matter (INNER, LEFT and ASOF all fail). The same query correlated on the first table, or on a single-table body, returns rows.

Reproduced on master 641aa5fee5.

```sql
CREATE TABLE o (ok INT, k INT, v INT);
INSERT INTO o VALUES (1, 10, 1), (2, 20, 2), (3, 30, 2);
CREATE TABLE t (ts TIMESTAMP, id INT, v INT) TIMESTAMP(ts);
INSERT INTO t VALUES ('2024-01-01T00:00:01', 1, 1), ('2024-01-01T00:00:03', 2, 2), ('2024-01-01T00:00:05', 3, 3);
CREATE TABLE p (ts TIMESTAMP, id INT, k INT) TIMESTAMP(ts);
INSERT INTO p VALUES ('2024-01-01T00:00:00', 1, 10), ('2024-01-01T00:00:02', 2, 20), ('2024-01-01T00:00:04', 2, 30), ('2024-01-01T00:00:06', 3, 10);

SELECT o.ok, s.id, s.pk
FROM o JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT t.id, p.k pk
    FROM t JOIN p ON t.id = p.id
    WHERE p.k = o.k
    ORDER BY t.id
    LIMIT 1
) s
ORDER BY 1, 2, 3;
```

Actual: `[0] Invalid column: __qdb_outer_ref__0_k` (the error position is 0).

Expected:

```
ok  id  pk
1   1   10
2   2   20
3   2   30
```

Variants:

- `t LEFT JOIN p` or `t ASOF JOIN p ON (id)`: same error.
- Select `p.k` without an alias: same error.
- Correlate on the first table instead (`WHERE t.v = o.v ORDER BY t.id, p.k LIMIT 1`): returns the correct rows.
- Single-table body (`FROM p WHERE p.k = o.k ORDER BY p.id LIMIT 1`): returns the correct rows.

### Describe the bug

`TestOs` decides whether to load a locally built sqllogictest library
(`core/rust/qdb-sqllogictest/target/{release,debug}/libqdbsqllogictest.*`) or the precompiled library
from `core/target/test-classes/io/questdb/bin/<os>-<arch>/`. To find the sources root, it takes the
precompiled library's path and cuts it at the first `/target/`:

```java
int targetIndex = absolutePathPreCompiled.indexOf("/target/");
```

(core/src/test/java/io/questdb/test/TestOs.java:95)

When the checkout lives under a directory named `target`, for example `/home/u/target/questdb`, the first
match is that outer directory, and the sources root resolves to `/home/u`. The dev library paths then point
at `/home/u/rust/qdb-sqllogictest/target/...`, which does not exist. Their timestamps read as 0, and
`TestOs` silently loads the precompiled library, ignoring the developer's fresh local build.

Tests still run, but against a stale sqllogictest library, with no message saying so.

### To reproduce

1. Check out the repo under a path that contains a `target` directory, e.g. `/tmp/target/questdb`.
2. Build `core/rust/qdb-sqllogictest` locally so its library is newer than the precompiled one.
3. Run any `AbstractCairoTest` subclass: stderr never shows `Loading DEV release sqllogictest library`.

### Expected

`TestOs` cuts at the `target` directory of the `core` module: `lastIndexOf("/target/")`.

### QuestDB version

body_text:
An unqualified column name in the `ON` clause of an INNER JOIN fails with
`Ambiguous column` when a table joined later has a column with the same name. The
`ON` clause can see only the tables joined so far, so standard SQL resolves the name
to the one table in that scope that has it. The same holds for an equality conjunct
in a LEFT/RIGHT/FULL JOIN `ON` clause (`LEFT JOIN f1 ON w = a0 ...`). A non-equality
conjunct in an outer join `ON` clause already resolves the name this way.

#### Reproduce (master 641aa5fee5)

```sql
CREATE TABLE f0 (a0 INT, b0 INT);
INSERT INTO f0 VALUES (2, null), (3, 1), (2, 2);
CREATE TABLE f1 (a1 INT, b1 INT, w INT);
INSERT INTO f1 VALUES (3, 2, 1), (2, 2, 2), (null, 1, 3), (3, 3, 2), (3, 1, 3);
CREATE TABLE f2 (a2 INT, b2 INT, w INT);
INSERT INTO f2 VALUES (3, 1, 2), (1, null, 3), (3, 3, null), (1, 2, 2), (1, 3, 3);

-- fails: Ambiguous column [name=w] (position 40)
SELECT * FROM f0 JOIN f1 ON b1 = b0 AND w > 1 JOIN f2 ON a2 = a0;

-- works: the same query with f1.w
SELECT * FROM f0 JOIN f1 ON b1 = b0 AND f1.w > 1 JOIN f2 ON a2 = a0;

-- fails: Ambiguous column [name=w] (position 33)
SELECT * FROM f0 LEFT JOIN f1 ON w = a0 JOIN f2 ON a2 = a0;
```

#### Expected

Both statements resolve `w` to `f1.w`, as the qualified form does. A name that more
than one of the tables joined so far has stays an error.

#### Notes

- `SqlOptimiser.processJoinConditions()` sends INNER `ON` conjuncts to the WHERE
  clause and equality conjuncts to `analyseEquals()`. Both resolve literals through
  `LiteralCollector` / `validateColumnAndGetModelIndex()`, which searches every table
  of the FROM clause, not the tables joined so far.
- It is an error, not a wrong result. Qualifying the name works around it.

body_text:
A column reference qualified with a quoted table name that contains a dot, such as
`"t.1".w`, fails in the select list and in the filter of an outer join `ON` clause.
The same reference works in `WHERE` and as an outer join key.

#### Reproduce (master 641aa5fee5)

```sql
CREATE TABLE f0 (a0 INT, b0 INT, v INT);
INSERT INTO f0 VALUES (2, null, 1), (3, 1, 3), (2, 2, 2);
CREATE TABLE 't.1' (a1 INT, b1 INT, w INT);
INSERT INTO 't.1' VALUES (3, 2, 1), (2, 2, 2), (null, 1, 3), (3, 3, 2), (3, 1, 3);

-- fails with an internal error: wtf? "t.1".w
SELECT "t.1".w FROM f0 JOIN 't.1' ON b1 = b0;

-- fails: [48] Invalid column: "t.1".w   (also with 't.1'.w)
SELECT * FROM f0 LEFT JOIN 't.1' ON b1 = b0 AND "t.1".w > 1;

-- work
SELECT * FROM f0 JOIN 't.1' ON b1 = b0 WHERE "t.1".w > 1;
SELECT * FROM f0 LEFT JOIN 't.1' ON "t.1".b1 = b0;
```

#### Expected

All four statements accept `"t.1".w` as a reference to column `w` of table `t.1`.
The select-list case should never surface an internal (`wtf?`) message.

#### Notes

`JoinRecordMetadata.getColumnIndexQuiet()` splits the reference at the last unquoted
dot and looks up the table part as written, quotes included. The table alias it
registered has no quotes. `QueryModel.getModelAliasIndex()` strips the quotes, which
may explain why the optimiser-side paths (WHERE, join keys) work. I have not traced
the select-list path.

Possibly related: #7478 (a quoted column alias containing dots is truncated at the last dot).

body_text:
### Description

When two tables that are already in scope of an outer join's ON clause share a column name, and the
ON clause uses that name unqualified in a filter conjunct, QuestDB rejects the query with
`Invalid column: <name>`. The column exists; the actual problem is that the name is ambiguous. The
same name in an INNER JOIN ON clause, in WHERE, or in an outer join's equality key reports
`Ambiguous column [name=<name>]`.

The misleading message makes users look for a missing or misspelled column instead of qualifying the
name.

### Reproduction

```sql
CREATE TABLE f1 (a1 INT, b1 INT, w INT);
INSERT INTO f1 VALUES (3, 2, 1), (2, 2, 2), (null, 1, 3), (3, 3, 2), (3, 1, 3);

SELECT * FROM f1 a LEFT JOIN f1 b ON b.a1 = a.a1 AND w > 1;
-- [53] Invalid column: w          <- expected: Ambiguous column [name=w]

SELECT * FROM f1 a JOIN f1 b ON b.a1 = a.a1 AND w > 1;
-- [48] Ambiguous column [name=w]

SELECT * FROM f1 a JOIN f1 b ON b.a1 = a.a1 WHERE w > 1;
-- [50] Ambiguous column [name=w]

SELECT * FROM f1 a LEFT JOIN f1 b ON w = a.b1;
-- [37] Ambiguous column [name=w]
```

RIGHT JOIN and FULL JOIN behave like LEFT JOIN (`Invalid column: w`).

### Expected

`Ambiguous column [name=w]` at the position of `w`, consistent with the other forms. Rejecting the
query is correct: `w` has two holders among the tables joined so far.

### Notes

- The likely throw site is `FunctionParser.createColumn()` (`SqlException.invalidColumn`), reached when
  `SqlCodeGenerator` compiles the outer join's filter: the lookup of the unqualified name in the join
  metadata returns no column, and the parser reports it as missing. (Inferred from the code; no stack

body_text:
### Describe the bug

An outer join (LEFT, RIGHT or FULL) whose ON clause references columns of
two earlier tables fails to compile when those two earlier tables are not
joined to each other by an equi-key (a CROSS JOIN, a comma join, or a
non-equi INNER join). The query is valid, but QuestDB rejects it with
`Invalid column: <earlier table>.<column>`. EXPLAIN fails the same way.

The optimiser runs the context-free earlier table (`c` below) after the
outer join. `SqlCodeGenerator.generateJoins` then compiles the outer join's
ON clause (`compileJoinFilter(slaveModel.getOuterJoinExpressionClause(), ...)`)
against join metadata that does not contain `c` yet, and `FunctionParser`
throws `Invalid column`.

On master e756069d95 the equi-key forms (`d.k = c.k AND d.k = a.k`) failed
with `AssertionError: wtf? c.k` in `generateSelectChoose` under `-ea` (an
`ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` without `-ea`) and leaked the hash-join map
(16,640 bytes of `NATIVE_JOIN_MAP` per attempt). Branch
`fix/join-optimiser-lost-rows` (b746306b14) changes that into the
`Invalid column` SqlException below and no longer leaks. The form with a
non-key predicate (`d.k + 0 = a.k`) fails with `Invalid column: a.k` on both
revisions.

### To reproduce

```sql
CREATE TABLE a (k INT, id INT);
INSERT INTO a VALUES (1, 1), (2, 2);
CREATE TABLE c (k INT, id INT);
INSERT INTO c VALUES (1, 10), (3, 30);
CREATE TABLE d (k INT, id INT);
INSERT INTO d VALUES (1, 100), (2, 200), (3, 300);

-- all fail with "Invalid column: c.k" (or a.k)
SELECT * FROM a CROSS JOIN c LEFT JOIN d ON d.k = c.k AND d.k = a.k ORDER BY a.id, c.id;
SELECT * FROM a CROSS JOIN c LEFT JOIN d ON d.k = a.k AND d.k = c.k ORDER BY a.id, c.id;
SELECT * FROM a, c LEFT JOIN d ON d.k = c.k AND d.k = a.k ORDER BY a.id, c.id;
SELECT * FROM a JOIN c ON c.id > a.id LEFT JOIN d ON d.k = c.k AND d.k = a.k ORDER BY a.id, c.id;
SELECT * FROM a CROSS JOIN c RIGHT JOIN d ON d.k = c.k AND d.k = a.k ORDER BY d.id;
SELECT * FROM a CROSS JOIN c FULL JOIN d ON d.k = c.k AND d.k = a.k ORDER BY d.id, a.id, c.id;
SELECT * FROM a CROSS JOIN c LEFT JOIN d ON d.k = c.k AND d.k + 0 = a.k ORDER BY a.id, c.id;
```

The sub-query form compiles and returns the expected result for the first
query:

```sql
SELECT * FROM (SELECT a.k ak, a.id aid, c.k ck, c.id cid FROM a CROSS JOIN c) t
LEFT JOIN d ON d.k = t.ck AND d.k = t.ak ORDER BY t.aid, t.cid;
```

```
ak  aid  ck  cid  k     id
1   1    1   10   1     100
1   1    3   30   null  null
2   2    1   10   null  null
2   2    3   30   null  null
```

### Expected fix direction

`SqlOptimiser.doReorderTables` appends a model without a join context and
without dependencies (the CROSS JOIN `c`) after every model it can order.
An outer join must run after every earlier table its ON clause references.
Record an ordering edge from each table the outer join's ON clause (key or
`outerJoinExpressionClause`) references to the outer join, or pin every
model before the outer join to run before it. The RIGHT/FULL prefix pinning
proposed for "equi RIGHT/FULL join runs before an earlier CROSS JOIN" would
cover the RIGHT/FULL forms but not LEFT.

### QuestDB version

master (e756069d95), and branch fix/join-optimiser-lost-rows (b746306b14)


### Status on #7674

On the branch of #7674 (`fix/join-optimiser-lost-rows`), the plain-key forms and the RIGHT/FULL forms above return rows. LEFT joins whose ON clause compares an earlier CROSS, comma or non-equi-joined table through a non-key condition still fail (checked at db69fb3f4a), for example:

```sql
CREATE TABLE f0 (a0 INT, b0 INT);
CREATE TABLE f1 (a1 INT, b1 INT);
CREATE TABLE f2 (a2 INT, b2 INT);
CREATE TABLE f3 (a3 INT, b3 INT);
SELECT * FROM f0 CROSS JOIN f1 JOIN f2 ON b2 = a0 LEFT JOIN f3 ON a3 = a0 AND b3 >= a1;
-- Invalid column: a1
```

Two fixes that add ordering edges from such conditions were tried and rejected in review: an edge can make an UNNEST the first model of the join order (#7693), and a join can count as ordered after its own edge was dropped, which lets a later join run before a table its ON clause reads.

### Describe the bug

QuestDB accepts a join ON clause that references a table joined later in
the same FROM clause. PostgreSQL rejects such a query with "invalid
reference to FROM-clause entry". QuestDB either compiles it or fails with
an `Invalid column` error that points at the forward reference, and some
shapes return wrong rows without an error.

- INNER JOIN forward references work when no RIGHT/FULL OUTER join
  follows: the optimiser moves the ON conjunct into the WHERE filter.
- LEFT JOIN (and other outer/ASOF) forward references only work when the
  LEFT JOIN happens to run after the referenced table. `doReorderTables`
  appends a context-free model to the end of the order
  (SqlOptimiser.java:3888-3895, :3935-3938 on branch
  `fix/join-optimiser-lost-rows`), and the LEFT JOIN's ON clause is
  compiled at its own position. In a differential fuzz run over 165 random
  chains with a LEFT JOIN forward reference and an equi RIGHT/FULL join,
  110 fail with `Invalid column` on master.
- A prefix ON clause that references the RIGHT/FULL OUTER join's slave has
  no defined meaning, because the outer join's master is the prefix.

### To reproduce

```sql
CREATE TABLE f0 (a0 INT, b0 INT);
INSERT INTO f0 VALUES (1, 1), (2, 3);
CREATE TABLE f1 (a1 INT, b1 INT);
INSERT INTO f1 VALUES (1, 2), (3, 1);
CREATE TABLE f2 (a2 INT, b2 INT);
INSERT INTO f2 VALUES (1, 4), (2, 2), (4, 1);
CREATE TABLE f3 (a3 INT, b3 INT);
INSERT INTO f3 VALUES (1, 1), (2, 9);
CREATE TABLE f4 (a4 INT, b4 INT);
INSERT INTO f4 VALUES (1, 1), (3, 3);

-- LEFT JOIN f1 reads a2 from the later f2: compiles, returns 2 rows
SELECT * FROM f0 LEFT JOIN f1 ON b1 = a2 JOIN f2 ON a2 = a0;

-- circular: f1's ON reads f2 and f2's ON reads f1. On master this returns
-- no rows. Evaluating f1's ON after f2 joins (sub-query form below) keeps
-- both f4 rows, NULL-extended, because the RIGHT JOIN preserves them.
-- SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM f0 CROSS JOIN f2)
--     LEFT JOIN f1 ON b1 < b2 WHERE b2 < b1) LEFT JOIN f3 ON a3 >= a1)
--     RIGHT JOIN f4 ON b4 = b0;
SELECT * FROM f0 LEFT JOIN f1 ON b1 < b2 JOIN f2 ON b2 < b1
    LEFT JOIN f3 ON a3 >= a1 RIGHT JOIN f4 ON b4 = b0;

-- prefix ON reads the RIGHT JOIN's slave
SELECT * FROM f0 JOIN f1 ON a1 < a3 CROSS JOIN f2 RIGHT JOIN f3 ON b3 = b0;
```

### Expected fix direction

Reject an ON clause that references a table joined after it, with an error
positioned at the offending column, as PostgreSQL does. If QuestDB keeps
accepting INNER JOIN forward references for compatibility, reject at least
the outer/ASOF join forms and any reference past a RIGHT/FULL OUTER join.
`LateralJoinRewriter` builds `__qdb_outer_ref__` joins whose ON clause
references later models (see the LATERAL issue), so the check must run on
the user's query before that rewrite or exempt the rewriter's joins.

### QuestDB version

master (e756069d95), and branch fix/join-optimiser-lost-rows (b746306b14)


### Status on #7674

On the branch of #7674 (`fix/join-optimiser-lost-rows`), an INNER ON equality that references the slave of a later LEFT, RIGHT, FULL, ASOF or LT join fails with `Invalid column`, as on master. The circular forward references ahead of a RIGHT/FULL join (the second example above) still return the same wrong rows as master. Rejecting forward references outright, as suggested above, would turn queries that master answers correctly into errors (for example INNER JOIN forward references with no RIGHT/FULL join after them), so #7674 does not do it.

body_text:
### To reproduce

A window specification written inline in `OVER (...)` that names a base window ignores the base window. The query compiles and returns rows computed without the base window's `PARTITION BY` and `ORDER BY`.

```sql
SELECT x, sum(x) OVER (w1 ORDER BY x) a
FROM long_sequence(5)
WINDOW w1 AS (PARTITION BY x % 2);
```

| x | actual `a` | expected `a` |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1.0 | 1.0 |
| 2 | 3.0 | 2.0 |
| 3 | 6.0 | 4.0 |
| 4 | 10.0 | 6.0 |
| 5 | 15.0 | 9.0 |

The actual column is the running sum over all rows. The plan shows no partitioning:

```
CachedWindowLight
  orderedFunctions: [[x] => [sum(x) over (rows between unbounded preceding and current row)]]
    long_sequence count: 5
```

The equivalent spellings return the expected rows (`1, 2, 4, 6, 9`):

```sql
-- the specification written out
SELECT x, sum(x) OVER (PARTITION BY x % 2 ORDER BY x) a FROM long_sequence(5);

-- the same inheritance through a second named window
SELECT x, sum(x) OVER w2 a
FROM long_sequence(5)
WINDOW w1 AS (PARTITION BY x % 2), w2 AS (w1 ORDER BY x);
```

Two more forms of the same defect:

```sql
-- a bare base window in brackets drops the whole definition: returns 15.0 on every row,
-- while OVER w1 without brackets returns 1, 2, 4, 6, 9
SELECT x, sum(x) OVER (w1) a
FROM long_sequence(5)
WINDOW w1 AS (PARTITION BY x % 2 ORDER BY x);

-- an undefined base window compiles and runs: returns 1, 3, 6, 10, 15,
-- while OVER nosuch fails with "[22] window 'nosuch' is not defined"
SELECT x, sum(x) OVER (nosuch ORDER BY x) a FROM long_sequence(5);
```

### QuestDB version:

`master` at f56e72425c. Reproduced on a branch based on that commit; the branch does not change the code involved.

### OS, in case of Docker specify Docker and the Host OS:

Linux. The defect is in SQL compilation and does not depend on the OS.

### File System, in case of Docker specify Host File System:

Not relevant.

### Full Name:

Andrei Pechkurov

### Affiliation:

QuestDB

### Additional context

`ExpressionParser` parses the inline form and stores the base name on the window column with `windowCol.setBaseWindowName(...)`. Nothing resolves it afterwards:

- `SqlOptimiser.resolveWindowInheritance()` walks only `model.getNamedWindows()`, the definitions of the `WINDOW` clause, so it merges a base into `w2 AS (w1 ORDER BY x)` and never visits a window column of the select list.
- `SqlOptimiser.resolveNamedWindows()` visits the select list, and handles only `isNamedWindowReference()`, the `OVER w` form.

So a select-list window that has a base keeps its own clauses only, and the "is not defined" check never runs for it.

A fix would resolve `hasBaseWindow()` for the window columns that `resolveNamedWindows()` already visits, including windows nested in expressions, with the same `resolveWindowInheritanceChain()` merge and the same "is not defined" error. The named-window syntax came in with #6746.

A window specification written inline in `OVER (...)` that names a base window ignores the base window. The query compiles and returns rows computed without the base window's `PARTITION BY` and `ORDER BY`.

```sql
SELECT x, sum(x) OVER (w1 ORDER BY x) a
FROM long_sequence(5)
WINDOW w1 AS (PARTITION BY x % 2);
```

| x | actual `a` | expected `a` |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1.0 | 1.0 |
| 2 | 3.0 | 2.0 |
| 3 | 6.0 | 4.0 |
| 4 | 10.0 | 6.0 |
| 5 | 15.0 | 9.0 |

The actual column is the running sum over all rows. The plan shows no partitioning:

```
CachedWindowLight
  orderedFunctions: [[x] => [sum(x) over (rows between unbounded preceding and current row)]]
    long_sequence count: 5
```

The equivalent spellings return the expected rows (`1, 2, 4, 6, 9`):

```sql
-- the specification written out
SELECT x, sum(x) OVER (PARTITION BY x % 2 ORDER BY x) a FROM long_sequence(5);

-- the same inheritance through a second named window
SELECT x, sum(x) OVER w2 a
FROM long_sequence(5)
WINDOW w1 AS (PARTITION BY x % 2), w2 AS (w1 ORDER BY x);
```

Two more forms of the same defect:

```sql
-- a bare base window in brackets drops the whole definition: returns 15.0 on every row,
-- while OVER w1 without brackets returns 1, 2, 4, 6, 9
SELECT x, sum(x) OVER (w1) a
FROM long_sequence(5)
WINDOW w1 AS (PARTITION BY x % 2 ORDER BY x);

-- an undefined base window compiles and runs: returns 1, 3, 6, 10, 15,
-- while OVER nosuch fails with "[22] window 'nosuch' is not defined"
SELECT x, sum(x) OVER (nosuch ORDER BY x) a FROM long_sequence(5);
```

### QuestDB version:

`master` at f56e72425c. Reproduced on a branch based on that commit; the branch does not change the code involved.

### OS, in case of Docker specify Docker and the Host OS:

Linux. The defect is in SQL compilation and does not depend on the OS.

### File System, in case of Docker specify Host File System:

Not relevant.

### Full Name:

Andrei Pechkurov

### Affiliation:

QuestDB

### Additional context

`ExpressionParser` parses the inline form and stores the base name on the window column with `windowCol.setBaseWindowName(...)`. Nothing resolves it afterwards:

- `SqlOptimiser.resolveWindowInheritance()` walks only `model.getNamedWindows()`, the definitions of the `WINDOW` clause, so it merges a base into `w2 AS (w1 ORDER BY x)` and never visits a window column of the select list.
- `SqlOptimiser.resolveNamedWindows()` visits the select list, and handles only `isNamedWindowReference()`, the `OVER w` form.

So a select-list window that has a base keeps its own clauses only, and the "is not defined" check never runs for it.

A fix would resolve `hasBaseWindow()` for the window columns that `resolveNamedWindows()` already visits, including windows nested in expressions, with the same `resolveWindowInheritanceChain()` merge and the same "is not defined" error. The named-window syntax came in with #6746.

body_text:
**Impact:** wrong rows, silently. Affects SPLICE JOIN queries written after a non-equi RIGHT/FULL OUTER JOIN (e.g. `RIGHT JOIN t4 ON t4.id > 1`), with no INNER join between them. Rare query shape.

**Location:** `core/src/main/java/io/questdb/griffin/SqlOptimiser.java`, `doReorderTables()` (master 641aa5fee5: method at line 3878, "add pure crosses at the end of ordered table list" at line 3933).

### Describe the bug

A SPLICE JOIN written after a non-equi RIGHT or FULL OUTER JOIN executes ahead of the outer join.
SPLICE emits slave rows that have no matching master row, with all master columns NULL. After the
reorder, the outer join pairs those slave-only rows with rows of its right-hand table, so they
come back with non-NULL values in columns that belong to the splice's master. When the outer join's
right side has several matching rows, the slave-only row is also duplicated.

In the written order, the splice's master is the outer join's output. That output has no designated
timestamp, so the query could reasonably be rejected with "left side of time series join has no
timestamp", as it already is for the equi form (`RIGHT JOIN t4 ON t4.id = t1.id`). Instead it runs
in a different order and returns different rows.

Cause: `SqlOptimiser.doReorderTables()` appends context-free joins last ("add pure crosses at the
end"), including the CROSS RIGHT/FULL join that a non-equi outer join becomes. The SPLICE join has
an implied dependency on the first model and runs before it.

### To reproduce

```sql
CREATE TABLE t1 (id INT, ts TIMESTAMP) TIMESTAMP(ts) PARTITION BY DAY;
INSERT INTO t1 VALUES (1, '2024-01-01T00:00:01'), (2, '2024-01-01T00:00:02'), (3, '2024-01-01T00:00:03');
CREATE TABLE t3 (id INT, ts TIMESTAMP) TIMESTAMP(ts) PARTITION BY DAY;
INSERT INTO t3 VALUES (1, '2024-01-01T00:00:00'), (3, '2024-01-01T00:00:04'), (2, '2024-01-01T00:00:05');
CREATE TABLE t4 (id INT, ts TIMESTAMP) TIMESTAMP(ts) PARTITION BY DAY;
INSERT INTO t4 VALUES (4, '2024-01-01T00:00:01');

SELECT t1.id, t3.id, t4.id FROM t1 RIGHT JOIN t4 ON t4.id > 1 SPLICE JOIN t3 ON t3.id = t1.id;
```

Plan: `Nested Loop Right Join (filter 1<t4.id) <- Splice Join(t1, t3)`, with t4 on the right.

Actual:
```
id    id1   id2
null  1     4
1     null  4
2     null  4
3     null  4
3     3     4
2     2     4
```

The written order, with the outer join's output materialized as a timestamped table and spliced:

```sql
CREATE TABLE m AS (SELECT t1.id a, t4.id c, t1.ts FROM t1 RIGHT JOIN t4 ON t4.id > 1 ORDER BY ts) TIMESTAMP(ts);
SELECT m.a, t3.id, m.c FROM m SPLICE JOIN t3 ON t3.id = m.a;
```
```
a     id    c
null  1     null
1     null  4
...
```

The first row differs: the slave-only t3 row carries `t4.id = 4` instead of NULL. The keyless form
`... SPLICE JOIN t3` behaves the same way.

### Expected behavior

Either reject the query with "left side of time series join has no timestamp", the same as the
equi RIGHT/FULL form, or keep the master columns of slave-only splice rows NULL. ASOF and LT joins
are not affected: they keep one row per master row, so they commute with the outer join.

### Environment

Reproduced on master 641aa5fee5.

### Suggested fix

Don't let a SPLICE join execute ahead of a CROSS RIGHT/FULL join written before it. Either pin the outer join before the SPLICE join in `doReorderTables()`, or have the code generator reject the query with "left side of time series join has no timestamp", as it already does for the equi RIGHT/FULL form.

### Where found

Found while reviewing PR #7674 (branch `fix/join-optimiser-lost-rows`). That PR stops collecting SPLICE joins as "time-series joins ahead" of a non-equi outer join, which fixes the variant with an INNER join between the outer join and the SPLICE. This variant, with no INNER join between, comes from master's `doReorderTables()` and is unchanged by the PR.

body_text:
### To reproduce

Two expressions in one query that differ only in the sub-query they read are treated as duplicates. The optimiser keeps the first and uses it for both, so the second returns the first one's values. The query compiles and returns wrong rows without an error.

**GROUP BY keys**

```sql
SELECT (x = (SELECT 1L)) k1, (x = (SELECT 2L)) k2, count() c
FROM long_sequence(3)
GROUP BY (x = (SELECT 1L)), (x = (SELECT 2L));
```

| actual `k1, k2, c` | expected `k1, k2, c` (any order) |
|---|---|
| true, true, 1 | true, false, 1 |
| false, false, 2 | false, true, 1 |
| | false, false, 1 |

The plan has one key:

```
VirtualRecord
  functions: [column,column,c]
    GroupBy vectorized: false
      keys: [column]
      values: [count(*)]
        long_sequence count: 3
```

**Aggregate arguments**

```sql
SELECT sum(CASE WHEN x = (SELECT 1L) THEN x ELSE 0 END) a,
       sum(CASE WHEN x = (SELECT 2L) THEN x ELSE 0 END) b
FROM long_sequence(3);
```

Returns `a = 1, b = 1`. Expected `a = 1, b = 2`. The plan computes one aggregate and projects it twice (`functions: [a,a]`).

**ORDER BY keys**

```sql
SELECT x FROM long_sequence(3) ORDER BY x = (SELECT 1L), x = (SELECT 2L);
```

Returns `2, 3, 1`. Expected `3, 2, 1`. The sort has one key.

**Window PARTITION BY keys**

A sub-query written in place inside a window key is refused (`query is not allowed here`), so this form needs declared sub-queries:

```sql
DECLARE @q1 := (SELECT 1L x), @q2 := (SELECT 3L x)
SELECT x,
       sum(x) OVER (PARTITION BY x = @q1) a,
       sum(x) OVER (PARTITION BY x = @q2) b
FROM long_sequence(3);
```

| x | actual `a` | actual `b` | expected `b` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1.0 | 1.0 | 3.0 |
| 2 | 5.0 | 5.0 | 3.0 |
| 3 | 5.0 | 5.0 | 3.0 |

The plan has one window function, partitioned by the first sub-query.

The same merge shows in window function arguments (`sum(CASE WHEN x = @q1 ...) OVER ()` next to the `@q2` form) and in `GROUP BY s IN (SELECT ...), s IN (SELECT ...)`. The window form returns the same wrong rows inside a view body, a CTE and an `INSERT ... SELECT`.

Not affected, all return the expected rows: a plain projection (`SELECT x = (SELECT 1L) a, x = (SELECT 2L) b`), `WHERE x = (SELECT 1L) OR x = (SELECT 2L)`, and the GROUP BY form without a `GROUP BY` clause (`SELECT x = @q1 k1, x = @q2 k2, count()`).

### QuestDB version:

`master` at f56e72425c. The branch of #7602 returns the same rows for every statement above; it does not change the code involved.

### OS, in case of Docker specify Docker and the Host OS:

Linux. The defect is in SQL compilation and does not depend on the OS.

### File System, in case of Docker specify Host File System:

Not relevant.

### Full Name:

Andrei Pechkurov

### Affiliation:

QuestDB

### Additional context

`ExpressionNode.compareNodesExact()` compares two nodes by type, token, arguments and window expression. A `QUERY` node has a null token and no arguments, and the comparison never looks at its query model, so any two `QUERY` nodes compare equal. `ExpressionNode.deepHashCode()` hashes them alike. A de-duplication built on the pair therefore merges expressions that differ only in a sub-query. `SqlOptimiser.findDuplicateWindowFunction()` is one such caller and matches the window form above. The GROUP BY key, aggregate argument and ORDER BY key forms show the same symptom in their plans; which call site merges each was not traced. Other callers of `compareNodesExact()` (more sites in `SqlOptimiser`, one in `QueryModel`, several in `LateralJoinRewriter`) were not probed one by one.

A fix would make `QUERY` nodes compare by their model (`a.queryModel == b.queryModel`) with a hash to match. Identity comparison also stops merging two reads of the same declared sub-query once each read parses its own copy, as #7602 does, so the declared form needs either a comparison by declaration or acceptance of the lost merge.

Interaction with #7602 (open):

- It adds spellings that reach the same merge and that `master` refuses at parse time: a declared value that holds a sub-query as an operand (`DECLARE @k1 := x = (SELECT 1L x)`), `AUDITED` declarations in a view body, and IN-list variables.
- It fixes a spurious `scalar sub-query returned more than one row` error for a declared `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1` sub-query that `FROM` and another clause both read. A statement of that shape that also holds two expressions differing only in a sub-query fails with that error on `master` and returns merged, wrong rows on the branch. Example:

```sql
DECLARE @q1 := (SELECT x FROM long_sequence(3) ORDER BY x LIMIT 1),
        @q2 := (SELECT x FROM long_sequence(3) ORDER BY x DESC LIMIT 1)
SELECT x,
       sum(x) OVER (PARTITION BY x = @q1) a,
       sum(x) OVER (PARTITION BY x = @q2) b
FROM (SELECT * FROM @q1 UNION ALL SELECT * FROM @q2 UNION ALL SELECT 2L x UNION ALL SELECT 2L x);
```

Also seen on both commits, with assertions enabled: `SELECT x = @q1 k1, x = @q2 k2, count() c FROM long_sequence(3) GROUP BY x = @q1, x = @q2`, with `@q1`/`@q2` declared as the `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1` sub-queries above, throws `java.lang.AssertionError` at `OrderedMap$FixedSizeKey.commit` under `GroupByRecordCursorFactory$GroupByRecordCursor.buildDataMap` instead of returning rows.

`findDuplicateWindowFunction()` came in with #6643. Draft #7710 lists window de-duplication among the passes it plans to re-evaluate.

### To reproduce

A declared variable that holds a sub-query, used as a whole window key, fails with an internal Java exception. The same sub-query written in place is refused with a positioned SQL error.

**PARTITION BY**

```sql
DECLARE @q := (SELECT 2L x)
SELECT x, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY @q) r FROM long_sequence(3);
```

```
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Unexpected column type: CURSOR
    at io.questdb.cairo.RecordSinkFactory.getSingleInstanceClass(RecordSinkFactory.java:1990)
    at io.questdb.cairo.RecordSinkFactory.getInstanceClass(RecordSinkFactory.java:408)
    at io.questdb.cairo.RecordSinkFactory.getInstance(RecordSinkFactory.java:260)
    at io.questdb.cairo.RecordSinkFactory.getInstance(RecordSinkFactory.java:201)
    at io.questdb.cairo.RecordSinkFactory.getInstance(RecordSinkFactory.java:111)
    at io.questdb.griffin.SqlCodeGenerator.generateSelectWindow(SqlCodeGenerator.java:11086)
```

In place: `SELECT x, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY (SELECT 2L x)) r FROM long_sequence(3)` fails with `[43] query is not allowed here`.

**ORDER BY**

```sql
DECLARE @q := (SELECT 2L x)
SELECT x, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY @q) r FROM long_sequence(3);
```

```
java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "java.lang.CharSequence.length()" because "columnName" is null
    at io.questdb.cairo.sql.RecordMetadata.getColumnIndexQuiet(RecordMetadata.java:78)
    at io.questdb.griffin.SqlUtil.getColumnIndexQuiet(SqlUtil.java:971)
    at io.questdb.griffin.SqlCodeGenerator.toOrderIndices(SqlCodeGenerator.java:1032)
    at io.questdb.griffin.SqlCodeGenerator.generateSelectWindow(SqlCodeGenerator.java:11584)
```

With a nested union in `FROM`, the same key fails earlier, in the optimiser:

```sql
DECLARE @q := (SELECT 2L x)
SELECT x, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY @q) r
FROM (SELECT x FROM long_sequence(2) UNION ALL SELECT x FROM long_sequence(2));
```

```
java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "java.lang.CharSequence.length()" because "seq" is null
    at io.questdb.std.Chars.indexOfLastUnquoted(Chars.java:845)
```

body_text:
### To reproduce

`COMPILE VIEW` leaks native memory when the view body reads a table function that holds native resources, such as `read_parquet()`.

```sql
CREATE VIEW vp AS (SELECT x FROM read_parquet('q.parquet'));
COMPILE VIEW vp;
```

Each `COMPILE VIEW vp` leaves 256 bytes of `NATIVE_PATH` allocated. Three statements in a row leave 768. In a test, `assertMemoryLeak()` around the two statements fails with:

```
java.lang.AssertionError: Memory usage by tag: NATIVE_PATH, difference: 256 expected:<512> but was:<768>
```

Controls that do not leak: `CREATE VIEW` alone, and `CREATE VIEW` followed by `SELECT * FROM vp`.

A second route leaks the same way. An `ALTER VIEW` or `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` that the cycle check refuses, over a body that reads a table function:

```sql
CREATE VIEW va AS (SELECT x FROM read_parquet('q.parquet'));
ALTER VIEW va AS (SELECT x FROM va);
-- [17] circular dependency detected: view 'va' cannot reference itself
```

The refused `ALTER VIEW` leaves 256 bytes of `NATIVE_PATH`. A two-view cycle (`va` altered to read `vb`, which reads `va`) leaves 512. `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW vr AS (SELECT x FROM vr)` over such a view leaves 256.

Not affected: `ALTER VIEW` / `CREATE VIEW` statements that fail in the optimiser or in code generation (unknown function, invalid column, invalid column name), and `EXPLAIN` over the view.

The parquet file in these runs holds `x` = 1..10 and sits under the configured input root.

### QuestDB version:

`master` at f56e72425c. The branch of #7602 leaks on the same statements, see below for a difference in size.

### OS, in case of Docker specify Docker and the Host OS:

Linux. The defect does not depend on the OS.

### File System, in case of Docker specify Host File System:

Not relevant.

### Full Name:

Andrei Pechkurov

### Affiliation:

QuestDB

### Additional context

`SqlCompilerImpl.compileView()` leases a pooled compiler, calls `compiler.generateExecutionModel()` on the view SQL and discards the model. The optimiser has already instantiated the table function of every model it optimised. Nothing generates the model, so nothing takes ownership of those factories and nothing closes them.

`SqlCompilerImpl.alterViewExecution()` has the same window between `generateExecutionModel()` and `SqlUtil.generateFactory()`: `validateNoCycle()` throws there, after optimisation and before generation. That is the second route above.

Interaction with #7602 (open):

- It adds a sweep in `generateSelectOneShot()` that closes the table-function factories a generated plan did not claim. The two paths above never generate, so the sweep does not run for them. `SqlCompiler` does not expose the sweep to a caller that discards the model.
- On that branch every read of a declared sub-query parses its own copy, so a view body that reads one declared sub-query over a table function N times leaks 256 x N bytes per `COMPILE VIEW` (512 for two reads, 768 for three), against 256 on `master`. The refused `ALTER VIEW` route scales the same way.
- In the other direction, the sweep removes leaks that `master` has outside these two paths, for example a `SELECT` or `CREATE VIEW` whose declared sub-query over a table function is never read.

Two fix directions: give callers of `generateExecutionModel()` that discard the model a way to release its table functions, or have the compiler close what is still unclaimed when it is cleared or returned to the pool.

Draft #7710 mentions fixing "pooled compilers leaking prepared factories". Whether that covers these two paths was not checked.

`COMPILE VIEW` leaks native memory when the view body reads a table function that holds native resources, such as `read_parquet()`.

```sql
CREATE VIEW vp AS (SELECT x FROM read_parquet('q.parquet'));

```

Each `COMPILE VIEW vp` leaves 256 bytes of `NATIVE_PATH` allocated. Three statements in a row leave 768. In a test, `assertMemoryLeak()` around the two statements fails with:

```
java.lang.AssertionError: Memory usage by tag: NATIVE_PATH, difference: 256 expected:<512> but was:<768>
```

Controls that do not leak: `CREATE VIEW` alone, and `CREATE VIEW` followed by `SELECT * FROM vp`.

A second route leaks the same way. An `ALTER VIEW` or `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` that the cycle check refuses, over a body that reads a table function:

```sql
CREATE VIEW va AS (SELECT x FROM read_parquet('q.parquet'));
ALTER VIEW va AS (SELECT x FROM va);
-- [17] circular dependency detected: view 'va' cannot reference itself
```

The refused `ALTER VIEW` leaves 256 bytes of `NATIVE_PATH`. A two-view cycle (`va` altered to read `vb`, which reads `va`) leaves 512. `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW vr AS (SELECT x FROM vr)` over such a view leaves 256.

Not affected: `ALTER VIEW` / `CREATE VIEW` statements that fail in the optimiser or in code generation (unknown function, invalid column, invalid column name), and `EXPLAIN` over the view.

The parquet file in these runs holds `x` = 1..10 and sits under the configured input root.

### QuestDB version:

`master` at f56e72425c. The branch of #7602 leaks on the same statements, see below for a difference in size.

### OS, in case of Docker specify Docker and the Host OS:

Linux. The defect does not depend on the OS.

### File System, in case of Docker specify Host File System:

Not relevant.

### Full Name:

Andrei Pechkurov

### Affiliation:

QuestDB

### Additional context

`SqlCompilerImpl.compileView()` leases a pooled compiler, calls `compiler.generateExecutionModel()` on the view SQL and discards the model. The optimiser has already instantiated the table function of every model it optimised. Nothing generates the model, so nothing takes ownership of those factories and nothing closes them.

`SqlCompilerImpl.alterViewExecution()` has the same window between `generateExecutionModel()` and `SqlUtil.generateFactory()`: `validateNoCycle()` throws there, after optimisation and before generation. That is the second route above.

Interaction with #7602 (open):

- It adds a sweep in `generateSelectOneShot()` that closes the table-function factories a generated plan did not claim. The two paths above never generate, so the sweep does not run for them. `SqlCompiler` does not expose the sweep to a caller that discards the model.
- On that branch every read of a declared sub-query parses its own copy, so a view body that reads one declared sub-query over a table function N times leaks 256 x N bytes per `COMPILE VIEW` (512 for two reads, 768 for three), against 256 on `master`. The refused `ALTER VIEW` route scales the same way.
- In the other direction, the sweep removes leaks that `master` has outside these two paths, for example a `SELECT` or `CREATE VIEW` whose declared sub-query over a table function is never read.

Two fix directions: give callers of `generateExecutionModel()` that discard the model a way to release its table functions, or have the compiler close what is still unclaimed when it is cleared or returned to the pool.

### To reproduce

`SAMPLE BY ... FILL(LINEAR) ALIGN TO CALENDAR TIME ZONE '...'` buckets on UTC boundaries when the query runs on the SAMPLE BY cursor, for example over a sub-query. The other fill modes shift the buckets by the time zone offset for the same query.

```sql
CREATE TABLE trades (sym SYMBOL, price DOUBLE, ts TIMESTAMP) TIMESTAMP(ts) PARTITION BY DAY;
INSERT INTO trades VALUES
    ('a', 1.0, '2024-01-01T10:00:00.000000Z'),
    ('b', 2.0, '2024-01-01T12:00:00.000000Z'),
    ('a', 4.0, '2024-01-01T19:00:00.000000Z'),
    ('b', 8.0, '2024-01-01T20:00:00.000000Z'),
    ('a', 16.0, '2024-01-02T19:00:00.000000Z');

-- FILL(NULL); FILL(NONE), FILL(PREV) and FILL(42) return the same buckets
SELECT ts, sum(price) FROM (SELECT ts, price FROM trades)
SAMPLE BY 1d FILL(NULL) ALIGN TO CALENDAR TIME ZONE '+05:30';

-- FILL(LINEAR)
SELECT ts, sum(price) FROM (SELECT ts, price FROM trades)
SAMPLE BY 1d FILL(LINEAR) ALIGN TO CALENDAR TIME ZONE '+05:30';
```

A `+05:30` day starts at 18:30Z of the previous UTC day.

| Query | Buckets (start, `sum`) |
|---|---|
| FILL(NONE), FILL(PREV), FILL(NULL), FILL(42) | `2023-12-31T18:30Z` 3.0, `2024-01-01T18:30Z` 12.0, `2024-01-02T18:30Z` 16.0 |
| FILL(LINEAR) | `2024-01-01T00:00Z` 15.0, `2024-01-02T00:00Z` 16.0 |

The keyed query (`SELECT ts, sym, sum(price) FROM (SELECT ts, sym, price FROM trades) SAMPLE BY 1d FILL(LINEAR) ALIGN TO CALENDAR TIME ZONE '+05:30'`) returns the same UTC buckets: `2024-01-01T00:00Z` (a = 5.0, b = 10.0) and `2024-01-02T00:00Z` (a = 16.0, b = null). A time zone name gives the same result: `TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata'` also returns the two UTC buckets. `LIMIT` makes no difference.

The plan of the FILL(LINEAR) queries is `Sample By` with `fill: linear`, which is `SampleByInterpolateRecordCursorFactory`.

### Expected

The same bucket boundaries as the other fill modes for the same `TIME ZONE`, or a compile-time error if FILL(LINEAR) does not support `TIME ZONE` on this path. Today the clause is accepted and has no effect on the boundaries.

### Cause

`SampleByInterpolateRecordCursorFactory.SampleByInterpolateRecordCursor` parses the time zone in `parseParams()` and computes `tzOffset` (from the numeric offset, or from the zone rules in `initTimestamps()`), but never applies it to a timestamp. The only read of `tzOffset` is the check `tzOffset == 0 && fixedOffset == Long.MIN_VALUE`, which chooses between first-observation and calendar alignment. The cursor has no DST handling either.

The other cursor-based fill modes extend `AbstractNoRecordSampleByCursor`, which adds `tzOffset` to each row's timestamp before rounding and adjusts it at DST transitions.

### Notes

- Not affected by this report: FILL(LINEAR) straight over a table, which takes a different path. `SampleByTest` has a `TIME ZONE` + `FROM`-`TO` + `FILL(LINEAR)` case there that honours the zone.
- A fix changes results for existing queries. At least one test pins the current output: `SampleByTest.testSampleCountFillLinearWithOffset` (`SAMPLE BY 3h FILL(LINEAR) ALIGN TO CALENDAR TIME ZONE 'Europe/Berlin' WITH OFFSET '00:45'`).
- Related: #4424 questions what `TIME ZONE` should do in SAMPLE BY in general and notes that FILL(LINEAR) has no DST code. This issue is the narrower, reproducible case: the cursor-path FILL(LINEAR) ignores the offset that the other fill modes apply.
- Found while fixing a different SAMPLE BY time zone bug in #7681 (a numeric `TIME ZONE` dropped under `LIMIT`). That fix doesn't touch `SampleByInterpolateRecordCursorFactory`.

### QuestDB version

Observed on the #7681 branch at `5994325d5b`. `SampleByInterpolateRecordCursorFactory.java` is identical on `master` at `f56e72425c`; the queries were not re-run on `master` itself.

### OS, in case of Docker specify Docker and the Host OS

Linux

### File System, in case of Docker specify Host File System

Not relevant.

### Additional context

By the code, the `WITH OFFSET` part of the clause is applied on this path (`sampler.setOffset(fixedOffset)` in `initTimestamps()`), and only the time zone is dropped. That part was read, not executed.
