**Versions:** Next.js 16.2.10, which bundles react-dom `19.3.0-canary-3f0b9e61-20260317` and `react-server-dom-turbopack` from the same build. Production build, Chrome.

### What happens

A client navigation through `<Link>`, or a `router.refresh()`, sometimes never commits. The RSC response has fully arrived and nothing is logged. The page stays on the old route until any unrelated state update reaches the root, and then it commits at once. On one of our pages this happens in 10–60% of clicks, depending on host load and how long the payload takes to stream.

Root state while stuck: `pendingLanes === suspendedLanes` (transition lanes), `pingedLanes === 0`, `callbackNode === null`, `cancelPendingCommit === null`.

### Sequence

We instrumented the production build and saw this sequence:

1. The render reaches a lazy element whose Flight chunk is still `pending`. `resolveLazy` → `readChunk` throws the chunk without subscribing to it. `handleThrow` takes the SuspendedOnImmediate path, and the work loop yields.
2. The chunk's row arrives. The chunk has no listeners, so `resolveModelChunk` leaves it `resolved_model` without decoding it.
3. On resume, `isThenableResolved` returns false for `resolved_model`, so the work loop goes `throwAndUnwindWorkLoop` → `throwException`. The boundary is already visible, so `renderDidSuspendDelayIfPossible()` sets the exit status to RootSuspendedWithDelay (4). Then `attachPingListener` calls `chunk.then(ping, ping)`.
4. `ReactPromise.prototype.then` initialises the `resolved_model` chunk and calls `ping` **synchronously**, inside the render.
5. `pingSuspendedRoot` sees `workInProgressRoot === root` and exit status 4. Because this is the render phase, it neither calls `prepareFreshStack` nor adds the lanes to `workInProgressRootPingedLanes`.
6. The render ends as RootSuspendedWithDelay, and `markRootSuspended` clears `root.pingedLanes` for those lanes. Nothing pings again.

### Suggested fix

We verified this on the compiled build: 30/30 navigations landed instead of 25/30, and 0/40 refreshes stalled instead of 3/40. In `pingSuspendedRoot`, in the render-phase case, record the ping:

```js
if ((executionContext & RenderContext) === NoContext) {
  prepareFreshStack(root, NoLanes);
} else {
  workInProgressRootPingedLanes = mergeLanes(workInProgressRootPingedLanes, pingedLanes);
}
```

Fixes on the Flight or reconciler side would also close it. Either treat `resolved_model` / `resolved_module` as resolved in `isThenableResolved`, initialising the chunk first, or subscribe in `readChunk` before throwing a pending chunk.

### Workaround

Any state update while the navigation is pending rescues it, for example a 1 s tick in a component that reads `useLinkStatus()`.

### Not verified

- We have no minimal standalone repro yet. The analysis comes from instrumenting our own app's production build.
- We think there may be a TODO comment in React's source on that render-phase branch, but could not check it, because the compiled build strips comments.
- Some rounds also show a `net::ERR_ABORTED` on an RSC request. Its source was not traced. It appears in rounds that commit as well as rounds that stick, so we don't think it causes the bug.

**Versions.** react 19.2.8 · react-dom 19.2.8 · next 15.5.25 (webpack build, deployed on Vercel; the app router). Not reproducible under `next dev`.

**Symptom.** On a production build, a `<Link>` click to the same pathname with different search params (`/page?tab=a` → `/page?tab=b`) sometimes never commits: the RSC request for the new page is sent and answered in full (200, complete payload), no error is thrown, nothing stays pending, and the URL and the DOM never change. Any later state update anywhere in the tree (a second click, an unrelated `setState`) makes the stuck navigation commit immediately. Measured across two days on one deployment: 11 of 125 such clicks stuck (about 1 in 11); each landed within milliseconds of a later unrelated state update.

**What the React root looks like while stuck** (read through a devtools hook installed before React loaded):

- `root.pendingLanes = 14336` (three transition lanes), `root.suspendedLanes = 14336`, `root.pingedLanes = 0`, `root.warmLanes = 14336`, `root.callbackNode = null`, `root.callbackPriority = 0`.
- The app router's `useState` hook (Next's `useActionQueue`) holds two unprocessed updates in its base queue, lanes 2048 and 8192, each a Promise whose React-tracked `status` is already `'fulfilled'`.

So every pending lane is marked suspended, nothing is pinged, and nothing is scheduled: `getNextLanes` returns 0 forever.

**The sequence** (one failing click, times in ms on the page's clock; a trap on `WeakMap.prototype.set`/`delete` named every `attachPingListener`/`pingSuspendedRoot` call):

```
+0      click (Link → startTransition → dispatch; Next takes its "aliased prefetch" path for a same-pathname navigation:
         the router state moves to the new URL at once with an EMPTY page cache node + the loading component;
         the page node's render issues the data fetch and suspends on Next's never-resolving `unresolvedThenable`)
+2      the navigation's deferred promise resolves (lane 2048)
+60     attachPingListener(Promise /* the lazy fetch */, lanes 2048)
+62     attachPingListener(Object /* unresolvedThenable, then = () => {} */, lanes 4096)   ← a deferred-value lane
+74     root: pending 6144 · suspended 6144 · warm 6144 · no callback
+319    RSC response headers
+342    ping fires for the lazy-fetch promise; Next dispatches ACTION_SERVER_PATCH → a second deferred promise (lane 8192)
+344    attachPingListener(Flight Chunk, status pending, lanes 14336)
+357    that chunk's ping fires → root: pending 14336 · suspended 14336 · pinged 14336 · callback scheduled   (healthy)
+360    RSC body ends
+360    attachPingListener(Flight Chunk, status "resolved_model", lanes 14336)  ─┐ same millisecond, inside the render
+360    pingSuspendedRoot for that same chunk                                     ─┘
+374    root: pending 14336 · suspended 14336 · pinged 0 · warm 14336 · no callback   ← STUCK; nothing more for 8+ s
+8000   (probe) hook.queue.dispatch(<the state React already holds>) → pushState and commit within 3 ms
```

**Why the ping is dropped, as far as I can read the build.** A React Flight `Chunk` in state `resolved_model` is not "resolved" to React (`isThenableResolved` checks for `'fulfilled'`/`'rejected'` only), so after the work loop yields with `SuspendedOnImmediate` and resumes with `SuspendedAndReadyToContinue` (reason 7), it goes to `throwAndUnwindWorkLoop` → `throwException` → `attachPingListener(root, chunk, lanes)` → `chunk.then(ping, ping)`. Flight's `Chunk.prototype.then` **initializes a `resolved_model` chunk synchronously and calls the callback synchronously** when it becomes `fulfilled`. So `pingSuspendedRoot` runs *inside* the render phase (`executionContext & RenderContext`). In `react-dom-client.production.js` 19.2.8:

```js
function pingSuspendedRoot(root, wakeable, pingedLanes) {
  var pingCache = root.pingCache;
  null !== pingCache && pingCache.delete(wakeable);
  root.pingedLanes |= root.suspendedLanes & pingedLanes;       // suspendedLanes for these lanes is 0 at this point (markRootUpdated cleared it)
  root.warmLanes &= ~pingedLanes;
  workInProgressRoot === root &&
    (workInProgressRootRenderLanes & pingedLanes) === pingedLanes &&
    (4 === workInProgressRootExitStatus || (3 === workInProgressRootExitStatus && …)
      ? 0 === (executionContext & 2) && prepareFreshStack(root, 0)   // in the render phase: nothing happens
      : (workInProgressRootPingedLanes |= pingedLanes),              // only taken when the exit status is not yet 3/4
    …);
  ensureRootIsScheduled(root);
}
```

When an earlier suspension in the same pass has already set `workInProgressRootExitStatus = 4` (RootSuspendedWithDelay), a ping arriving from inside the render phase takes the first branch, which is a no-op in the render context, and is **not** recorded in `workInProgressRootPingedLanes`. The listener has already been deleted from `pingCache`. The pass then ends in `markRootSuspended(root, lanes, …)`, which marks every render lane suspended (`suspendedLanes |= lanes`, `pingedLanes &= ~lanes`, `warmLanes |= lanes`), and no listener remains to ping them. `ensureRootIsScheduled` then finds no unsuspended, unpinged, non-warm lane and schedules nothing.

Any later `markRootUpdated` (which resets `suspendedLanes`/`pingedLanes`/`warmLanes`) lets the stuck lanes render again, which is why an unrelated state update "fixes" it.

**Workaround in the app.** A navigation watchdog: at the start of every navigation (`onRouterTransitionStart` in `instrumentation-client.ts`) arm a timer; if the URL has not moved after 1.2 s, trigger a no-op state update in a root-level client component. The stuck navigation then commits in ~3 ms. The failure rate on a later deployment: 2 of 48 clicks stuck, both recovered at 1.2 s.

**A reproduction.** It needs a production build, a page with a `loading.tsx` (so Next's aliased-prefetch branch applies — it only runs when `NODE_ENV !== 'development'` and the seeded entry carries a loading component), a same-pathname search-param `<Link>`, and a page payload large enough to still be streaming when the server patch is applied (ours is ~108 KB). The race is timing-dependent (about 1 in 11 on our site). I can share the read-only Playwright probes that (a) read the root's lanes and the router hook's queue after a click, and (b) trap the ping cache's WeakMap to name every listener, if that helps.

### Website or app

https://gist.github.com/Elehiggle/ea271e796f304a4de2ef223137879009

### Repro steps

1. Save the linked repro's six files in one directory.
2. Run `npm ci --ignore-scripts --no-audit --no-fund`.
3. Run `npm run reproduce`. Tested with Node 24.18.0 and npm 11.16.0.

### What kind of issue is this?

- [x] React Compiler core (the JS output is incorrect, or your app works incorrectly after optimization)
- [ ] babel-plugin-react-compiler (build issue installing or using the Babel plugin)
- [ ] eslint-plugin-react-hooks (build issue installing or using the eslint plugin)
- [ ] react-compiler-healthcheck (build issue installing or using the healthcheck script)

### Link to repro

https://playground.react.dev/#N4Igzg9grgTgxgUxALhAGwQFwAQAcEB2AJgJYEDm2AvNgOQBuAhmlArQNwA6B3CAHrggwcAMygE4mEhALYAwhAC2ggoUwAKAJTZg3bNjgywOABaNiGOWhJwA1tWxbqAPh179BozkO4Ang-xiMnIuWQ9A0goHAig0NFCPTwJIDAA6NAhydR9fTXZsAHoC7H58SQQiZDomFjZ3AF8E7BgsWFkAHgAjKExMGWwZKxtbKmAzCwQhu3rnKdt2gu7emWdQ+u4QABoQQwIREnIUEF0wosNlEjRGKRkAWQgiBCrOEGY0F+56rfATCAB3ACSBEwCBgBGYYBQIghCHqQA

### Repro steps

Inside a function nested in a component (an event handler, for example), a local copy of a module-level `let` is replaced by the module variable itself. When the handler then reassigns the variable, every later use of the "copy" sees the new value.

Input:

```js
let pending = 'value';

export function Component() {
  const handleClick = () => {
    const copy = pending;
    pending = null;
    console.log(copy); // expected: 'value'
  };
  return <button onClick={handleClick}>Click</button>;
}
```

Output (the handler is outlined to `_temp`):

```js
function _temp() {
  pending = null;
  console.log(pending); // logs null
}
```

`const copy = pending` is dropped and `copy` is rewritten to `pending`, which is read after the assignment. The copy has to survive because the variable is reassigned before it is read.

What I checked with babel-plugin-react-compiler directly (the same output in `1.0.0` and `0.0.0-experimental-a1856f3-20260507`):

- **Outlining is not required.** When the handler captures a prop and stays inline, the copy is still dropped (`value = null; console.log(label, value);`).
- **Sync or async makes no difference.**
- **Only functions inside components are affected.** The same function outside a component compiles unchanged. In the render body itself, the compiler bails out of the component, as expected.

How we hit it in production: a PWA install button kept Chrome's `beforeinstallprompt` event in a module-level variable (it fires before the component mounts). The click handler did `const event = deferred; deferred = null; await event.prompt();`, which compiled to `deferred = null; await deferred.prompt();`, so every press threw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'prompt')`. Workaround: move that logic into a plain function outside the component (or use `'use no memo'`).

Possibly related to other bugs in how the compiler handles closures and `_temp` outlining (#34901, #35342, #35386), though those are about locally scoped variables lost when a function is moved out to module scope. Here the variable already is module-scoped.

### How often does this bug happen?

Every time

### What version of React are you using?

19.3.0 (Next.js 16.3.8, `reactCompiler: true`)

### What version of React Compiler are you using?

babel-plugin-react-compiler 1.0.0 (also reproduced on 0.0.0-experimental-a1856f3-20260507 and the current Playground)

body_text:
## Expected Behavior
XREAD should support multiple ID, one per stream

Redis XREAD syntax is
```
XREAD [COUNT count] [BLOCK milliseconds] STREAMS key [key ...] id [id ...]
```

Redis XREAD support reading from multiple streams, redis-cli mandates that each stream has own ID. That is logical as each stream can be trimmed very differently,  Unique ID needed when reading streams larger than COUNT, ID used to continue streaming from right location.

```
127.0.0.1:6379> XREAD COUNT 100 STREAMS stream-1 stream-2 1769414803181-0 1769417819561-0
```

Also Java lettuce for example support own ID for multiple stream, see redis-cli>monitor output. See XREAD command given by lettuce when reading 3 separate streams

```
1769435290.365489 [0 172.18.0.1:63222] "XREAD" "COUNT" "1000" "STREAMS" "stream-1" "stream-2" "stream-3" "1769414825724-0" "1769418971541-0" "0"

```


## Current Behavior
In Go-Redis when XREAD is used to read multiple streams []string it is possible to set only one ID (string). 

This result that same ID is used for reading all streams. This means that client needs to select one of the ID and that results 
- data lost if highest ID taken, because COUNT might have limited the number of messages
- same data read multiple times if smallest ID is taken. 

Monitor when go-redis is used, second XREAD after one of the returned ID is passed to next requests

```
1769439443.897530 [0 192.168.65.1:23864] "xread" "count" "1000" "streams" "uid-stream" "session-id-stream" "jti-stream" "1769438569498-0" "1769438569498-0" "1769438569498-0"
```


## Possible Solution

The problem originates to [XReadArgs ](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/master/stream_commands.go#L172). ID is defined as string, thus only one value can be passed.
```
type XReadArgs struct {
    Streams []string  // slice allows multiple streams
    Count int64
    Block time.Duration
    ID string   // ID incorrectly string, only one allowed
}
```
Options

1. Change ID to []string and pass ID to Redis as expected. This is potentially breaking change
2. Ad new fields IDs, which is used when set, fallback to single ID for compatibility
3. Change ID type to interface. When creating redis XREAD ID, check if type is string, then keep current behavior, if type is []string then apply multiple. If len(streams) != len(ID), just pass to Redis. Redis will return error

Workaround:
When using XREAD pass only one stream to API. When multiple streams needs to be read then multiple calls are required.
Also using the smallest ID might work but result reading same data multiple times.

Multiple streams are needed to simulate different TTL for each stream, and single XREAD is preferable way to read multiple streams.

## Steps to Reproduce

1.  Add data to stream-1: XADD stream-1 cmd ADD key XXX value expired ttl 200
2.  Add data to stream-2: XADD stream-2 cmd ADD key YYY value expired ttl 200
3. Turn on cli monitor in redis
4. Read both stream in single XREAD, start from beginning XREAD COUNT 100 STREAMS stream-1 stream-2 "0" "0", note in go-redis you can pass only one id, in reply you get ID for both stream. In first call ID is normally "0".
4. Add mode data to both stream, you can use same XADD data ow new one with different values.
5. Now you should use per stream ID to read data  XREAD COUNT 100 STREAMS stream-1 stream-2 "last-id-1" "last-id2", but in go-redis you can only pass one id. 

## Context (Environment)
redis 8.4 in docker 
Windows 11 go-redis 9.17.2
go 1.24.2

## Detailed Description

I think the above description is detailed enough

## Possible Implementation

This is solution for option 3 (use ID type interface

```
type XReadArgs struct {
    Streams []string  // slice allows multiple streams
    Count int64
    Block time.Duration
    ID interface{}   // interface for backward compatibility
}
```

Issue is here [Same ID set to every stream](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/master/stream_commands.go#L197)

```
	switch v := a.ID.(type) {

## Expected Behavior

A matched field that cannot be decoded should either report an unsupported-type error or have its successful no-op behavior documented. Could maintainers confirm whether returning an error for non-byte slice fields without a custom decoder is acceptable in v9, should be reserved for v10, or whether the current behavior should be preserved?

## Current Behavior

`MapStringStringCmd.Scan` and `SliceCmd.Scan` return nil for a matched `[]string` field but leave its previous value unchanged. `internal/hscan.decodeSlice` assigns only when the element kind is uint8 and otherwise returns nil. This report does not request automatic JSON or CSV deserialization.

## Possible Solution

Return the existing `decodeUnsupported` error for the non-byte case, preserving byte slices and custom decoding dispatch. This changes observable behavior from nil to an error and can stop scanning subsequent fields, so I would like to agree on the compatibility scope before submitting a PR.

## Steps to Reproduce

The public result types reproduce this without a Redis server:

```go
package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"

    "github.com/redis/go-redis/v9"
)

func main() {
    dst := struct {
        Values []string `redis:"values"`
    }{Values: []string{"old"}}
    cmd := redis.NewMapStringStringCmd(context.Background(), "hgetall", "key")
    cmd.SetVal(map[string]string{"values": "a,b"})
    err := cmd.Scan(&dst)
    fmt.Printf("err=%v values=%q\n", err, dst.Values)
}
```

Public regression tests against the original production code observe nil with the original slice retained. `NewSliceCmd(ctx, "hmget", "key", "values")` with `SetVal([]interface{}{"a,b"})` behaves the same way.

## Context (Environment)

- go-redis master commit `f813adcb8569821e5bf117af6216163128dc8eca`, module v9.
- Go 1.26.4, darwin/arm64.
- Redis version: no server was used; this is public result decoding.

## Detailed Description

The non-byte slice no-op is longstanding, so a caller relying on nil while retaining a tagged slice would be affected by an error-return change. An unsupported field can also stop later assignments. I am asking for a compatibility decision rather than assuming that new regression expectations authorize a v9 behavior change.

## Possible Implementation

A local draft returns nil after byte assignment and `decodeUnsupported` otherwise. Independently rerunning the public and internal regressions against original production code fails; the draft passes those regressions and the entire internal/hscan race suite. Byte content, a custom named-slice scanner, unmatched fields and existing command errors remain covered. Full Redis integration and all-module checks have not been run. No PR has been submitted.

## Problem

`Client.EphemeralConn()` (#4039) is the API for session-scoped work: `SELECT`, `AUTH`, `HELLO`, `RESET`, `CLIENT TRACKING`. `Close` discards the connection, so that state never returns to the pool.

With client-side caching on (RESP3, `DB: 0`, cache attached), those commands still fail on an `EphemeralConn`:

```go
conn := rdb.EphemeralConn()
err := conn.Select(ctx, 1).Err() // errSelectWithCSC
```

`Client.conn()` copies the parent's `cscActive` onto the derived client, and `cscCommandError` uses it to reject the commands above. `Conn()` needs that guard. `EphemeralConn()` inherits it from the same shared code path.

## Why the guard is not removed outright

`EphemeralConn` takes an idle connection from the parent pool. With CSC on, that connection has `CLIENT TRACKING ON`, and the parent cache owns entries read through it. They are evicted only when the connection is removed (`cscEvictOnRemoveHook`, `EvictByConn(connID)`).

If the user runs `RESET`, `CLIENT TRACKING OFF`, or `HELLO 2` on it, the server stops sending invalidations for those keys. The parent cache then serves the entries stale until `Close` evicts them. A long-lived `EphemeralConn` makes that window long. The guard prevents this. Discard-on-close does not.

## Proposal

When CSC is on, give an `EphemeralConn` a newly dialed connection that is not tracked, instead of an idle pooled one.

1. **Fresh dial.** Add a mode to `StickyConnPool` (next to `DiscardOnClose`): on the first `Get`, call `ConnPool.NewConn` instead of `ConnPool.Get`.
2. **No tracking.** In `Client.conn(true)`, do not copy `cscActive` and do not call `attachCSC`. `cscTrackingRequested()` is then false, so:
   - `initConn` does not send `CLIENT TRACKING ON`;
   - `cscCommandError` allows all session commands;
   - no cache entry is owned by this connection, so the parent cache cannot go stale through it.
3. **Matching removal.** `NewConn` does not take a pool turn, so `Close` must use `ConnPool.RemoveWithoutTurn`, not `Remove`. `Remove` would free a turn that was never taken.

The sticky client already never serves or fills the cache, so nothing else changes.

This can apply only when the parent's CSC is active, so an `EphemeralConn` without CSC keeps reusing idle connections. Or it can always dial fresh, which is simpler and behaves the same with or without CSC. To decide.

## Trade-offs

- **One dial per `EphemeralConn`, every time.** The current godoc says `Get` reuses an idle pooled connection; that changes.

`Client.EphemeralConn()` (#4039) is the API for session-scoped work: `SELECT`, `AUTH`, `HELLO`, `RESET`, `CLIENT TRACKING`. `Close` discards the connection, so that state never returns to the pool.

body_text:
#### Summary

When `ContextTimeoutEnabled` is enabled, go-redis respects context deadlines for socket I/O, but a pure `context.Cancel()` does not reliably interrupt a command that is already blocked in a socket read.

This is especially visible with blocking commands such as `BLMOVE`, `BLPOP`, `XREAD BLOCK 0`, or `XREADGROUP BLOCK 0`: after the caller cancels the context, the command may continue until `ReadTimeout` expires.

This appears to be a v8 to v9 behavior regression. Related discussion: [#2682](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/issues/2682), [#2556](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/issues/2556), and [#2276](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/issues/2276).

#### Reproduction

The following reproducer uses a Redis-compatible server that accepts the command but does not produce a reply within the test window. The timing behavior was reproduced with `github.com/redis/go-redis/v9` v9.21.0. The relevant synchronous I/O path was also checked against the current upstream `master` at commit `760b98dc0b7d8621f09e1d91d7a6b32fe555bebe`.

```go
ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background())

client := redis.NewClient(&redis.Options{
    Addr: "127.0.0.1:6379",
    ReadTimeout: 10 * time.Second,
    ContextTimeoutEnabled: true,
})

done := make(chan error, 1)
go func() {
    _, err := client.BLMove(ctx, "src", "dst", "RIGHT", "LEFT", 0).Result()
    done <- err
}()

time.Sleep(200 * time.Millisecond)
cancel()

select {
case err := <-done:
    fmt.Println(err)
case <-time.After(1 * time.Second):
    t.Fatal("command was not interrupted by context cancellation")
}
```

Observed behavior: with `ReadTimeout` set to 10 seconds, the pure-cancellation case returned after approximately 10 seconds instead of returning within the 1-second test window. The observed result was `context.Canceled`, but only after the socket read timeout elapsed.

The reproduction environment was Go 1.26.4 on Darwin arm64. The test used a controlled Redis-compatible endpoint and did not use production data or credentials.

Expected behavior: with `ContextTimeoutEnabled: true`, the command should return within a bounded time after cancellation and return an error matching `context.Canceled`.

#### Proposed semantics

I would like to propose the following behavior:

- `ContextTimeoutEnabled: false` keeps the existing behavior for compatibility.
- `ContextTimeoutEnabled: true` makes in-flight socket reads and writes respect both context deadlines and pure context cancellation.
- A pure cancellation returns `context.Canceled`.
- A context deadline returns `context.DeadlineExceeded`.
- If a command may already have been written to Redis, the client must not automatically retry it after context cancellation, because the command may have been executed already.
- If the RESP stream is not known to be fully consumed, the connection should be removed rather than returned to the pool.
- A reply that was fully decoded before cancellation should keep its successful result.

The first change would focus on interrupting in-flight I/O and safe connection handling. Bounded reply draining and connection reuse would be a separate follow-up concern.

#### Relation to existing work

[PR #3946](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/pull/3946) proposes draining the remaining reply after a context error so that a connection can sometimes be reused. That addresses connection reuse after an error, but it does not solve the case where a pure cancellation cannot wake the blocked socket read in the first place.

I would prefer to keep these concerns separate:

1. First, make in-flight I/O respond to pure context cancellation safely.
2. Then, if appropriate, add bounded drain/reuse with explicit coverage for pipelines, transactions, RESP3 push frames, and client-side caching.

#### Questions

Would the maintainers be open to extending the meaning of `ContextTimeoutEnabled: true` to include pure context cancellation, without adding another public option?

Would removing the affected connection by default be an acceptable first implementation, before attempting any drain/reuse optimization?

I would be happy to prepare a focused PR with regression tests for blocking commands, ordinary commands, pipelines, transactions, connection reuse, and race conditions.

Following up on the discussion in #4104 for the PubSub rewrite started in #4017.

In a realtime broker, we need to know when a subscription is ready before publishing from another connection. Correlating replies by channel name is not enough:

1. Subscribe to a channel, with its reply delayed.
2. Unsubscribe, then subscribe to the same channel again.
3. The first reply arrives and can be mistaken for confirmation of the second subscription.

A consumer-side FIFO also breaks across reconnects: automatic resubscription restores the current channel set, not the original command sequence.

Could the new implementation expose a way to wait for confirmation of a specific subscribe operation? Old replies and automatic resubscription replies should not complete a newer operation. Connection retirement or close should settle pending waits, and canceling one caller’s wait should not cancel a shared subscription.

The API shape can follow the new engine. #4104 has a prototype and regression tests for delayed replies, reconnects, and cancellation that may be useful.

body_text:
## Problem

`FailoverClient` resolves the master on every new data-node dial. `sentinelFailover.MasterAddr` (`sentinel.go:1009`) runs `getMasterAddr` against the cached sentinel (`:1015`) for each caller, and concurrent callers are not coalesced. A burst of N concurrent dials therefore sends N `SENTINEL get-master-addr-by-name` queries, and the sentinel client's pool grows to serve them, up to its `PoolSize`.

Measured with a fake sentinel and a real master, `PoolSize: 100` and 200 concurrent Pings on a cold client:

| Build | Sentinel connections | `get-master-addr-by-name` queries |
|---|---|---|
| master | 100 | 100 |
| master, `MinIdleConns: 20` | 101-103 | 100 |
| prototype: concurrent `MasterAddr` calls share one query | 2 | 1 |
| prototype + sentinel clients built with `MinIdleConns: 0` | 2 | 2 |

The sentinel clients inherit the data-node pool options (`PoolSize`, `MinIdleConns`), so `MinIdleConns` also keeps idle connections open to every sentinel.

## Suggested fix

- Coalesce concurrent `MasterAddr` / `replicaAddrs` lookups (singleflight-style, per `sentinelFailover`, not package-level). Waiters must keep their own context: a waiter whose ctx ends returns early without cancelling the shared lookup.
- Build sentinel clients with `MinIdleConns: 0` (and a small `PoolSize`), since they only serve lookups and the `+switch-master` subscription.

## Notes

- #4020 adds a `SentinelOptionsOverride` struct whose main use case is limiting sentinel connections. With the fix above, most of that use case is covered without new API.
- #4069 rewrites `MasterAddr` / `replicaAddrs` error handling, so the two changes need to be ordered.

Found while reviewing #4020.

body_text:
Clients using `StreamingCredentialsProvider` retain closed Pub/Sub connections and their buffers after the sockets close and the provider subscriptions end.

The [Pub/Sub close path](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/v9.23.0/redis.go#L2903-L2932) bypasses `ReAuthPoolHook.OnRemove`, leaving credential listeners and pending reauthentication state in the client's registries.

Open fix PR:
- https://github.com/redis/go-redis/pull/4119

Retention also reproduces on the shared-connection rewrite at 338eb3bc41577461cd772785618379e0be3f9e57. The adapted repro checks provider unsubscription and retained listeners without the removed `PubSubPool` field. Sharing reduces connection creation while other handles remain open, but listeners still accumulate when physical Pub/Sub connections close and reopen.

- https://github.com/redis/go-redis/pull/4116

## Impact

Repeated reconnects, such as during network instability, accumulate retained connections and can create memory pressure in long-lived clients even with few active subscriptions. Growth follows connection churn, not message volume.

## Reproduction

The test closes Pub/Sub connections and checks that the client's listener registry is empty. The provider holds no listener references and sends no credential updates.

<details>
<summary>Test and run instructions</summary>

Start a disposable Redis instance in another terminal:

```sh
redis-server --bind 127.0.0.1 --port 16379 --save '' --appendonly no --requirepass old-token

body_text:
Commands can overrun their context deadlines while acquiring streaming credentials, even with `ContextTimeoutEnabled: true`.

Connection initialization calls [`StreamingCredentialsProvider.Subscribe`](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/v9.23.0/redis.go#L971-L988) synchronously, without a context. The command cannot stop waiting until the provider returns, even if its context has expired. The interface has no cancellation parameter, so this is a missing client/provider contract rather than a socket-timeout setting.

The same wait occurs with go-redis-entraid when `Subscribe` waits behind the token manager's [in-progress acquisition lock](https://github.com/redis/go-redis-entraid/blob/v1.0.7/manager/entraid_manager.go#L71-L118); it does not require a permanently blocked custom provider.

The PING reproduction below also fails on the open Pub/Sub rewrite at 338eb3bc41577461cd772785618379e0be3f9e57. That rewrite bounds the caller's wait during Pub/Sub setup, while credential acquisition can continue in the background; it does not fix ordinary command waits.

- https://github.com/redis/go-redis/pull/4116

## Impact

In an HTTP service, slow token acquisition can keep a Redis call running after the incoming request times out. The handler and any concurrency slot it holds remain occupied until acquisition returns. Under sustained traffic, overdue calls can consume worker capacity and delay other requests.

## Reproduction

A blocked provider and an in-memory connection isolate the credential wait from Redis I/O. The test specifies a bounded caller wait, without prescribing cancellation of arbitrary provider code or an exact timeout error type. No Redis server is needed.

<details>
<summary>Test and run instructions</summary>

In a `go-redis v9.23.0` checkout, save this as `deadline_repro_test.go` in the repository root.

```go
package redis_test

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"net"
	"testing"
	"time"

	"github.com/redis/go-redis/v9"
	"github.com/redis/go-redis/v9/auth"
)

type blockedReproProvider struct{ entered, release chan struct{} }

func (p *blockedReproProvider) Subscribe(auth.CredentialsListener) (auth.Credentials, auth.UnsubscribeFunc, error) {
	close(p.entered)
	<-p.release
	return nil, nil, errors.New("acquisition released by test cleanup")
}

func TestCredentialWaitHonorsDeadline(t *testing.T) {
	p := &blockedReproProvider{make(chan struct{}), make(chan struct{})}
	clientEnd, serverEnd := net.Pipe()
	defer serverEnd.Close()
	c := redis.NewClient(&redis.Options{
		StreamingCredentialsProvider: p,
		ContextTimeoutEnabled:        true,
		MaxRetries:                   -1,
		Dialer: func(context.Context, string, string) (net.Conn, error) {
			return clientEnd, nil
		},
	})
	t.Cleanup(func() { c.Close() })
	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), time.Second)
	defer cancel()
	done := make(chan error, 1)
	finished := make(chan struct{})
	go func() {
		defer close(finished)
		done <- c.Ping(ctx).Err()
	}()
	t.Cleanup(func() { close(p.release); <-finished })
	select {
	case <-p.entered:
	case <-ctx.Done():
		t.Fatal("setup failed: Subscribe was not entered")
	}
	<-ctx.Done()
	select {
	case err := <-done:
		if err == nil {
			t.Fatal("expected the overdue command to return an error")
		}
	case <-time.After(100 * time.Millisecond):
		t.Fatal("Ping still blocked in Subscribe after its deadline")
	}
}
```

```sh
go test -race -count=1 -run '^TestCredentialWaitHonorsDeadline$' .
```

Desired behavior: the command's deadline bounds its wait for credentials. The cancellation contract and returned error type need to be defined across the client/provider interface. The current test fails with:

```text
Ping still blocked in Subscribe after its deadline
```

Verified with:
- Go: `go1.27.1 linux/amd64`
- go-redis: `v9.23.0`

</details>

Cancellation must also clean up a subscription that completes after the caller returns; abandoning the wait alone can leave a listener or acquisition goroutine behind.

			t.Fatal("expected the overdue command to return an error")
		}
	case <-time.After(100 * time.Millisecond):
		t.Fatal("Ping still blocked in Subscribe after its deadline")
	}
}
```

```sh
go test -race -count=1 -run '^TestCredentialWaitHonorsDeadline$' .
```

Desired behavior: the command's deadline bounds its wait for credentials. The cancellation contract and returned error type need to be defined across the client/provider interface. The current test fails with:

```text
Ping still blocked in Subscribe after its deadline
```

Verified with:
- Go: `go1.27.1 linux/amd64`
- go-redis: `v9.23.0`

</details>

Cancellation must also clean up a subscription that completes after the caller returns; abandoning the wait alone can leave a listener or acquisition goroutine behind.

## Background

Cluster topology refresh (`JedisClusterInfoCache.renewClusterSlots()`) is currently triggered from several places, each with its own ad-hoc policy:

- `ClusterCommandExecutor.handleConnectionProblem` — after 2 consecutive connection failures + backoff
- `ClusterCommandExecutor` — immediately on `MOVED` redirect
- `ClusterConnectionProvider.getConnectionFromSlot` — when a slot has no mapped pool
- `JedisClusterInfoCache.TopologyRefreshTask` — scheduled, fixed delay

Current safeguard against renewal storms is `rediscoverLock.tryLock()`, which dedups *concurrent* renewals but not *serial* ones. There is no time-based gate, no backoff coordination across call sites. Under concurrency, a brief hiccup on one node can fan out into repeated full-topology refreshes.

This came up in #4154 / #4544: adding a refresh trigger on the `getConnectionFromSlot` command path would bypass the executor's existing throttling. We took the safe short-term fix (#4555, expose a manual refresh) and deferred the real redesign here. See also the existing TODO at `ClusterCommandExecutor.java:338`.

## Explore how to 

Introduce a single component that owns refresh *policy* (separate from `JedisClusterInfoCache`, which owns the topology *data*):

- **Grace period / rate limit** — minimum interval between reactive refreshes
- **Configurable** thresholds/intervals.

## Goals

- Eliminate renewal storms without losing self-healing responsiveness.
- Consolidate the scattered triggers behind one policy.
- Keep the manual `refreshClusterTopology()` (#4555) as a thin entry into the same path.

## References

- #4154, #4544, #4555
- TODO: `ClusterCommandExecutor.java:338`

## Summary

The scenario tests added in #4707 do not exercise the fault injector's `maintenance_mode` trigger (`data_movement_conn_drop` / `maintenance_mode`). The trigger leaves the node in maintenance mode, which makes the following tests on the same environment fail with `Target node cannot accommodate [...]`. Other clients' maintenance-notification tests do not exercise it either. This issue tracks a dedicated test with a verified cleanup.

## Proposed change

- After each `maintenance_mode` test and after the test database is deleted, call the fault injector's `reset_cluster` action with only `clean_maintenance_mode` set, and fail if any node is reported as not reset (`nodes_failed`). This is awaited and verified, unlike the trigger's `automatically_clean_mm` flag, which restores the node from a background 10 s timer with no confirmation.
- Add `FaultInjectorClient#clearMaintenanceMode()` for that call.
- Add the trigger to `MaintNotificationsIT.movingScenarios()` and restore it in `MaintenanceTrafficResilienceIT.scenarios()`.

## Acceptance criteria

- The `maintenance_mode` scenario passes in both tests.
- No node remains in maintenance mode afterwards; teardown fails loudly otherwise.

body_text:
## Bug Report

#### Current Behavior

Lettuce can repeatedly reuse a stale physical cluster connection when AWS ElastiCache replaces nodes while retaining the same node DNS names.

During a node-type change, ElastiCache can temporarily advertise two different node IDs for the same hostname and port: an old node and its replacement. DNS for that hostname changes to the replacement IP, but an existing Lettuce connection can remain connected to the old IP.

When the role moves to the replacement node:

1. The old node returns `MOVED` with the same stable hostname.
2. Lettuce retries using that hostname and port.
3. The existing cached connection for that endpoint is reused without a new DNS resolution.
4. The retry reaches the old node and receives `MOVED` again.
5. Adaptive and periodic topology refreshes run and discover the new node IDs, but do not replace the stale physical connection.

This is consistently reproduced only on the **second consecutive resize without restarting the client**:

- Resize 1: 28,204 internally handled `MOVED`; zero surfaced failures.
- Resize 2: 7,697,720 additional internally handled `MOVED` and **1,539,725 surfaced `MOVED` failures**.
- Failure window: approximately 6 minutes 25 seconds, about 4,000 surfaced failures per second.
- All ten workers were affected while the shared cluster connection remained open.
- No data mismatches occurred.

Tested and reproduced in Lettuce `6.3.2.RELEASE`. The client recovers only after the old sockets disconnect and normal reconnect resolves the stable hostnames to the replacement IPs.

Example masked topology during replacement:

```text
id=<old-node-id> uri=redis://cache-node-0003-002.<cluster-domain>:6379 flags=[SLAVE, REPLICA]
id=<new-node-id> uri=redis://cache-node-0003-002.<cluster-domain>:6379 flags=[MASTER]
```

Example connection transition when recovery finally occurs:

```text
DisconnectedEvent [... -> cache-node-0003-002.<cluster-domain>/10.x.x.211:6379]
ConnectedEvent    [... -> cache-node-0003-002.<cluster-domain>/10.x.x.221:6379]
```

<summary>Stack trace</summary>

</details>

#### Input Code

<details>
<summary>Input Code</summary>

```java
Security.setProperty("networkaddress.cache.ttl", "5");

Duration timeout = Duration.ofSeconds(5);
RedisURI seed = RedisURI.builder()
        .withHost("<configuration-endpoint>")
        .withPort(6379)
        .withSsl(true)
        .withTimeout(timeout)
        .build();

ClientResources resources = ClientResources.builder()
        .socketAddressResolver(SocketAddressResolver.create(
                new DirContextDnsResolver()))
        .build();

RedisClusterClient client = RedisClusterClient.create(resources, List.of(seed));

ClusterTopologyRefreshOptions refreshOptions =
        ClusterTopologyRefreshOptions.builder()
                .enableAllAdaptiveRefreshTriggers()
                .enablePeriodicRefresh(Duration.ofSeconds(30))
                .dynamicRefreshSources(true)
                .closeStaleConnections(true)
                .build();

ClusterClientOptions options = ClusterClientOptions.builder()
        .topologyRefreshOptions(refreshOptions)
        .socketOptions(SocketOptions.builder()
                .connectTimeout(timeout.dividedBy(2))
                .keepAlive(true)
                .build())
        .autoReconnect(true)
        .validateClusterNodeMembership(false)
        .build();

client.setOptions(options);

// One thread-safe connection is shared by all ten workers.
StatefulRedisClusterConnection<String, String> connection = client.connect();
RedisAdvancedClusterCommands<String, String> commands = connection.sync();

// Each worker performs 1,000 idempotent SET/GET cycles per second.
commands.set(key, value);
String actual = commands.get(key);
```

Reproduction procedure:

1. Start the client against a TLS-enabled, three-shard cluster with one replica per shard.
2. Keep the same client process and shared connection running throughout the test.
3. Change the node type from size A to size B and wait until the cluster is available.
4. Without restarting the client, change the node type from size B back to size A.
5. Observe repeated surfaced `MOVED` failures during the second replacement.

</details>

#### Expected behavior/code

After topology identifies a replacement node—or after a command receives repeated `MOVED` responses for the same target—Lettuce should verify that the cached connection still represents the expected node generation.

A stable hostname and port should not by themselves establish that an existing physical connection is valid when the node ID, role, resolved address, or channel generation has changed.

The client should establish a connection to the replacement node without waiting for AWS to close the old socket. Concurrent commands should not be failed unnecessarily, and delayed callbacks from an old channel must not disconnect a newer channel.

#### Environment

- Lettuce versions: `6.3.2.RELEASE`, official `7.7.0.RELEASE`
- Runtime: Java 17
- Service: AWS ElastiCache cluster mode enabled, TLS
- Engine: Valkey/Redis 7 compatible
- Topology: three shards, one replica per shard
- Routing: default upstream/write routing
- One shared `StatefulRedisClusterConnection` across ten worker threads
- `autoReconnect=true`
- All adaptive refresh triggers enabled
- Periodic topology refresh every 30 seconds
- `dynamicRefreshSources=true`
- Java DNS cache TTL: 5 seconds

#### Possible Solution

Cached cluster connections should carry identity beyond hostname and port, including the expected node ID, routing role/intent, resolved remote address, and physical channel generation.

When a repeated `MOVED` indicates that a connection still reaches an old node, Lettuce could:

1. Atomically stop routing new commands to the expected stale generation.
2. Resolve the hostname again and establish a replacement generation.
3. Ensure a delayed callback can retire only the physical generation that dispatched the redirected command.
4. Allow already-sent commands on the old channel to drain, with a bounded retirement timeout.
5. Route redirected commands through the replacement connection.

A forced disconnect and auto-reconnect prototype eliminated surfaced `MOVED` failures in this workload, but it can replay commands whose server-side outcome is unknown. Therefore, blindly reconnecting and resending is not generally safe for non-idempotent commands. A production fix should explicitly preserve or document the resulting delivery semantics.

#### Additional context

The first resize succeeding is not evidence that the issue is fixed. At startup, write connections existed for the original master endpoint names. The first resize promoted the alternate endpoint names, causing cache misses and fresh DNS resolution. The second resize promoted the original names again, at which point cached connections for those stable names still targeted the previous physical nodes.

`MOVED_REDIRECT` adaptive refresh events occurred throughout the failure window, and topology updates contained the new node IDs. This indicates that adaptive refresh was triggered correctly; refreshed metadata still led to reuse of the stale host/port connection.

The redirect counters stopped increasing immediately after the final old channel disconnected and reconnected to the replacement address.

The test used only idempotent `SET`/`GET` operations.

        .withHost("<configuration-endpoint>")
        .withPort(6379)
        .withSsl(true)
        .withTimeout(timeout)
        .build();

ClientResources resources = ClientResources.builder()
        .socketAddressResolver(SocketAddressResolver.create(
                new DirContextDnsResolver()))
        .build();

RedisClusterClient client = RedisClusterClient.create(resources, List.of(seed));

ClusterTopologyRefreshOptions refreshOptions =
        ClusterTopologyRefreshOptions.builder()
                .enableAllAdaptiveRefreshTriggers()
                .enablePeriodicRefresh(Duration.ofSeconds(30))
                .dynamicRefreshSources(true)
                .closeStaleConnections(true)
                .build();

ClusterClientOptions options = ClusterClientOptions.builder()
        .topologyRefreshOptions(refreshOptions)
        .socketOptions(SocketOptions.builder()
                .connectTimeout(timeout.dividedBy(2))
                .keepAlive(true)
                .build())
        .autoReconnect(true)
        .validateClusterNodeMembership(false)
        .build();

client.setOptions(options);

// One thread-safe connection is shared by all ten workers.
StatefulRedisClusterConnection<String, String> connection = client.connect();
RedisAdvancedClusterCommands<String, String> commands = connection.sync();

// Each worker performs 1,000 idempotent SET/GET cycles per second.
commands.set(key, value);
String actual = commands.get(key);
```

Reproduction procedure:

1. Start the client against a TLS-enabled, three-shard cluster with one replica per shard.
2. Keep the same client process and shared connection running throughout the test.
3. Change the node type from size A to size B and wait until the cluster is available.
4. Without restarting the client, change the node type from size B back to size A.
5. Observe repeated surfaced `MOVED` failures during the second replacement.

</details>

#### Expected behavior/code

After topology identifies a replacement node—or after a command receives repeated `MOVED` responses for the same target—Lettuce should verify that the cached connection still represents the expected node generation.

A stable hostname and port should not by themselves establish that an existing physical connection is valid when the node ID, role, resolved address, or channel generation has changed.

The client should establish a connection to the replacement node without waiting for AWS to close the old socket. Concurrent commands should not be failed unnecessarily, and delayed callbacks from an old channel must not disconnect a newer channel.

#### Environment

- Lettuce versions: `6.3.2.RELEASE`, official `7.7.0.RELEASE`
- Runtime: Java 17
- Service: AWS ElastiCache cluster mode enabled, TLS
- Engine: Valkey/Redis 7 compatible
- Topology: three shards, one replica per shard
- Routing: default upstream/write routing
- One shared `StatefulRedisClusterConnection` across ten worker threads
- `autoReconnect=true`
- All adaptive refresh triggers enabled
- Periodic topology refresh every 30 seconds
- `dynamicRefreshSources=true`
- Java DNS cache TTL: 5 seconds

#### Possible Solution

Cached cluster connections should carry identity beyond hostname and port, including the expected node ID, routing role/intent, resolved remote address, and physical channel generation.

When a repeated `MOVED` indicates that a connection still reaches an old node, Lettuce could:

1. Atomically stop routing new commands to the expected stale generation.
2. Resolve the hostname again and establish a replacement generation.
3. Ensure a delayed callback can retire only the physical generation that dispatched the redirected command.
4. Allow already-sent commands on the old channel to drain, with a bounded retirement timeout.
5. Route redirected commands through the replacement connection.

A forced disconnect and auto-reconnect prototype eliminated surfaced `MOVED` failures in this workload, but it can replay commands whose server-side outcome is unknown. Therefore, blindly reconnecting and resending is not generally safe for non-idempotent commands. A production fix should explicitly preserve or document the resulting delivery semantics.

#### Additional context

The first resize succeeding is not evidence that the issue is fixed. At startup, write connections existed for the original master endpoint names. The first resize promoted the alternate endpoint names, causing cache misses and fresh DNS resolution. The second resize promoted the original names again, at which point cached connections for those stable names still targeted the previous physical nodes.

`MOVED_REDIRECT` adaptive refresh events occurred throughout the failure window, and topology updates contained the new node IDs. This indicates that adaptive refresh was triggered correctly; refreshed metadata still led to reuse of the stale host/port connection.

The redirect counters stopped increasing immediately after the final old channel disconnected and reconnected to the replacement address.

The test used only idempotent `SET`/`GET` operations. body_text:
### Redis version

7.2.16

### Redisson version

3.52.0

### Redisson configuration

```java
Config config = new Config();
config.useReplicatedServers()
      .addNodeAddress("redis://<endpoint>:6379")
      .setReadMode(ReadMode.MASTER)
      .setTimeout(3000)
      .setRetryAttempts(4);
// lockWatchdogTimeout default 30000
RLock lock = redisson.getLock("mylock");
if (lock.tryLock(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
    try { ... } finally { lock.unlock(); }
}
```

### What is the Expected behavior?

The lock acquire script runs at most once on Redis per `tryLock()` call. If Redis answers after `timeout`, either the call fails with `RedisResponseTimeoutException` (as it does in single server mode) or it succeeds with `getHoldCount() == 1`. One `unlock()` then releases the lock.

### What is the Actual behavior?

In replicated servers mode, when Redis answers the acquire EVALSHA later than `timeout`, Redisson cancels the attempt and sends the same EVALSHA again after the retry delay. Redis executes the script twice. The second execution finds the hash field `<clientId>:<threadId>` already present and takes the reentrant `hincrby` branch. One `tryLock()` returns `true` with `getHoldCount() == 2`.

The caller calls `unlock()` once, the hash field stays at 1 and the key stays locked. Every later `tryLock()` by the same thread is reentrant and refreshes `pexpire`, so as long as the owning thread keeps using the lock (a scheduler thread in our case) the phantom hold never expires. All other threads time out on `tryLock()` until the key is deleted by hand. We had this in production for several hours.

`redis-cli MONITOR` during the reproducer below, one `tryLock()` on the Java side:

```text
1790065841.836655 [0 172.17.0.1:56760] "EVALSHA" "149c5a8bf18676fd99e9e6e24923bd64d9b62f94" "1" "[test]f20c96e9-..." "30000" "92c2ec07-...:1"
1790065843.153746 [0 172.17.0.1:56760] "EVALSHA" "149c5a8bf18676fd99e9e6e24923bd64d9b62f94" "1" "[test]f20c96e9-..." "30000" "92c2ec07-...:1"
```

Same script, same key, same `<clientId>:<threadId>`, same connection, 1.3 s apart (timeout 1000 ms + retry delay 200 ms + round trip). `HGETALL` of the key afterwards returns the field with value `2`.

The same test with `useSingleServer()` behaves as expected: `tryLock()` throws `RedisResponseTimeoutException`, the EVALSHA is sent once, the hash holds at most 1.

### Additional information

**Where I believe the resend comes from.** `RedissonLock.tryLockInnerAsync` goes through `RedissonBaseLock.evalWriteSyncedNoRetryAsync` → `CommandAsyncService.syncedEvalNoRetry`, so the intent is clearly that the acquire script is never resent. The `retry=false` flag is honoured in the single server branch but lost in the batch branch:

- [`CommandAsyncService.syncedEval` 3.52.0, L1062-L1073](https://github.com/redisson/redisson/blob/3d8945a7225a8909f5ffa8000e81dab193760e43/redisson/src/main/java/org/redisson/command/CommandAsyncService.java#L1062-L1073): `isSingleConfig()` → `evalWriteNoRetryAsync` when `retry` is false.
- [same method, L1164-L1165](https://github.com/redisson/redisson/blob/3d8945a7225a8909f5ffa8000e81dab193760e43/redisson/src/main/java/org/redisson/command/CommandAsyncService.java#L1164-L1165): all other modes create a `CommandBatchService` and call `executorService.evalWriteAsync(...)`; `retry` is not passed on.
- [`CommandBatchService` 3.52.0, L482-L483](https://github.com/redisson/redisson/blob/3d8945a7225a8909f5ffa8000e81dab193760e43/redisson/src/main/java/org/redisson/command/CommandBatchService.java#L482-L483): `new RedisCommonBatchExecutor(..., referenceType, false)`, `noRetry` hard-coded to `false`.
- [`RedisExecutor.isResendAllowed` 3.52.0, L485-L489](https://github.com/redisson/redisson/blob/3d8945a7225a8909f5ffa8000e81dab193760e43/redisson/src/main/java/org/redisson/command/RedisExecutor.java#L485-L489): `attempt < attempts && !noRetry && (command == null || ...)`. The batch executor has `command == null`, so the per-command `isNoRetry()` check is skipped as well.

body_text:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

Since 3.52.0 the connection pool hands out the most recently released connection first (#5151, #6768). That works well for idle discard, but it interacts badly with response timeouts: when an attempt times out, its connection is released to the head of the free deque, so the retry scheduled `retryInterval` later polls that same connection again, unless another command happened to release one in between. New commands are handed the stalled connection the same way. Of course, a timeout does not necessarily mean a stalled connection, and the connection could well serve the next command well. But to try and handle _possibly stalled_ connections better, we might want to enqueue at the back.

We see this in production on 3.52.0 (single server mode, AWS ElastiCache Serverless, `timeout=500`, `retryAttempts=3`, `retryInterval=100`, `connectionPoolSize=connectionMinimumIdleSize=32`). Occasionally one client stops getting responses for 7–24s while other clients connected to the same server IP keep working. Every `RedisResponseTimeoutException` from the affected client reports `after 3 of 3 retry attempts`, and the channel in the message, which is the connection the final attempt used, is the **same** one every time.

LIFO release is a possible explanation why the final attempt keeps landing on the stalled one.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Keep LIFO for healthy connections, but release a connection whose attempt ended in a response timeout to the **tail** of the free deque instead of the head. The retry, and other new commands, then get a different connection, while #5151's idle-discard behaviour is preserved.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

- Closing the connection on response timeout: stronger, but more reconnect churn, and a slow response doesn't always mean the connection is broken.
- `pingConnectionInterval`: we saw no failed pings during these stalls, and lowering the interval would at best shorten a stall rather than let the retry avoid it.
- Pinning a version before 3.52.0 (round-robin): loses the idle-discard fix (though might be viable in our case since we set min=max connections).

**Expected behavior**

After a slot is migrated to another master (e.g. online resharding / scale-out of a Redis Cluster), listeners of `RShardedTopic` and `RLocalCachedMap` (which uses a sharded topic when sharding is supported) keep receiving messages.

**Actual behavior**

Listeners on channels whose slot was migrated stop receiving messages forever. For `RLocalCachedMap` with `SyncStrategy.UPDATE`/`INVALIDATE`, the local cache on other instances is never updated again until the application restarts. `PUBSUB SHARDNUMSUB` on the new owner of the slot shows 0 subscribers.

**Root cause**

`PublishSubscribeService.reattachPubSub(int slot)` resubscribes sharded channels with `codec` (the codec of the *regular* channel, which is always `null` for a sharded channel) instead of `scodec`:

```java
Codec scodec = pubSubEntry.getConnection().getShardedChannels().get(entry.getKey().getChannelName());
if (scodec != null) {
    Queue<RedisPubSubListener<?>> listeners = pubSubEntry.getListeners(entry.getKey().getChannelName());
    unsubscribe(entry.getKey().getChannelName(), pubSubEntry, PubSubType.SUNSUBSCRIBE);
    ssubscribe(codec, ChannelName.newList(entry.getKey().getChannelName()), listeners.toArray(new RedisPubSubListener[0]));
    //         ^^^^^ null here, should be scodec
}
```

`RedisPubSubConnection.ssubscribe()` puts the codec into a `ConcurrentHashMap`, which throws `NullPointerException` for a null value, so the resubscription fails after the old subscription has already been removed. Nothing retries it.

**Steps to reproduce or test case**

1. Redis 7+ cluster (3 masters), `shardedSubscriptionMode` = `AUTO` (default).
2. Two Redisson clients `A` and `B`, both get `RLocalCachedMap` with `SyncStrategy.UPDATE` (or `RShardedTopic` with a listener on `B`).
3. `A` keeps writing to the map / publishing.
4. Migrate the slot of the map/channel to another master (`CLUSTER SETSLOT ... IMPORTING/MIGRATING/NODE`, or `redis-cli --cluster reshard`).
5. `B` no longer receives updates; its local cache stays stale indefinitely.

A test case (`RedissonShardedTopicTest.testSlotMigrationInCluster`, mirroring the existing `RedissonTopicTest.testSlotMigrationInCluster`) is included in the PR.

**Redis version**

7.0.10 (also reproduced locally with 7.2)

**Redisson version**

3.52.0, and the code is unchanged on current `master`.

**Redisson configuration**

Cluster servers config, `subscriptionMode: MASTER`, `readMode: MASTER`, `scanInterval: 1000`, default `shardedSubscriptionMode`.

**Workaround**

Set `shardedSubscriptionMode: OFF` (on all instances at once) or restart the application after resharding.

body_text:
### Summary: 
If Redis/Valkey rejects writes for a short time (for example while a replica reconnects), an RReliableTopic listener can stop receiving messages forever. Redisson tries once to refresh the subscriber's registration or status, and if that one attempt fails it never tries again. The listener then quietly stops reading. No error reaches the application, and messages pile up unread until the service is restarted.

### Expected behavior

A transient write failure, such as `NOREPLICAS` while a replica reconnects, should not permanently stop an `RReliableTopic` listener. Once the server accepts writes again, the subscriber should keep its registration (or re-create it) and keep consuming messages.

### Actual behavior

There are two related failure paths in `RedissonReliableTopic`. Both stop the poll loop permanently. No exception reaches the caller, and the subscriber still looks registered until it dies.

**1. A failed watchdog renewal is never rescheduled.**
`renewExpiration()` reschedules itself only when the renewal succeeds. When the renewal script fails, for example with `NOREPLICAS`, it logs this once and never renews again:

```
ERROR org.redisson.RedissonReliableTopic - Can't update reliable topic testFailedRenewal expiration time
org.redisson.client.RedisNoReplicasException: NOREPLICAS Not enough good replicas to write. script: 422be3f551b99935463b2c32454148831f31afd9, on @user_script:1..
```

The subscriber's score in `{<name>}:timeout` stops moving and expires after `reliableTopicWatchdogTimeout`. Nothing is visible yet: the blocked `XREADGROUP` still delivers.

On the next message, the listener receives it. Then the post-poll status-update script runs `zrangebyscore … 0 now-1`, finds the subscriber's own expired id, and destroys its own consumer group. With no groups left, `score` stays `92233720368547758`. Lua 5.1 `tostring()` formats that as `9.2233720368548e+16`, so the script calls `XRANGE <stream> 9.2233720368548e+16-0 +`, and that fails:

```
ERROR org.redisson.RedissonReliableTopic - Unable to update subscriber status
org.redisson.client.RedisException: ERR Invalid stream ID specified as stream command argument script: e584bfe0230f6e59051ef5a8a125585d0f7f1c94, on @user_script:1..
```

The `updateFuture` error branch returns without calling `poll(id)`, so the subscriber is dead. Later messages stay unread in the stream. The topic now has no consumer group and no `{name}:timeout` entry, but `listeners` still contains the listener, and `subscribed` is still `true`, so `addListener` on the same instance will not re-subscribe.

(You can confirm the formatting with `EVAL "return tostring(92233720368547758) .. '-0'" 0`, which returns `9.2233720368548e+16-0`.)

**2. A failed status update stops polling even if renewals keep working.**
This needs no renewal failure. Any single failure of the post-poll update script stops polling, because `poll(id)` is not rescheduled after "Unable to update subscriber status". In the test below it is `NOPERM` for a few ms:

```
ERROR org.redisson.RedissonReliableTopic - Unable to update subscriber status
org.redisson.client.RedisException: NOPERM User default has no permissions to run the 'evalsha' command.
```

Renewals keep succeeding, so the consumer group and the `{name}:timeout` entry stay valid and unexpired. The subscriber looks healthy, but it never reads again: `last-delivered-id` stays put while the stream grows.

These look like modes 5 and 6 in the contributor analysis on #7262 (Aug 22), which were listed as not covered by #7263, #7310 or #7300. #7299 / #7300 (4.8.0) fixed only the listener-exception path. Both tests below still fail on 4.8.0.

### Steps to reproduce or test case
See attachment

[reproduce.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33535783/reproduce.zip)


### Redis version

Production: Valkey 8.1.10, cluster mode, TLS, 1 primary + 1 replica, `min-replicas-to-write 1`, `min-replicas-max-lag 10`. Reproduced with the tests above on `redis:8.10` and `valkey/valkey:8.1.10-alpine3.24`, standalone.

### Redisson version

Reproduced on 4.8.0.

### Redisson configuration

Production: `ClusterServersConfig`, `readMode = MASTER`, TLS (mTLS with short-lived client certificates), default `reliableTopicWatchdogTimeout` (600 000 ms). Tests: single server, default config, `reliableTopicWatchdogTimeout = 3000` for the renewal test.

Production trigger: a replica lost its replication link for about 4 minutes, so writes were rejected with `NOREPLICAS`. Every reliable-topic subscriber across several services logged "Can't update reliable topic … expiration time" in that window. Then each one died on its first message after expiry, up to 23 hours later. Only a restart recovered them.

A transient write failure, such as `NOREPLICAS` while a replica reconnects, should not permanently stop an `RReliableTopic` listener. Once the server accepts writes again, the subscriber should keep its registration (or re-create it) and keep consuming messages.

### Actual behavior

There are two related failure paths in `RedissonReliableTopic`. Both stop the poll loop permanently. No exception reaches the caller, and the subscriber still looks registered until it dies.

**1. A failed watchdog renewal is never rescheduled.**
`renewExpiration()` reschedules itself only when the renewal succeeds. When the renewal script fails, for example with `NOREPLICAS`, it logs this once and never renews again:

```
ERROR org.redisson.RedissonReliableTopic - Can't update reliable topic testFailedRenewal expiration time
org.redisson.client.RedisNoReplicasException: NOREPLICAS Not enough good replicas to write. script: 422be3f551b99935463b2c32454148831f31afd9, on @user_script:1..
```

The subscriber's score in `{<name>}:timeout` stops moving and expires after `reliableTopicWatchdogTimeout`. Nothing is visible yet: the blocked `XREADGROUP` still delivers.

On the next message, the listener receives it. Then the post-poll status-update script runs `zrangebyscore … 0 now-1`, finds the subscriber's own expired id, and destroys its own consumer group. With no groups left, `score` stays `92233720368547758`. Lua 5.1 `tostring()` formats that as `9.2233720368548e+16`, so the script calls `XRANGE <stream> 9.2233720368548e+16-0 +`, and that fails:

```
ERROR org.redisson.RedissonReliableTopic - Unable to update subscriber status
org.redisson.client.RedisException: ERR Invalid stream ID specified as stream command argument script: e584bfe0230f6e59051ef5a8a125585d0f7f1c94, on @user_script:1..
```

The `updateFuture` error branch returns without calling `poll(id)`, so the subscriber is dead. Later messages stay unread in the stream. The topic now has no consumer group and no `{name}:timeout` entry, but `listeners` still contains the listener, and `subscribed` is still `true`, so `addListener` on the same instance will not re-subscribe.

(You can confirm the formatting with `EVAL "return tostring(92233720368547758) .. '-0'" 0`, which returns `9.2233720368548e+16-0`.)

**2. A failed status update stops polling even if renewals keep working.**
This needs no renewal failure. Any single failure of the post-poll update script stops polling, because `poll(id)` is not rescheduled after "Unable to update subscriber status". In the test below it is `NOPERM` for a few ms:

```
ERROR org.redisson.RedissonReliableTopic - Unable to update subscriber status
org.redisson.client.RedisException: NOPERM User default has no permissions to run the 'evalsha' command.
```

Renewals keep succeeding, so the consumer group and the `{name}:timeout` entry stay valid and unexpired. The subscriber looks healthy, but it never reads again: `last-delivered-id` stays put while the stream grows.

These look like modes 5 and 6 in the contributor analysis on #7262 (Aug 22), which were listed as not covered by #7263, #7310 or #7300. #7299 / #7300 (4.8.0) fixed only the listener-exception path. Both tests below still fail on 4.8.0.

### Steps to reproduce or test case
See attachment

[reproduce.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33535783/reproduce.zip)


### Redis version

Production: Valkey 8.1.10, cluster mode, TLS, 1 primary + 1 replica, `min-replicas-to-write 1`, `min-replicas-max-lag 10`. Reproduced with the tests above on `redis:8.10` and `valkey/valkey:8.1.10-alpine3.24`, standalone.

### Redisson version

Reproduced on 4.8.0.

### Redisson configuration

Production: `ClusterServersConfig`, `readMode = MASTER`, TLS (mTLS with short-lived client certificates), default `reliableTopicWatchdogTimeout` (600 000 ms). Tests: single server, default config, `reliableTopicWatchdogTimeout = 3000` for the renewal test.

Production trigger: a replica lost its replication link for about 4 minutes, so writes were rejected with `NOREPLICAS`. Every reliable-topic subscriber across several services logged "Can't update reliable topic … expiration time" in that window. Then each one died on its first message after expiry, up to 23 hours later. Only a restart recovered them.

### Reproduction

## Reproduction

Minimal reproduction repo: https://github.com/Duduceretta/react-router-link-freeze-repro (mirrors the nested `createBrowserRouter` guard→layout→page structure and the persistent sidebar `<Link>` items described below; README has exact repro steps).

Steps that reproduce reliably in the full app:

- `react-router-dom`: `7.18.3`
- `react` / `react-dom`: `19.x`
- App structure: `createBrowserRouter` with nested routes — `ProtectedRoute` (auth guard using `useLocation()` + `Navigate`) → layout route (persistent sidebar + `<Outlet/>`, itself using `useLocation()` and a `useEffect` keyed on `location.pathname`) → leaf page routes.
- Sidebar renders several `<Link to={itemPath}>` items; each real mouse click on a different item navigates to a different leaf route.
- Click real, physical mouse clicks on 2+ different sidebar `<Link>` items back-to-back, as fast as physically possible, for ~10-20 clicks. The tab becomes unresponsive to further input (clicks, and even opening/using DevTools on that tab) for many seconds.

### What did NOT reproduce it

- A flat `createBrowserRouter` with 2 routes and no nested layout/guard, navigating via `router.navigate()` in a plain `<button onClick>` (no `<Link>` involved) — clicked as fast as physically possible, never froze.
- Removing every custom side-effect layer we had (a SignalR listener, several `useEffect`s, a custom ripple effect, various context providers) while still using `<Link>` for navigation — still froze.
- Programmatic/synthetic clicks (`element.click()`, CDP-driven automation) never reproduced this at all, even at a much higher rate than physically possible with a mouse. Only real, physical rapid mouse clicks reproduce it.

### What DID resolve it

Replacing `<Link to={item.path}>` with:

```tsx
const navigate = useNavigate();
<button type="button" onClick={() => { if (!isActive) navigate(item.path); }}>
  ...
</button>
```

No other change. Same routes, same layout, same guards. This alone made the freeze stop occurring, tested with 30+ real rapid clicks across every route, repeatedly.

We also tried `<RouterProvider useTransitions={false}>`, which measurably reduced (but did not eliminate) the accumulated work — only combined with the `<Link>` → `<button>` swap did the freeze fully disappear.

### System Info

```shell
## System Info


System:
  OS: Windows 11 10.0.22631
  CPU: (12) x64 12th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-12450H
  Memory: 2.91 GB / 15.71 GB
Binaries:
  Node: 24.16.0
  npm: 11.17.0
Browsers:
  Edge: Chromium (152.0.4191.53)
npmPackages:
  react: 19.2.8
  react-dom: 19.2.8
  react-router-dom: 7.18.3
  vite: 8.2.2
```

### Used Package Manager

npm

### Expected Behavior

## Expected Behavior

Rapid repeated clicks on different `<Link>` targets should be coalesced/interrupted the same way rapid `navigate()` calls apparently are — not accumulate into a backlog that takes over a minute (relative to the ~10s input burst) to drain, and never freeze the tab's responsiveness to unrelated input (scrolling kept working throughout; only click handling and page reactivity stalled).

### Actual Behavior

## Actual Behavior

Clicking a `<Link to={path}>` repeatedly and rapidly (dozens of clicks in a few seconds, real mouse clicks — not synthetic/programmatic ones) causes the entire tab to stop responding to input for many seconds, with **no console error, no unhandled rejection, and low CPU usage** on the affected thread. The page eventually recovers on its own after ~15-25s without any further interaction.

### Performance trace findings

We captured a ~30s Chrome Performance trace spanning the freeze. Key findings:

- CPU usage stayed low throughout (confirmed via both the trace and the OS Task Manager) — this is a single-thread saturation issue, not a busy CPU-bound loop, which is why total system CPU looked unremarkable on a multi-core machine.
- The renderer main thread had **no idle gaps larger than ~800ms** across the entire 30s window — it was continuously processing work.
- We stopped clicking at ~9.6s into the recording (36 real clicks total), but `RunTask` events on the main thread continued at a high, roughly constant rate (150-250 tasks per 500ms bucket) for **another ~16 seconds** after input stopped, only tapering off around the 25.5s mark.
- Interestingly, opening/using Chrome DevTools' "inspect element" tool against the frozen tab also failed to respond during the freeze (it depends on the same main thread), even though `document.elementFromPoint()` executed from an already-open Console (attached before the freeze) returned correctly and `1+1` evaluated fine in that Console — so the JS engine itself wasn't deadlocked; it was continuously busy processing a backlog that outlived the input by more than a minute of wall-clock ratio to the input window.

We don't have a minimal reproduction narrowed down to a single React Router internal yet (we found this via progressive app-level isolation, not by reading the router's source), but the shape of the evidence (continuous, non-blocking-looking work that vastly outlives the triggering input, present with `<Link>` and absent with an equivalent `navigate()` call in a plain event handler) points at something in `<Link>`'s click handling / transition scheduling accumulating faster than it can drain under a burst of rapid real clicks.

## Additional context

Happy to share the full captured trace JSON (~55MB uncompressed) and a minimal repro repo if useful — let us know the preferred way to share a large trace file on this tracker.

[Trace-20260913T133445.json.gz](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32165841/Trace-20260913T133445.json.gz)

## Reproduction

Minimal reproduction repo: https://github.com/Duduceretta/react-router-link-freeze-repro (mirrors the nested `createBrowserRouter` guard→layout→page structure and the persistent sidebar `<Link>` items described below; README has exact repro steps).

Steps that reproduce reliably in the full app:

- `react-router-dom`: `7.18.3`
- `react` / `react-dom`: `19.x`
- App structure: `createBrowserRouter` with nested routes — `ProtectedRoute` (auth guard using `useLocation()` + `Navigate`) → layout route (persistent sidebar + `<Outlet/>`, itself using `useLocation()` and a `useEffect` keyed on `location.pathname`) → leaf page routes.
- Sidebar renders several `<Link to={itemPath}>` items; each real mouse click on a different item navigates to a different leaf route.
- Click real, physical mouse clicks on 2+ different sidebar `<Link>` items back-to-back, as fast as physically possible, for ~10-20 clicks. The tab becomes unresponsive to further input (clicks, and even opening/using DevTools on that tab) for many seconds.

### What did NOT reproduce it

- A flat `createBrowserRouter` with 2 routes and no nested layout/guard, navigating via `router.navigate()` in a plain `<button onClick>` (no `<Link>` involved) — clicked as fast as physically possible, never froze.
- Removing every custom side-effect layer we had (a SignalR listener, several `useEffect`s, a custom ripple effect, various context providers) while still using `<Link>` for navigation — still froze.
- Programmatic/synthetic clicks (`element.click()`, CDP-driven automation) never reproduced this at all, even at a much higher rate than physically possible with a mouse. Only real, physical rapid mouse clicks reproduce it.

### What DID resolve it

Replacing `<Link to={item.path}>` with:

```tsx
const navigate = useNavigate();
<button type="button" onClick={() => { if (!isActive) navigate(item.path); }}>
  ...
</button>
```

No other change. Same routes, same layout, same guards. This alone made the freeze stop occurring, tested with 30+ real rapid clicks across every route, repeatedly.

We also tried `<RouterProvider useTransitions={false}>`, which measurably reduced (but did not eliminate) the accumulated work — only combined with the `<Link>` → `<button>` swap did the freeze fully disappear.

### System Info

```shell

  Memory: 2.91 GB / 15.71 GB
