  npm: 11.17.0
Browsers:
  Edge: Chromium (152.0.4191.53)
npmPackages:
  react: 19.2.8
  react-dom: 19.2.8
  react-router-dom: 7.18.3
  vite: 8.2.2
```

### Used Package Manager

npm

### Expected Behavior

## Expected Behavior

Rapid repeated clicks on different `<Link>` targets should be coalesced/interrupted the same way rapid `navigate()` calls apparently are — not accumulate into a backlog that takes over a minute (relative to the ~10s input burst) to drain, and never freeze the tab's responsiveness to unrelated input (scrolling kept working throughout; only click handling and page reactivity stalled).

### Actual Behavior

## Actual Behavior

Clicking a `<Link to={path}>` repeatedly and rapidly (dozens of clicks in a few seconds, real mouse clicks — not synthetic/programmatic ones) causes the entire tab to stop responding to input for many seconds, with **no console error, no unhandled rejection, and low CPU usage** on the affected thread. The page eventually recovers on its own after ~15-25s without any further interaction.

### Performance trace findings

We captured a ~30s Chrome Performance trace spanning the freeze. Key findings:

- CPU usage stayed low throughout (confirmed via both the trace and the OS Task Manager) — this is a single-thread saturation issue, not a busy CPU-bound loop, which is why total system CPU looked unremarkable on a multi-core machine.
- The renderer main thread had **no idle gaps larger than ~800ms** across the entire 30s window — it was continuously processing work.
- We stopped clicking at ~9.6s into the recording (36 real clicks total), but `RunTask` events on the main thread continued at a high, roughly constant rate (150-250 tasks per 500ms bucket) for **another ~16 seconds** after input stopped, only tapering off around the 25.5s mark.
- Interestingly, opening/using Chrome DevTools' "inspect element" tool against the frozen tab also failed to respond during the freeze (it depends on the same main thread), even though `document.elementFromPoint()` executed from an already-open Console (attached before the freeze) returned correctly and `1+1` evaluated fine in that Console — so the JS engine itself wasn't deadlocked; it was continuously busy processing a backlog that outlived the input by more than a minute of wall-clock ratio to the input window.

We don't have a minimal reproduction narrowed down to a single React Router internal yet (we found this via progressive app-level isolation, not by reading the router's source), but the shape of the evidence (continuous, non-blocking-looking work that vastly outlives the triggering input, present with `<Link>` and absent with an equivalent `navigate()` call in a plain event handler) points at something in `<Link>`'s click handling / transition scheduling accumulating faster than it can drain under a burst of rapid real clicks.

## Additional context

Happy to share the full captured trace JSON (~55MB uncompressed) and a minimal repro repo if useful — let us know the preferred way to share a large trace file on this tracker.

### Reproduction

 Steps:                                                                                                                                                                        
  1. `yarn install && yarn build && yarn start`, serve over HTTP/2 (the repo includes a small h2 proxy: `yarn h2`)                                                              
  2. Open https://localhost:3443/ in Chrome, DevTools → Network, enable the "Priority" column, throttle to "Slow 4G"                                                            
  3. Reload: `<Scripts>` emits ~150 `<link rel="modulepreload">` (all **High**) that React 19 hoists into `<head>`, next to the render-blocking stylesheet                      
  4. The stylesheet finishes only after most of the JS; first paint (= LCP) waits for it                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                                
  Workaround to compare: `WORKAROUND=1 yarn start` rewrites the SSR stream to add `fetchPriority="low"` to route preloads (all except `manifest.url` and                        
  `manifest.entry.module`).                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                                                
  Our production app measurements (Lighthouse 12.8, devtools throttling: mobile, RTT 150 ms, 1.6 Mbps, 4× CPU, HTTP/2, 3 runs each; 195 modulepreloads, 104 KB gz CSS):         
                                                                                                                                                                                
  | | Default (High) | Route preloads `fetchPriority="low"` |                                                                                                                   
  |---|---|---|                                                                                                                                                                 
  | LCP − TTFB | 7544 / 7524 / 7522 ms | 1558 / 1549 / 1547 ms |                                                                                                                
  | Stylesheet load time | ~7.4 s | ~1.4 s |                                                                                                                                    
  | JS requested before stylesheet finished | ~1.1 MB | 3 files, 70 KB |                                                                                                        
  | CLS | 0.013 | 0.013 |                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                                                                                
  Trade-off: route JS arrives ~2 s later, so hydration moves later too.                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                
  Prior art: TanStack Start fixed the same issue at the framework level (TanStack/router#8546). Angular CLI hit it too (angular/angular-cli#27490). A caveat from               
  rangojs/rango#1026: don't lower the entry module, or hydration can queue behind images.

### System Info

```shell
System:                                                                                                                                                                       
    OS: macOS 15.7.2                                                                                                                                                            
    CPU: (12) arm64 Apple M4 Pro                                                                                                                                                
    Memory: 24.00 GB                                                                                                                                                            
    Shell: 5.9 - /bin/zsh                                                                                                                                                       
  Binaries:                                                                                                                                                                     
    Node: 26.4.0                                                                                                                                                                
    Yarn: 3.2.0                                                                                                                                                                 
    npm: 11.17.0                                                                                                                                                                
  Browsers:                                                                                                                                                                     
    Chrome: 155.0.8059.85                                                                                                                                                       
    Firefox: 151.0                                                                                                                                                              
    Safari: 18.6                                                                                                                                                                
  npmPackages:                                                                                                                                                                  
    @react-router/dev: 7.18.1                                                                                                                                                   
    @react-router/node: 7.18.1                                                                                                                                                  
    @react-router/serve: 7.18.1                                                                                                                                                 
    react-router: 7.18.1                                                                                                                                                        
    vite: 5.4.21                                                                                                                                                                
  Also verified: <Scripts> output is unchanged in react-router 7.18.4 and 8.5.0
```

### Used Package Manager

yarn

### Expected Behavior

 On an SSR'd document, route-module preloads shouldn't compete with render-blocking CSS for bandwidth, or at least there should be a supported way to control their priority.  
  For example:                                                                                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                                                
  - a `<Scripts>` prop: `<Scripts modulePreloadFetchPriority="low" />`, applied to entry imports + route modules but not to `manifest.url` / `manifest.entry.module`, or        
  - a per-link callback: `<Scripts getModulePreloadProps={(href) => ({ fetchPriority: "low" })} />`, or                                                                         
  - `fetchPriority="low"` by default for route preloads on SSR'd documents (as TanStack Start did), with one of the above as an escape hatch.                                   
                                                                                                                                                                                
  Hints stay in the HTML, so there's still no import waterfall; Chrome just fetches the stylesheet first. 

### Actual Behavior

 `<Scripts>` renders every module of the matched routes' static import graph as `<link rel="modulepreload">` (195 on our home page), forwarding only `crossOrigin`, `integrity`
  and `nonce`. Chrome fetches `modulepreload` at High and doesn't hold it back during "tight mode", so over HTTP/2 the render-blocking stylesheet shares one connection with ~1 
  MB of JS. On a throttled mobile profile our 104 KB (gz) stylesheet took ~7.4 s instead of ~1.4 s, and first paint/LCP waited for it, even though the server-rendered page     
  needs none of that JS to paint.                                                                                                                                               
                                                                                                                                                                                
  The only workaround today is to rewrite the SSR HTML stream in `entry.server.tsx` with a regex, which depends on `<Scripts>`' exact serialized attribute order and would break
  silently if that changes.

### Reproduction

Framework mode: https://stackblitz.com/edit/github-ov7fjxvh (scenario 1)
Data mode: https://stackblitz.com/edit/vitejs-vite-fhmxctzv (scenario 2)

Open the preview in its own tab, pick the scenario in the in-app guide and click the highlighted steps. The repro logs every `document.startViewTransition()` call with its `types`. The counts are the same without that logging (checked by observing `document.activeViewTransition` / `animationstart`) and without the guide UI.

Setup: persistent `<ViewTransition>` around `<Outlet>` in the root layout, as in the 8.5 migration guide. Animations slowed to 600 ms, `/slow` has a 300 ms loader.

Steps, framework mode, scenario 1 (plain layout, `/fast` has no loader):
1. On `/`, run `startTransition(() => { addTransitionType('forward'); navigate('/fast') })`.

Steps, data mode, scenario 2 (layout calls `useNavigation()` for a global loading indicator):
1. On `/`, `navigate('/fast')`.
2. Click `<Link to="/slow">` (route with loader).

Related proposal: #15669

### System Info

```shell
System:
    OS: Linux 5.0 undefined (StackBlitz WebContainer)
    CPU: (8) x64 Intel(R) Core(TM) i9-9880H CPU @ 2.30GHz
    Shell: 1.0 - /bin/jsh
  Binaries:
    Node: 22.22.3
    npm: 10.8.2
  npmPackages:
    react-router: 8.5.0
    react: 19.3.1
    react-dom: 19.3.1
    vite: 8.3.4
    @vitejs/plugin-react: 6.1.2
  Browsers:
    Chromium 145 (headless, Playwright)

```

### Used Package Manager

npm

### Expected Behavior

One view transition per navigation, when the new page renders, carrying the transition types added with `addTransitionType`.


### Actual Behavior

An extra view transition for the `navigation.state = "loading"` commit (URL unchanged, content unchanged). The page swap only starts after that one has finished, so the swap is delayed by the animation duration (the URL has already changed). The transition types go to the first one: the unchanged page visibly slides out and back in, then the new page cross-fades with `types: null`.

```
startViewTransition  URL /      types ["forward"]   ← navigation.state = "loading"
startViewTransition  URL /fast  types null          ← page swap, starts after the first finished
```

- **Framework mode:** every navigation, even to routes without a loader and with a plain layout (also reproduced in a minimal app whose root renders only `<ViewTransition><Outlet /></ViewTransition>`). Same with dev, a production build, and `routeDiscovery: { mode: "initial" }`. With default animations and a loader route, there can be a third view transition, because route discovery emits a second `loading` state.
- **Data mode:** for navigations that don't resolve synchronously (loader or `lazy`), when the component rendering `<ViewTransition>` re-renders on navigation state (e.g. `useNavigation()`). Moving the `useNavigation()` consumer to a sibling doesn't help if it updates the DOM (e.g. a loading bar); only a consumer with no DOM change avoids the extra view transition. Without such a consumer there is one view transition, but the page swap still has `types: null` (scenario 3).

Navigations that resolve synchronously in data mode produce a single view transition with the expected types.

As far as I can tell, while a `<ViewTransition>` is mounted, React starts a view transition for any transition commit that changes the DOM or re-renders the boundary. The question is whether the router's `loading` commit should be one of them (it runs in `React.startTransition`, inside the caller's transition).

`InMemoryRegistryStore.putIfAbsent(key, value)` can return `null` without storing `value` when it waits for a concurrent `computeIfAbsent` whose mapping function fails.

Reproduced on upstream `master` at `a8a33164256ddb6e4bbc168f5c47ac34a348ee7f`, using Java 21, with both platform and virtual threads.

### Reproduction

1. Thread A enters `computeIfAbsent("key", mappingFunction)` and blocks inside the mapping function. The registry now holds its incomplete future.
2. Thread B calls `putIfAbsent("key", "candidate")` and waits in `future.join()`.
3. Allow A's mapping function to throw.
4. B catches the failed future's exception and returns `null`, but never retries insertion. After both calls finish, `find("key")` is empty.

With two waiting `putIfAbsent` calls, both can return `null` and both candidates are lost. The same problem occurs if initialization throws `CancellationException`.

### Expected behavior

After initialization fails, a waiting registration should atomically insert its candidate or return the value inserted by another contender. A failed initialization should not turn a successful-looking registration into a no-op.

### Proposed fix and tests

Retry `putIfAbsent` after conditionally removing the failed future with `entryMap.remove(key, future)`. Conditional removal protects a newer entry from another contender or from the failed initializer's cleanup. Keep mapping functions and future waits outside map locks.

The accompanying JUnit regression test holds initialization pending until each registration thread is waiting, then releases it. It checks the stored value as well as the return values, using one and two contenders on platform and virtual threads. Successful initialization is also covered to preserve existing behavior. The existing `putIfAbsentShouldReturnNullWhenConcurrentComputeIfAbsentFails` test only checks the return value and does not force the registration to wait before releasing initialization.

Prepared with AI assistance; validation details and the regression test will be included in the pull request.

Resilience4j version: master after #2506 (2.4.1-SNAPSHOT)

Java version: 21

Follow-up to #1592 / #2506, which made the Reactor `BulkheadOperator` acquire its permission with the non-blocking `Bulkhead#acquirePermissionAsync()`.

The RxJava 2 and RxJava 3 `BulkheadOperator`s (`SingleBulkhead`, `MaybeBulkhead`, `CompletableBulkhead`, `ObserverBulkhead`, `FlowableBulkhead`) still call `Bulkhead#tryAcquirePermission()` in `subscribeActual`. With `maxWaitDuration > 0` that parks the subscribing thread — e.g. an RxJava computation thread or a Netty event loop — for up to the wait duration; the same problem #1592 described for Reactor ("Seems like rxjava2 and rxjava3 versions are also blocking").

**Proposal** — mirror the Reactor change in both modules:

* acquire with `acquirePermissionAsync()`: an already granted permission subscribes upstream exactly as today, an already rejected one emits `BulkheadFullException` as today;
* a pending permission hands the downstream a deferred `Disposable` (via RxJava's `DisposableHelper`) or, for `Flowable`, a deferred `Subscription` (`SubscriptionArbiter`, the primitive `delaySubscription` uses) which accumulates requests, subscribes upstream once the permission is granted, cancels the pending request on dispose, and releases a permission granted concurrently with a dispose;
* release keeps happening in the existing `Bulkhead*Observer` / `BulkheadSubscriber` hooks; the public `BulkheadOperator` API is unchanged, so existing `maxWaitDuration > 0` configurations are fixed transparently.

I am preparing a PR with the same test coverage as the Reactor change (queueing, FIFO, timeout, cancellation while waiting, cancellation after a queued grant, error release, `Flowable` backpressure) and will reference this issue.

Resilience4j version: master after #2506 (2.4.1-SNAPSHOT)

Java version: 21

Follow-up to #1592 / #2506.

`Bulkhead.executeSuspendFunction` and `Flow.bulkhead` acquire the permission through `acquirePermissionSuspend()`, which for `maxWaitDuration > 0` runs the blocking `acquirePermission()` inside `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)`. That keeps the caller's dispatcher free but still occupies one IO thread per waiting coroutine for up to the wait duration, and coroutine cancellation cannot interrupt the wait: when the coroutine is cancelled while waiting, `withContext` throws `CancellationException` on return even if `acquirePermission()` succeeded in the meantime, and that permission is never released.

**Proposal:** `acquirePermissionAsync().await()` — `CompletionStage.await()` is part of `kotlinx-coroutines-core` since 1.7 (the project is on 1.11.0). Waiting then costs no thread, cancelling the coroutine cancels the queued request (`await()` cancels the future), and a permission granted concurrently with the cancellation is handed back instead of leaking. The fast path (permission available) stays synchronous because the returned future is already completed, and `maxWaitDuration = 0` keeps failing fast with `BulkheadFullException`.

I am preparing a PR and will reference this issue.

Resilience4j version: master after #2506 (2.4.1-SNAPSHOT)

Java version: 21

Follow-up to #1592 / #2506. Since #2506 a `SemaphoreBulkhead` with `maxWaitDuration > 0` queues asynchronous permission requests (`acquirePermissionAsync()`, Reactor operator). That queue is bounded only by time (`maxWaitDuration`) and its depth is not observable. @RobWin's original sketch in #1592 used a bounded queue of permission requests, so this closes the remaining gap to that design.

**Proposal**, mirroring the `ThreadPoolBulkhead` naming:

1. `Bulkhead.Metrics#getQueueDepth()` — the number of permission requests currently waiting (default `0`, so custom `Bulkhead` implementations are unaffected). Exposed by the Micrometer binder as `resilience4j.bulkhead.queue.depth` next to `available.concurrent.calls` / `max.allowed.concurrent.calls`, and by the Dropwizard adapter.
2. `BulkheadConfig#queueCapacity` — the maximum number of waiting permission requests. The default `Integer.MAX_VALUE` keeps today's behavior; when the queue is full, further asynchronous requests fail immediately with `BulkheadFullException` and publish `CallRejected`, exactly like a full `ThreadPoolBulkhead` queue. Wired through `CommonBulkheadConfigurationProperties` (Spring Boot / Micronaut) and the commons-configuration adapter. The blocking `acquirePermission()` / `tryAcquirePermission()` paths are unaffected: they wait on the semaphore, not in the queue.

I am preparing a PR and will reference this issue.

**resilience4j version:** `main` (Spring Boot 4 module, added in #2384)

body_text:
## Problem

`resilience4j.retry.calls` tells me how many calls succeeded or failed, with and without retry attempts. It does not tell me how much time the retries add. A retry configured with 100 ms waits and one configured with 10 s exponential backoff produce the same counters, but have very different effects on latency.

Today the only way to get this is to register an `onRetry` listener on every `Retry` and maintain a custom meter, which is easy to get wrong with dynamically created retries.

## Proposal

Do for retries what `AbstractCircuitBreakerMetrics` already does for call durations: register a `Timer` in the shared metrics base class and feed it from the event publisher. `RetryOnRetryEvent#getWaitInterval()` already carries the wait that was scheduled before the next attempt.

```java
Timer backoff = Timer.builder(names.getBackoffMetricName())
    .description("The wait scheduled between retry attempts")
    .tag(TagNames.NAME, retry.getName())
    .tags(customTags)
    .register(meterRegistry);
retry.getEventPublisher().onRetry(event -> backoff.record(event.getWaitInterval()));
```

- New `RetryMetricNames#getBackoffMetricName()` and `Builder#backoffMetricName(String)`, default `resilience4j.retry.backoff` (Prometheus: `resilience4j_retry_backoff_seconds_count/_sum/_max`).
- `TaggedRetryMetrics` and `TaggedRetryMetricsPublisher` (used by the Spring Boot auto-configuration) both extend `AbstractRetryMetrics`, so both get the meter, and it is removed together with the other meters of a retry.
- No change to `Retry` itself. The value is the scheduled wait, not the measured sleep time, which would differ for interrupted or non-blocking (reactive/async) retries. The description would say so.

## Questions

1. Is an always-on meter fine (one extra meter per `Retry`, like the call `Timer` of the circuit breaker), or would you prefer it opt-in?
2. Is `resilience4j.retry.backoff` an acceptable name?

I have checked that there is no existing issue or PR for this. If the shape is fine for you I will send a PR against `master` with tests (and adjust the meter-count assertions in the existing retry metrics tests).

Today the only way to get this is to register an `onRetry` listener on every `Retry` and maintain a custom meter, which is easy to get wrong with dynamically created retries.

## Proposal

Do for retries what `AbstractCircuitBreakerMetrics` already does for call durations: register a `Timer` in the shared metrics base class and feed it from the event publisher. `RetryOnRetryEvent#getWaitInterval()` already carries the wait that was scheduled before the next attempt.

```java
Timer backoff = Timer.builder(names.getBackoffMetricName())
    .description("The wait scheduled between retry attempts")
    .tag(TagNames.NAME, retry.getName())
    .tags(customTags)
    .register(meterRegistry);
retry.getEventPublisher().onRetry(event -> backoff.record(event.getWaitInterval()));
```

- New `RetryMetricNames#getBackoffMetricName()` and `Builder#backoffMetricName(String)`, default `resilience4j.retry.backoff` (Prometheus: `resilience4j_retry_backoff_seconds_count/_sum/_max`).
- `TaggedRetryMetrics` and `TaggedRetryMetricsPublisher` (used by the Spring Boot auto-configuration) both extend `AbstractRetryMetrics`, so both get the meter, and it is removed together with the other meters of a retry.
- No change to `Retry` itself. The value is the scheduled wait, not the measured sleep time, which would differ for interrupted or non-blocking (reactive/async) retries. The description would say so.

## Questions

1. Is an always-on meter fine (one extra meter per `Retry`, like the call `Timer` of the circuit breaker), or would you prefer it opt-in?
2. Is `resilience4j.retry.backoff` an acceptable name?

I have checked that there is no existing issue or PR for this. If the shape is fine for you I will send a PR against `master` with tests (and adjust the meter-count assertions in the existing retry metrics tests).

Resilience4j version: 2.4.0 (also `master`, b7c00698)

Java version: 21

### Summary

`RateLimiterEvent` carries `numberOfPermits` (`AbstractRateLimiterEvent.getNumberOfPermits()`), but it is not exposed in two places where users typically look:

- `AbstractRateLimiterEvent.toString()` only prints `type`, `rateLimiterName` and `creationTime` (https://github.com/resilience4j/resilience4j/blob/b7c00698/resilience4j-ratelimiter/src/main/java/io/github/resilience4j/ratelimiter/event/AbstractRateLimiterEvent.java#L55-L61)
- `RateLimiterEventDTO` (`/actuator/ratelimiterevents`) only has `rateLimiterName`, `type` and `creationTime` (https://github.com/resilience4j/resilience4j/blob/b7c00698/resilience4j-framework-common/src/main/java/io/github/resilience4j/common/ratelimiter/monitoring/endpoint/RateLimiterEventDTO.java)

So a mismatch between the permits a call was supposed to consume and the permits it actually consumed (#2546 is one example) is invisible in logs and in the actuator endpoint. Today it can only be seen by calling `event.getNumberOfPermits()` from a custom consumer, or indirectly through the `resilience4j.ratelimiter.available.permissions` metric.

### Proposal

Add `numberOfPermits` to `AbstractRateLimiterEvent.toString()` and to `RateLimiterEventDTO` (set in `RateLimiterEventDTO.createRateLimiterEventDTO`, which the Spring Boot 3/4 `RateLimiterEventsEndpoint` uses). The DTO change is additive; `toString()` only changes its output format, and nothing in the repository asserts on that string.

Split out of #2546 so it is not lost when that issue is closed by its fix. If the maintainers agree with the direction, I can open a PR for this (it is independent of #2548).

**Resilience4j version:**
2.4.0

**Java version:**
any

**Problem description:**

`resilience4j-spring-boot3` 2.4.0 has this in its `Import-Package`:

```
io.github.resilience4j.ratelimiter.internal
```

No bundle in the 2.4.0 release exports that package. `resilience4j-ratelimiter` contains the classes but exports only `io.github.resilience4j.ratelimiter`, `.event` and `.utils`, which looks deliberate given no `.internal` package is exported anywhere in the release. So the bundle cannot resolve.

It stands out in the manifest: every other entry carries a version range from the exporting bundle, that one does not, because bnd found no exporter to take a version from.

```
io.github.resilience4j.ratelimiter;version="[2.4,3)"
io.github.resilience4j.ratelimiter.event;version="[2.4,3)"
io.github.resilience4j.ratelimiter.internal
```

**Why it appeared in 2.4.0.** The code has reached into that package since 2.0.x: `RateLimitersHealthIndicator` does `instanceof AtomicRateLimiter` and then calls `getDetailedMetrics()`. What changed is the packaging. In 2.3.0 `resilience4j-spring-boot3` shipped without a `Bundle-SymbolicName` and without an `Import-Package` header at all; in 2.4.0 it is a bundle with 119 imports. `resilience4j-spring6`, `resilience4j-framework-common` and `resilience4j-micrometer` became bundles in 2.4.0 too. So the dependency was always there, the manifest just started describing it.

I scanned every artifact published at 2.4.0 and this is the only package in your own namespace that is imported without being exported, so it looks like a single loose end rather than a pattern.

I did not want to guess the fix, since the options differ a lot in what they commit to:

- export `io.github.resilience4j.ratelimiter.internal`, which makes an internal package public API
- give the health indicator a way to get `nanosToWait` without the cast, so the import disappears
- mark the import optional, though the `instanceof` would then throw `NoClassDefFoundError` rather than simply not match, so this one needs care

Happy to put up a PR for whichever direction you prefer.

**Java version:**
any

**Problem description:**

`resilience4j-spring-boot3` 2.4.0 has this in its `Import-Package`:

```
io.github.resilience4j.ratelimiter.internal
```

No bundle in the 2.4.0 release exports that package. `resilience4j-ratelimiter` contains the classes but exports only `io.github.resilience4j.ratelimiter`, `.event` and `.utils`, which looks deliberate given no `.internal` package is exported anywhere in the release. So the bundle cannot resolve.

It stands out in the manifest: every other entry carries a version range from the exporting bundle, that one does not, because bnd found no exporter to take a version from.

```
io.github.resilience4j.ratelimiter;version="[2.4,3)"
io.github.resilience4j.ratelimiter.event;version="[2.4,3)"
io.github.resilience4j.ratelimiter.internal
```

**Why it appeared in 2.4.0.** The code has reached into that package since 2.0.x: `RateLimitersHealthIndicator` does `instanceof AtomicRateLimiter` and then calls `getDetailedMetrics()`. What changed is the packaging. In 2.3.0 `resilience4j-spring-boot3` shipped without a `Bundle-SymbolicName` and without an `Import-Package` header at all; in 2.4.0 it is a bundle with 119 imports. `resilience4j-spring6`, `resilience4j-framework-common` and `resilience4j-micrometer` became bundles in 2.4.0 too. So the dependency was always there, the manifest just started describing it.

I scanned every artifact published at 2.4.0 and this is the only package in your own namespace that is imported without being exported, so it looks like a single loose end rather than a pattern.

I did not want to guess the fix, since the options differ a lot in what they commit to:

- export `io.github.resilience4j.ratelimiter.internal`, which makes an internal package public API
- give the health indicator a way to get `nanosToWait` without the cast, so the import disappears
- mark the import optional, though the `instanceof` would then throw `NoClassDefFoundError` rather than simply not match, so this one needs care

Happy to put up a PR for whichever direction you prefer.

Two paths in `transitionOnResult` do not apply the requested transition on current `master` (`b7c00698`).

1. Returning `TransitionCheckResult.transitionToOpen()` throws `IllegalArgumentException` instead of opening the breaker with the configured wait duration. The state still reports `CLOSED`, but subsequent permission requests are rejected because `isClosed` was already set to false.
2. When `recordResult` marks a result as a failure, `onResult` records the failed call but skips `transitionOnResult`. A callback returning `transitionToOpenAndWaitFor(...)` never opens the breaker on that path.

Minimal first case:

```java
CircuitBreaker cb = CircuitBreaker.of("example", CircuitBreakerConfig.custom()
    .transitionOnResult(result -> TransitionCheckResult.transitionToOpen())
    .build());
cb.onError(0, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS, new RuntimeException("failed"));
// throws IllegalArgumentException; expected cb.getState() == OPEN
```

For the second case, add `.recordResult("POISON"::equals)`, return `transitionToOpenAndWaitFor(Duration.ofSeconds(60))`, and call `cb.onResult(0, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS, "POISON")`. The failed-call metric becomes 1, but the state remains `CLOSED`.

I reproduced both with JDK 21 regression tests on the current source and will prepare a focused fix. The expected default-duration behavior also matches the design described in #1387. No new transition API is needed.

body_text:
## Output of `restic version`

```
restic 0.18.1 compiled with go1.25.1 on darwin/arm64
```

(reproduced with the official release binary; also relevant to any version using minio-go v7 with the `backend-error-redesign` watchdog, which is beta = enabled by default in 0.18.1)

## What happened?

Backing up to S3/MinIO, the upload froze for the entire duration of a stalled connection **without printing a single error or retry line**. When the connection eventually started working again, the backup instantly resumed at full speed.

The interesting part: restic 0.18.1 *does* have protection for this — the `backend-error-redesign` watchdog cancels requests that make no progress for 5 minutes (`StuckRequestTimeout` in `internal/backend/http_transport.go`). I can show that it fires — but its cancellation is silently absorbed by minio-go's internal retry loop, so each watchdog timeout just starts another 5-minute stall with no user-visible output.

## Steps to reproduce

Deterministic, self-contained, single command (downloads and sha256-pins restic 0.18.1 and a MinIO server binary, then SIGSTOPs the server mid-PUT — the kernel keeps ACKing TCP for the frozen process, so from restic's side the connection stays ESTABLISHED while the peer never responds):

```bash
./repro.sh            # freezes the server for 12 minutes (2.4x the watchdog timeout)
```

Repo: https://github.com/schickling-repros/2026-08-restic-s3-stall (includes the full recorded timeline)

In short: 1 GiB of random data → `restic backup --limit-upload 4096` against `s3:http://127.0.0.1:39093/repro` → once bytes are flowing, `kill -STOP` the MinIO process → wait → `kill -CONT`.

## Expected behavior

A stalled connection should surface to the user within a bounded, visible time. Since the watchdog cancels stuck requests after 5 minutes, at the latest ~5 minutes into the freeze the user should see retry lines like `Save(<data/…>) returned error, retrying after …`.

## Actual behavior

Measured during a 723-second freeze (full 10s-resolution timeline in the repro repo):

```
09:38:19 | >>> FREEZING minio (SIGSTOP) mid-upload -- 40232 KiB already stored, error/retry lines so far: 0
09:43:21 | frozen 302s: stored=40232KiB error/retry_lines_total=0 est_conns=6 NEW_SILENT_RECONNECT(client_port(s): 64662 64663 64664 64665 )
09:48:22 | frozen 603s: stored=40232KiB error/retry_lines_total=0 est_conns=7 NEW_SILENT_RECONNECT(client_port(s): 49684 49685 49686 49687 49701 )
09:50:22 | >>> UNFREEZING minio (SIGCONT) after 723s -- bytes stored during entire freeze: 40232 KiB -> 40232 KiB, error/retry lines surfaced: 0
09:54:38 | restic exit status: 0
```

- 12 minutes (= 2.4× the watchdog timeout): **zero** new bytes stored, **zero** error/retry lines printed.
- The watchdog does fire under the hood — visible only as silent TCP reconnect storms at exactly ~300s and ~600s (27 distinct client ports used during the freeze) — but each minio-go retry just stalls for another 5 minutes, invisible to the user.
- After SIGCONT the backup resumed instantly and completed with exit 0.

### Why this compounds to multi-hour freezes

From source (restic 0.18.1, minio-go v7.0.95):

- minio-go retries internally up to `MaxRetry = 10` times (`retry.go`), silently, before an error reaches restic,
- each attempt stalls for the full 5-minute watchdog timeout before cancellation → one restic-level `Save` needs ≈ 11 × 5 min ≈ **55 minutes** before the first user-visible retry line,
- restic's own retry layer then repeats the cycle (`retry.New(be, 15*time.Minute, …)`), so a permanently dead path means roughly 2¾ hours of silence before the backup finally aborts (extrapolation from source, not measured).

This matches what we saw in production against a MinIO endpoint over a WAN link: recurring freezes of minutes-to-hours (longest observed: 2h37m) with no errors, NAS receive counters flat, and sudden full-speed recovery.

## Do you have an idea how to fix it?

Making the watchdog timeout (or a shorter stall budget) propagate as a visible, logged condition — e.g. surfacing minio-go's internal retries to restic's retry/report layer, or capping the total time a single `Save` may spend inside minio-go's internal retry loop — would turn silent multi-hour freezes into visible retry behavior.

## Did restic help you today?

Yes, massively — restic has been quietly excellent except for this failure mode being hard to diagnose precisely because it's silent.

```
restic 0.18.1 compiled with go1.25.1 on darwin/arm64
```

(reproduced with the official release binary; also relevant to any version using minio-go v7 with the `backend-error-redesign` watchdog, which is beta = enabled by default in 0.18.1)

## What happened?

Backing up to S3/MinIO, the upload froze for the entire duration of a stalled connection **without printing a single error or retry line**. When the connection eventually started working again, the backup instantly resumed at full speed.

The interesting part: restic 0.18.1 *does* have protection for this — the `backend-error-redesign` watchdog cancels requests that make no progress for 5 minutes (`StuckRequestTimeout` in `internal/backend/http_transport.go`). I can show that it fires — but its cancellation is silently absorbed by minio-go's internal retry loop, so each watchdog timeout just starts another 5-minute stall with no user-visible output.

## Steps to reproduce

Deterministic, self-contained, single command (downloads and sha256-pins restic 0.18.1 and a MinIO server binary, then SIGSTOPs the server mid-PUT — the kernel keeps ACKing TCP for the frozen process, so from restic's side the connection stays ESTABLISHED while the peer never responds):

```bash
./repro.sh            # freezes the server for 12 minutes (2.4x the watchdog timeout)
```

Repo: https://github.com/schickling-repros/2026-08-restic-s3-stall (includes the full recorded timeline)

In short: 1 GiB of random data → `restic backup --limit-upload 4096` against `s3:http://127.0.0.1:39093/repro` → once bytes are flowing, `kill -STOP` the MinIO process → wait → `kill -CONT`.

## Expected behavior

A stalled connection should surface to the user within a bounded, visible time. Since the watchdog cancels stuck requests after 5 minutes, at the latest ~5 minutes into the freeze the user should see retry lines like `Save(<data/…>) returned error, retrying after …`.

## Actual behavior

Measured during a 723-second freeze (full 10s-resolution timeline in the repro repo):

```
09:38:19 | >>> FREEZING minio (SIGSTOP) mid-upload -- 40232 KiB already stored, error/retry lines so far: 0
09:43:21 | frozen 302s: stored=40232KiB error/retry_lines_total=0 est_conns=6 NEW_SILENT_RECONNECT(client_port(s): 64662 64663 64664 64665 )
09:48:22 | frozen 603s: stored=40232KiB error/retry_lines_total=0 est_conns=7 NEW_SILENT_RECONNECT(client_port(s): 49684 49685 49686 49687 49701 )
09:50:22 | >>> UNFREEZING minio (SIGCONT) after 723s -- bytes stored during entire freeze: 40232 KiB -> 40232 KiB, error/retry lines surfaced: 0
09:54:38 | restic exit status: 0
```

- 12 minutes (= 2.4× the watchdog timeout): **zero** new bytes stored, **zero** error/retry lines printed.
- The watchdog does fire under the hood — visible only as silent TCP reconnect storms at exactly ~300s and ~600s (27 distinct client ports used during the freeze) — but each minio-go retry just stalls for another 5 minutes, invisible to the user.
- After SIGCONT the backup resumed instantly and completed with exit 0.

### Why this compounds to multi-hour freezes

From source (restic 0.18.1, minio-go v7.0.95):

- minio-go retries internally up to `MaxRetry = 10` times (`retry.go`), silently, before an error reaches restic,
- each attempt stalls for the full 5-minute watchdog timeout before cancellation → one restic-level `Save` needs ≈ 11 × 5 min ≈ **55 minutes** before the first user-visible retry line,
- restic's own retry layer then repeats the cycle (`retry.New(be, 15*time.Minute, …)`), so a permanently dead path means roughly 2¾ hours of silence before the backup finally aborts (extrapolation from source, not measured).

This matches what we saw in production against a MinIO endpoint over a WAN link: recurring freezes of minutes-to-hours (longest observed: 2h37m) with no errors, NAS receive counters flat, and sudden full-speed recovery.

## Do you have an idea how to fix it?

Making the watchdog timeout (or a shorter stall budget) propagate as a visible, logged condition — e.g. surfacing minio-go's internal retries to restic's retry/report layer, or capping the total time a single `Save` may spend inside minio-go's internal retry loop — would turn silent multi-hour freezes into visible retry behavior.

## Did restic help you today?

Yes, massively — restic has been quietly excellent except for this failure mode being hard to diagnose precisely because it's silent.

## Summary

Append-only mode (rest-server `--append-only`) is designed to let a *compromised backup client* keep writing without being able to delete or overwrite existing data. That protects the stored pack files. It does **not** protect the correctness of `forget` retention decisions, and I think that gap is worth closing or at least documenting more prominently.

## The problem

`restic backup` accepts `--time`, `--host`, and `--tag` as free-form client-supplied values, and `restic forget` keeps the *last* snapshot in each time bucket. A client that can append (which is the whole point of append-only) can create arbitrary snapshots that land in any bucket the retention policy uses.

An attacker who has compromised a client with append-only credentials can therefore:

1. Back up an empty directory repeatedly with `--time` set to the end of each day/week/month/year within the retention window, and with `--host`/`--tag` matching the legitimate client so snapshot filters don't distinguish them.
2. These fake snapshots become the "keepers" for `--keep-daily` / `--keep-weekly` / `--keep-monthly` / etc.
3. On the next `forget --prune` run from the trusted host, the real snapshots — no longer selected by the policy — are removed, and prune deletes the underlying data.

The attacker never deletes anything themselves. Append-only holds. The data is destroyed by the operator's own trusted pruning, using attacker-planted metadata. This defeats the specific threat model append-only exists to address.

## Expected behavior

A compromised append-only client should not be able to influence which snapshots the operator's retention policy keeps or discards.

## Possible directions for a fix

Looking for maintainer guidance on which is acceptable:

- **Server-side timestamp enforcement:** an option for rest-server / the repo to reject or ignore client-supplied `--time` that deviates from the server's clock beyond a small tolerance, so snapshots can't be backdated/postdated into arbitrary buckets.
- **`forget` safety heuristics:** warn (or refuse without `--force`) when a `forget` run would drop snapshots in favor of newly-appeared empty/near-empty ones, or when many snapshots share suspicious timestamps.

Output of `restic version`
--------------------------
restic 0.19.1 compiled with go1.26.4 on windows/amd64 (Windows)
restic 0.18.1 compiled with go1.25.0 on linux/amd64 (Linux)

What backend/service did you use to store the repository?
---------------------------------------------------------
My VPS, running Ubuntu 26.
So the backup and restore commands looked like:
"restic -r sftp:my_name@my_vps.com:/path-to-repo backup ."
"restic -r sftp:my_name@my_vps.com:/path-to-repo restore latest --target ."



Problem description / Steps to reproduce
----------------------------------------

I performed a "backup" command on Linux, to backup some files. One directory in the backup data accidentally had a space at the end of the directory name - e.g.
```
data/dir-a/aaa.txt
data/dir-b /bbb.txt <- note the space
data/dir-c/ccc.txt
```

The backup completed with no errors.

I then restored that snapshot on Windows. The backup reported errors:
"Unable to set timestamp of file data\dir-b\bbb.txt - no such file or directory"
All files were restored. The 'dir-b' did not have a space at the end (which I think Windows forbids anyway). 

I went back to Linux, removed the space, and did a new backup snapshot. The new snapshot restored on Windows without errors.

Expected behavior
-----------------

Not sure :) Maybe warn about spaces at the end of path components on Linux? Or a more meaningful error message on Windows.

Actual behavior
---------------

See above

------------------------------------------------------------

Restic is awesome! Keep up the good work.

Output of `restic version`
--------------------------

restic 0.19.1 compiled with go1.26.4 on darwin/arm64

What backend/service did you use to store the repository?
---------------------------------------------------------

Azure Blob Storage, authenticated with `AZURE_ACCOUNT_NAME` and `AZURE_ACCOUNT_KEY`.

Problem description / Steps to reproduce
----------------------------------------

Any command that opens an existing repository blocks for 15 minutes when the Azure container does not exist, then fails. `restic init` against the same location creates the container right away.

1. Pick a storage account and a container name that does not exist in it.
2. Run a command that opens the repository:

    ```sh
    export AZURE_ACCOUNT_NAME=<account>
    export AZURE_ACCOUNT_KEY=<key>
    export RESTIC_PASSWORD=<password>
    restic -r azure:does-not-exist:/repo cat config
    ```

3. restic retries for 15 minutes before it exits.

For comparison, a missing `config` blob in a container that does exist fails at once with `repository does not exist`.

Expected behavior
-----------------

A missing container fails immediately, the same as a missing config file:

```txt
Fatal: repository does not exist: unable to open config file: ...
Is there a repository at the following location?
```

Actual behavior
---------------

restic retries the `Stat` of the config file until the 15-minute retry limit runs out:

```
Stat(<config/>) returned error, retrying after 1.106390407s: blob.GetProperties: HEAD https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net/does-not-exist/repo%2Fconfig
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
RESPONSE 404: 404 The specified container does not exist.
ERROR CODE: ContainerNotFound
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Response contained no body
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Stat(<config/>) returned error, retrying after 1.377195697s: blob.GetProperties: HEAD https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net/does-not-exist/repo%2Fconfig
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
RESPONSE 404: 404 The specified container does not exist.
ERROR CODE: ContainerNotFound
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Response contained no body
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

...
repeated for 15mins
...


Fatal: unable to open config file: blob.GetProperties: HEAD https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net/does-not-exist/repo%2Fconfig
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
RESPONSE 404: 404 The specified container does not exist.
ERROR CODE: ContainerNotFound
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Response contained no body
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

azure:does-not-exist:/repo
```

Then it exits with the generic error instead of `ErrNoRepository`:

```
Fatal: unable to open config file: ... ContainerNotFound
```

Do you have any idea what may have caused this?
-----------------------------------------------

The Azure backend classifies `ContainerNotFound` as neither "not exist" nor permanent, so the retry backend keeps retrying it.

- `hasRepositoryConfig` calls `Stat` on the config file through the retry-wrapped backend
([global.go#L341-L349](https://github.com/restic/restic/blob/v0.19.1/internal/global/global.go#L341-L349)). The wrapper is set up with a 15-minute limit
([global.go#L615](https://github.com/restic/restic/blob/v0.19.1/internal/global/global.go#L615)).
- The retry `Stat` stops early only when `IsNotExist` is true ([backend_retry.go#L231-L251](https://github.com/restic/restic/blob/v0.19.1/internal/backend/retry/backend_retry.go#L231-L251)).
- Azure `IsNotExist` only matches `BlobNotFound` ([azure.go#L204-L206](https://github.com/restic/restic/blob/v0.19.1/internal/backend/azure/azure.go#L204-L206)), and `IsPermanentError` only adds
401, 403 and 416 ([azure.go#L208-L220](https://github.com/restic/restic/blob/v0.19.1/internal/backend/azure/azure.go#L208-L220)). A 404 `ContainerNotFound` matches neither.

My preferred fix would be to make `IsNotExist` also match `bloberror.ContainerNotFound`: A missing container means every object in it is missing, and `hasRepositoryConfig` then returns `ErrNoRepository`.

Another possibility is to add it to `IsPermanentError`, which stops the retries; but it keeps the generic error as the cause, and I'm pretty sure 404 was omitted from this for a reason.

> **Disclaimer:** AI-drafted, verified by me before filing. I answer follow-ups. When the sftp backend cannot start its ssh session, restic sometimes exits without printing ssh's own error line (`subprocess ssh: ssh: connect to host ... Connection refused`). restic's own message is the same whatever ssh said, so the lost line is the only one that says why the connection failed. Our backup scripts tell an unreachable target (a quiet skip) from a real failure (an alert) by that line, so a busy host reported an unreachable target as a failed backup. On a host under CPU load it went missing in about a quarter of runs; without extra load it never did. ## Output of `restic version`

restic 0.19.1, linux/amd64

## What happens

On some filesystems `fallocate` can be accepted and never return. `restic restore` then stops at the first file larger than one blob. Files are created empty and nothing further happens. A goroutine dump shows every writer blocked in `fallocate`, via `ensureSize` → `fs.PreallocateFile`.

A timeout doesn't help. Reproduced with a FUSE filesystem that accepts `fallocate` and never replies:

- the kernel holds the inode lock, so `pwrite`, `ftruncate` and `unlink` on that file also block, and a blocked `unlink` blocks its directory;
- the thread is in `D` state (`request_wait_answer`) and ignores `SIGKILL`, so the process can't exit;
- `FALLOC_FL_KEEP_SIZE` behaves the same.

Preallocation is only an optimisation: the file can be written without it. But `--sparse` doesn't skip it for files larger than one blob without zero chunks, and nothing else lets restore avoid the call. `restic dump | tar -x` works.

## Proposed fix

Since the file can be written without preallocating, check in a child process whether the filesystem answers `fallocate` before calling it for a file, and skip preallocation where it doesn't. PR to follow.

## Output of `restic version`

```
restic 0.19.1 compiled with go1.26.4 on linux/arm64
```

Also reproduced with 0.19.0 on linux/arm64 and 0.19.1 on darwin/arm64. First observed with 0.19.0 on linux/amd64.

## What backend/service did you use to store the repository?

Local directory in the repro below. We first saw it with an S3 repository restoring onto an NFS (Amazon EFS) volume.

## Problem description / Steps to reproduce

`restic restore --overwrite if-changed` (and `--overwrite always`) silently produces a corrupt file when the target file is a hard link (link count > 1) whose content differs from the snapshot in only some blobs. The restored file has the correct size and mtime, but every blob that already matched the old content is left as zeros. Restic exits 0 and reports no error.

We hit this when pre-seeding a restore target with a hard-link copy of the previous restore (`cp -al` / `rsync --link-dest`) so that unchanged files keep sharing an inode.

This script reproduces it in the official image (`docker run --rm --entrypoint /bin/sh -v $PWD:/work restic/restic:0.19.1 /work/repro.sh`):

```sh
#!/bin/sh
set -e
export RESTIC_REPOSITORY=/tmp/repo RESTIC_PASSWORD=test
cd /tmp
restic init -q
mkdir src
head -c 8388608 /dev/urandom > src/file.bin
touch -d "2026-03-10 00:00:00" src/file.bin
restic backup -q --host h src
restic restore -q latest --target base
# change 7 bytes in the middle, new mtime
printf 'CHANGED' | dd of=src/file.bin bs=1 seek=4194304 conv=notrunc 2>/dev/null
touch -d "2026-09-23 00:00:00" src/file.bin
restic backup -q --host h src
# pre-seed the target with hard links to the earlier restore
cp -al base new
stat -c 'before: links=%h size=%s' new/src/file.bin
restic restore -q latest --target new --overwrite if-changed
stat -c 'after:  links=%h size=%s' new/src/file.bin
cmp -s new/src/file.bin src/file.bin && echo "restored file matches source" || echo "restored file DIFFERS from source"
echo "non-zero bytes: $(tr -d '\000' < new/src/file.bin | wc -c) of $(stat -c %s src/file.bin)"
```

## Expected behavior

`new/src/file.bin` matches the second snapshot, and `base/src/file.bin` is left untouched.

## Actual behavior

```
before: links=2 size=8388608
after:  links=1 size=8388608
restored file DIFFERS from source
non-zero bytes: 3414334 of 8388608
```

`base/src/file.bin` is intact. The new file was unlinked and recreated, but only the changed blobs were written to it. A later `restore --overwrite if-changed` trusts the corrupt file because its size and mtime match, so the damage persists across restores. On macOS the recreated file ends up shorter than expected instead of zero-filled, presumably because preallocation does not extend the file there.

## Cause

The two parts of the overwrite logic from #4838 and #4864 disagree when a file has more than one link:

1. `withOverwriteCheck` / `verifyFile` in `internal/restorer/restorer.go` reads the existing file and records which blobs already match (`fileState`).
2. `filerestorer.go` skips those blobs (`!file.state.HasMatchingBlob(idx)`).
3. `createFile` in `internal/restorer/fileswriter.go` sees `ex.Links > 1` and replaces the file with a new, empty one ("nuke the existing file and start with a fresh one"), then `ensureSize` extends it to full size.

After step 3 the blob-match state from step 1 no longer describes the file on disk, but the restore still writes only the non-matching blobs.

A possible fix is to treat a file with a link count above 1 as having no matching blobs (restore it fully, since it will be replaced anyway). Another is to break the link by copying before writing only the changed blobs.

## Do you have any idea what may have caused this?

See above.

## Did restic help you today? Did it make you happy in any way?

Yes. Content-aware `--overwrite if-changed` is otherwise exactly what we needed.

restric is crashing.

Output of `restic version`
--------------------------

restic 0.19.1 compiled with go1.26.5 on darwin/arm64
Repository format version 2.

What backend/service did you use to store the repository?
---------------------------------------------------------

AWS S3, region eu-west-1, using the s3:s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/<bucket> form.

Versioning is enabled. Object Lock is enabled, with no default retention.
restic uploads everything as STANDARD (no s3.storage-class option). A bucket lifecycle rule later transitions data packs to DEEP_ARCHIVE after 14 days. Tree packs, the index and snapshots stay STANDARD.
The IAM user restic uses has s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject, s3:RestoreObject and s3:ListBucket (plus tagging and multipart permissions) on the bucket.

Problem description / Steps to reproduce
----------------------------------------

Restoring a single file whose data pack is in DEEP_ARCHIVE, with the s3-restore feature enabled:

export RESTIC_FEATURES=s3-restore=true
restic --no-lock restore \
  -o s3.enable-restore=true -o s3.restore-tier=Standard \
  -o s3.restore-days=7 -o s3.restore-timeout=1m \
  latest --target /tmp/out -v \
  --include '/mnt/hdd/music/.../desktop.ini'
(It's the same with the default timeout, --no-lock removed, Bulk tier, or several files.)

The feature flag and options do reach restic. Without RESTIC_FEATURES it refuses to start with:

Fatal: ... feature flag `s3-restore` is required to use `-o s3.enable-restore=true`
With the flag set, the repository opens normally.

Expected behavior
-----------------

restic requests a restore of the pack, prints warming up 1 packs from cold storage, this may take a while..., waits until the object is readable, then restores the file.

Actual behavior
---------------

No "warming up" message. No restore request is ever made: head-object on the pack still shows "Restore": null afterwards. restic goes straight to reading the pack and retries forever:

Load(<data/2f36a891c4>, 288, 13122927) returned error, retrying after 746.373065ms: The operation is not valid for the object's storage class
Load(<data/2f36a891c4>, 288, 13122927) returned error, retrying after 2.241984321s: The operation is not valid for the object's storage class
...
Load(<data/2f36a891c4>, 288, 13122927) returned error, retrying after 1m9.396474371s: The operation is not valid for the object's storage class
The pack really is archived, and the same credentials can thaw it. With the same access key restic uses, from the AWS CLI:

$ aws s3api head-object --bucket <bucket> --key data/2f/2f36a891c4a6...1611 \
    --query '{Class:StorageClass,Restore:Restore}'
{ "Class": "DEEP_ARCHIVE", "Restore": null }

$ aws s3api restore-object --bucket <bucket> --key data/2f/2f36a891c4a6...1611 \
    --restore-request 'Days=7,GlacierJobParameters={Tier=Standard}'
(succeeds)

$ aws s3api head-object ...
{ "Class": "DEEP_ARCHIVE", "Restore": "ongoing-request=\"true\"" }
Thawing the needed packs this way (restore-object on each, waiting until ongoing-request="false"), then running restic restore with no s3-restore options, works perfectly: 12 files, 77 packs, all verified with --verify.

Do you have any idea what may have caused this?
-----------------------------------------------

Not for certain. Reading v0.19.1:

- filerestorer.go should print the "warming up" message whenever StartWarmup returns any handles. Since it printed nothing, Backend.Warmup in internal/backend/s3/s3.go must have returned an empty list without an error.
- That happens if getWarmupStatus considers the object warm, for example if objectInfo.Metadata.Get("X-Amz-Storage-Class") doesn't come back as DEEP_ARCHIVE for this object.
- It also happens if RestoreObject returns InvalidObjectState, which requestRestore treats as "already warm" without logging it.
One thing that may be unusual here: the objects reached DEEP_ARCHIVE through a lifecycle transition rather than being uploaded with that storage class. I haven't tried a debug build. Happy to run one, or test a patch, if that would help.

Did restic help you today? Did it make you happy in any way?
------------------------------------------------------------

It's a very good backup program with the right emphasis IMO on a quality design. That's what I'm using it.
Restic's index, cat tree and find --show-pack-id made it easy to work out exactly which packs to thaw by hand to avoid the above bug so I'm not blocked by it. Always good to have an alternative! restore --verify confirmed that files come back intact from Deep Archive.

The system I have configured is intended to be ransomware safe and with cheap storage costs. I'm identifying the big data packs and tagging them. I then have a rule to transition tagged files to DEEP_ARCHIVE. My original intention was to transition all of /data, but that prevented me browsing the repo, hence the tagging approach. I had hoped to use governance mode, but it prevented the Restic lock mechanism working, so I have enabled versioning and prevented delete-object, etc. It would be nice if my scheme was supported natively by Restic someday.

Output of `restic version`
--------------------------

```
restic 0.19.1 compiled with go1.26.4 on linux/amd64
```

What backend/service did you use to store the repository?
---------------------------------------------------------

Local filesystem (ext4 on NVMe). The same symptom appeared earlier with a repository on a
CIFS/SMB-mounted share and on a vfat USB disk, so it does not look backend-specific.

Expected behavior
-----------------

`restic check --read-data` either confirms the repository is intact, or reports packs that really
are damaged.

Actual behavior
---------------

Most runs report blobs whose data "is wrong", usually recovered on a retry, and then declare the
repository damaged — while the repository is provably intact. Different packs are reported on every
run, and some runs are clean.

```
check successful on second attempt, original error pack 50d8ae14… contains 2 errors:
  [blob 82385e18…: read blob <data/82385e18> from pack 50d8ae14…: wrong data returned, hash is f821add6…]
...
The repository is damaged and must be repaired.
Fatal: repository contains errors
```

One run reported 17 affected packs (19 blobs), all recovered on the second attempt. Occasionally a
pack is *not* recovered and is reported as damaged — a later `repair packs` then salvaged every
blob from such a pack, and `repair snapshots --forget` reported `no snapshots were modified`.

Problem description / Steps to reproduce
----------------------------------------

Repository: 631 pack files, ~11 GB, 13 snapshots, mixed file sizes. Machine: 24-core CPU
(i9-14900K), 32 GB non-ECC RAM, Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 7.0.0-38, ext4 on NVMe.

Commands, all against the same unchanged repository (`$R` = `--repo <REPO> --password-file <FILE>`):

```bash
restic $R check --read-data                  # errors in 7 of 7 runs
GOMAXPROCS=1 restic $R check --read-data     # clean in 3 of 4 runs
restic $R check --read-data --no-cache       # still fails -> not the cache
DEBUG_LOG=/tmp/dbg.log restic $R check --read-data   # still fails -> not hidden by logging
```

| Run configuration | Runs | Result |
|---|---|---|
| default concurrency | 4 | errors every run: 2–13 blobs recovered on retry, 0–3 not recovered |
| default concurrency, with `DEBUG_LOG` | 3 | errors every run: 4–6 recovered, 1–2 not recovered |
| `GOMAXPROCS=1` | 4 | 3 runs clean, 1 run with 2 recovered reads |
| `--no-cache` | 1 | errors |

One further data point: a repository on a CIFS-mounted share passed `check --read-data` cleanly,
and the failures started appearing once the same data was on a fast local disk — consistent with a
timing-sensitive problem rather than a storage one.

The repository itself is intact; verified two ways, both independent of restic:

- **Every pack file hashed against its own name** (restic names packs by content hash), with plain
  buffered reads, 3 passes / 33 GB total: **0 mismatches**.
  ```python
  import hashlib, os, sys
  root = sys.argv[1] + "/data"
  bad = [f for d, _, fs in os.walk(root) for f in fs
         if hashlib.sha256(open(os.path.join(d, f), "rb").read()).hexdigest() != f]
  print(len(bad), "mismatches")
  ```
- **One pack reported as bad, re-read 5× with `dd iflag=direct`** (page cache bypassed): identical
  hashes every time, equal to its filename.

Hardware was ruled out before filing:

- 4 processes × 256 MB, each rehashing its own unchanging buffer for 60 s: 565 GB hashed,
  **0 mismatches**.
- 8 and 16 **threads in a single process** hashing one shared read-only buffer (`hashlib` releases
  the GIL, so this is genuinely parallel on shared memory): 1.6 TB and 3.1 TB hashed,
  **0 mismatches**.
- Seen under two different kernels (7.0.0-31 and 7.0.0-38); no MCE/EDAC events; non-ECC memory, so
  a silent flip is possible in principle, but ~4.6 TB of parallel hashing without a single error
  makes it an unlikely explanation for ~1 bad read per 2–3 GB in restic.

Debug log
---------

`DEBUG_LOG` works in the release binary, the problem reproduces with it enabled, and the log
contains only pack/blob IDs and source locations — no file or directory names — so this excerpt is
unredacted apart from the repository path. Each run produced ~57 MB; the full log can be supplied
on request.

The failing read comes from the pack blob iterator:

```
repository/repository.go:1258  repository.(*packBlobIterator).Next  71    process blob <data/818136d1>, skipped 0, <Blob (data) 818136d1, offset 5650617, …
repository/repository.go:1291  repository.(*packBlobIterator).Next  71  read blob data/818136d1…548a from pack 223e109a…5584: wrong data returned, hash is fe7f4e8c…aeba
repository/check.go:109        repository.checkPackInner.func1      71    check blob 818136d1…548a: <data/818136d1>
repository/check.go:111        repository.checkPackInner.func1      71    error verifying blob 818136d1…548a: read blob <data/818136d1> from pack 223e109a…5584: wrong data returned, hash is fe7f4e8c…aeba
```

Two more failures in the same run, on other goroutines:

```
repository/repository.go:1291  repository.(*packBlobIterator).Next  71  read blob data/2dd11f92…aa88 from pack 33447426…d09e: wrong data returned, hash is 94d4f348…540b
repository/repository.go:1291  repository.(*packBlobIterator).Next  72  read blob data/73b860b9…cd31 from pack 75b04af3…af0f: wrong data returned, hash is 9ed56c9c…b767
```

`restic stats --mode debug` is not included: the report is not about memory or cache size.

Do you have any idea what may have caused this?
-----------------------------------------------

The dependence on parallelism, and the fact that every failure surfaces in
`(*packBlobIterator).Next`, point at the concurrent pack-read path in `check --read-data` — a data
race or a reused/shared buffer, where a blob is hashed against data another goroutine has already
overwritten. That would explain all of it: random packs, success on retry, occasional
clean runs, and near-disappearance at `GOMAXPROCS=1` (which removes parallelism but not
concurrency, matching the one residual failure).

A related-looking failure appears in `copy` at full concurrency:

```
Fatal: Detected data corruption while saving blob <id>: hash mismatch
```

which also succeeded when simply retried.

Do you have an idea how to solve the issue?
-------------------------------------------

Not a specific patch — the reporter has not read the relevant code. If it is buffer reuse, the fix
is presumably to stop sharing the buffer whose contents are hashed, or to hash before the buffer can
be handed back to a pool.

As a workaround, the affected commands are being run with `GOMAXPROCS=1`, and "recovered on second
attempt" is treated as a warning rather than a failure, since the data turns out to be fine. The
cost is roughly 11 s → 24 s for a full `--read-data` pass on 11 GB.

Output of `restic version`
--------------------------

restic 0.19.0 compiled with go1.26.4 on linux/amd64

What should restic do differently? Which functionality do you think we should add?
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

We are using Restic to back up all our data, including the data stored in S3 compatible buckets in Ceph.  Currently we are using `s3fs` fuse mount to accomplish this, it presents an S3 bucket as a normal POSIX filesystem, or as close as it gets.  I've seen others use `rclone mount` to do the same thing.

Since Restic already has full client library for talking to S3, it seems reasonable that Restic was able to read data directly rather than going via a FUSE layer.

What are you trying to do? What problem would this solve?
---------------------------------------------------------

The FUSE layer is RAM hungry, especially for wide directories.  A native backup tool can be a lot more efficient and explicit in what it caches (FUSE implicitly uses kernel buffer cache).  It would also be able to support a few degenerate object names in S3:

 * An object name can have the same name as a directory.  Either the directory or the object will be ignored from the backup.
 * An object name can contain "//" and it is different from the object name with just "/".  FUSE will collapse "//" when presenting the filenames, and attempts to download the object will fail since it uses the wrong object name (with single "/").
 * An object name can contain "." and "..".  Similar to above (but probably less common).

I have a series of patches implemented already which have been tested and are about to go into production here.  It implements `restic backup --from-s3 BUCKET-URI` and otherwise leaves functionality unchanged.  

Did restic help you today? Did it make you happy in any way?
------------------------------------------------------------

Restic is great 🥇

Output of `restic version`

-->
`restic 0.19.1 compiled with go1.26.4 on windows/amd64`

What should restic do differently? Which functionality do you think we should add?
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

<!--
Please describe the feature you'd like us to add here.
-->
On the current version, restic does skip a lot, if not all, reparse points configured on Windows.
This means e.g. when WSL is installed files as `C:\Users\of4710\AppData\Local\Microsoft\WindowsApps\bash.exe`.


What are you trying to do? What problem would this solve?
---------------------------------------------------------

<!--
This section should contain a brief description what you're trying to do, which
would be possible after implementing the new feature.
-->
One could say those files contain no real data.
I would argue against that those are, sadly another variant of, symlinks used in the Windows world.
And it would be very helpful if restic could also backup those. Because this would eanle restic to become a full drive backup solution for Windows systems.
I.e. when my Windows drive fails, recreate NTFS partition, restore backup from restic, boot up Windows, and be happy. (Like you can do on Linux.)

Did restic help you today? Did it make you happy in any way?
------------------------------------------------------------

<!--
Answering this question is not required, but if you have anything positive to share, please do so here!
Sometimes we get tired of reading bug reports all day and a little positive end note does wonders.
Idea by Joey Hess, https://joeyh.name/blog/entry/two_holiday_stories/
-->
Yes. I hope restic can become a real open source full drive backup solution for Windows, like you know many for Linux.

Context
-------

I saw many issues around the `unsupported file type "irregular"` messages those reparse points to currently trigger. But none were framed as a feature request, thats why I created this issue.

-----------------

--------------------------

restic 0.19.1 compiled with go1.26.5-X:nodwarf5 on linux/amd64

What backend/service did you use to store the repository?
---------------------------------------------------------

GCS (but I believe the bug is backend-independent)

Problem description / Steps to reproduce
----------------------------------------

A backup with `--exclude=/path/**/A/**/*.go` includes the file /path/A/B.go.

I attached a script that shows this behavior: [restic_wildcard_exclude_bug.sh](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33790001/restic_wildcard_exclude_bug.sh)


Expected behavior
-----------------

I would expect `--exclude=/path/**/A/**/*.go` excluding the file /path/A/B.go.

Actual behavior
---------------

File /path/A/B.go is included in the backup.


Do you have any idea what may have caused this?
-----------------------------------------------

I believe the bug is there in restic/internal/filter/filter.go:

``` 
func match(pattern Pattern, strs []string) (matched bool, err error) {
	if ok, pos := hasDoubleWildcard(pattern); ok {
		// gradually expand '**' into separate wildcards
		newPat := make([]patternPart, len(strs))
		// copy static prefix once
		copy(newPat, pattern.parts[:pos])
		for i := 0; i <= len(strs)-len(pattern.parts)+1; i++ {
```
The bound of the for loop assumes that other double wildcards will match at least one path component.

I can probably send a PR to fix that.

Did restic help you today? Did it make you happy in any way?
------------------------------------------------------------
restic is a very nice backup system.

Output of `restic version`
--------------------------

```
restic 0.19.1 compiled with go1.26.4 on linux/amd64
```

What backend/service did you use to store the repository?
---------------------------------------------------------

S3-compatible storage over HTTPS. This affects every backend restic connects to over TLS.

Problem description / Steps to reproduce
----------------------------------------

<!--
This section should include at least:

 * A description of the problem you are having with restic.

 * The complete command line and any environment variables you used to
   configure restic's backend access. Make sure to replace sensitive values!

 * The output of the commands, what restic prints gives may give us much
   information to diagnose the problem!

 * The more time you spend describing an easy way to reproduce the behavior (if
   this is possible), the easier it is for the project developers to fix it!
-->
On 2026-10-20 it was disclosed that the private keys of eight eMudhra (emSign) intermediate CA certificates were compromised (https://emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/, https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=2083449). Anyone holding those keys can issue certificates that chain to a trusted root.

Go shipped an urgent fix that makes `crypto/x509` refuse chains containing these intermediates: https://go.dev/issue/82345 (CVE-2026-111943). The Go team recommends upgrading immediately. Go 1.26.10 and 1.27.3 are the current releases.

The restic 0.19.1 release binaries are built with go1.26.4, so they don't include this check. Whether a connection is protected then depends on the operating system: Windows and macOS have to distrust the certificates
themselves, and on Linux it depends on the installed `ca-certificates` package. Someone who can intercept a restic client's traffic, for example on an untrusted network, could impersonate the repository backend and obtain its credentials.

`go.mod` on master already has `toolchain go1.26.9`, but that's also older than the fix, and the Go version used for release binaries is set at release time.

Expected behavior
-----------------

<!--
Describe what you'd like restic to do differently.
-->
A patch release (e.g. 0.19.2) whose release binaries and Docker image are built with a Go version that includes the fix for golang/go#82345.

Actual behavior
---------------

<!--
In this section, please try to concentrate on observations, so only describe
what you observed directly.
-->
The latest release binaries are built with go1.26.4 and don't block the compromised intermediates.

Do you have any idea what may have caused this?
-----------------------------------------------

<!--
Did something noteworthy happen on your system, Internet connection, backend services, etc?
-->
The binaries predate Go's fix.

Did restic help you today? Did it make you happy in any way?
------------------------------------------------------------

<!--

Sometimes we get tired of reading bug reports all day and a little positive end note does wonders.
Idea by Joey Hess, https://joeyh.name/blog/entry/two_holiday_stories/
-->
I don't have any specific story to share but would like to thank you for this project. It is great! Absolutely love it! 
I tried to create a joke together with my AI about backups to include here, but this was the best we could come up with:
> Data loss is nature's way of telling you that you should have made a backup.

Output of `restic version`

```
restic 0.19.1 compiled with go1.26.4 on linux/amd64
```

What backend/service did you use to store the repository?
---------------------------------------------------------

S3-compatible storage over HTTPS. This affects every backend restic connects to over TLS.

Problem description / Steps to reproduce
----------------------------------------

<!--
This section should include at least:

 * A description of the problem you are having with restic.

 * The complete command line and any environment variables you used to
