   this is possible), the easier it is for the project developers to fix it!
-->
On 2026-10-20 it was disclosed that the private keys of eight eMudhra (emSign) intermediate CA certificates were compromised (https://emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/, https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=2083449). Anyone holding those keys can issue certificates that chain to a trusted root.

Go shipped an urgent fix that makes `crypto/x509` refuse chains containing these intermediates: https://go.dev/issue/82345 (CVE-2026-111943). The Go team recommends upgrading immediately. Go 1.26.10 and 1.27.3 are the current releases.

The restic 0.19.1 release binaries are built with go1.26.4, so they don't include this check. Whether a connection is protected then depends on the operating system: Windows and macOS have to distrust the certificates
themselves, and on Linux it depends on the installed `ca-certificates` package. Someone who can intercept a restic client's traffic, for example on an untrusted network, could impersonate the repository backend and obtain its credentials.

`go.mod` on master already has `toolchain go1.26.9`, but that's also older than the fix, and the Go version used for release binaries is set at release time.

-----------------

-->
A patch release (e.g. 0.19.2) whose release binaries and Docker image are built with a Go version that includes the fix for golang/go#82345.

---------------

-->
The latest release binaries are built with go1.26.4 and don't block the compromised intermediates.

restic 0.19.1 compiled with go1.26.4 on windows/amd64


What should restic do differently? Which functionality do you think we should add?
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The image repository specified in the `backup` command with the `-r` option should always automatically be excluded from the backup, as otherwise the restic repo will infinitely and circularly clone itself until there is no more drive space left.


What are you trying to do? What problem would this solve?
---------------------------------------------------------


I was using restic for the first time and wanted to put my restic repo inside my backup folder as the way you would do it with a git repo but then I noticed that it started getting larger, than the actual files it was supposed to clone and I saw that it indefinitely kept cloning its own files.
I think this would really improve usability for new users coming from git and just generally be a quality of life improvement.
I do not see any scenario in which you would not want to do this, 
as not automatically excluding the restic repository will always result in infinite cloning,
bloating disk space.
Though absolute paths should then be used to distinguish from the actual repo and perhaps a repo of the same name, that is somewhere deeper in the stuff you actually want to clone.


Did restic help you today? Did it make you happy in any way?
------------------------------------------------------------

Other than that restic is still exactly what I am looking for. A CLI tool like git to version your stuff, only made for large backups instead of code versioning.

### Expected Behavior / Situation

Please provide a supported signed/trusted Windows native distribution that works with Smart App Control enabled. When Windows rejects a module that exists on disk, the loader should distinguish this from a missing optional dependency.

### Actual Behavior / Situation

Observed with rollup 4.63.2, @rollup/rollup-win32-x64-msvc 4.63.2, Node.js v24.19.0 on Windows with Smart App Control enforced.

Starting a Vite project using `npm run dev -- --configLoader runner` fails. The top-level message says `Cannot find module @rollup/rollup-win32-x64-msvc` and suggests reinstalling dependencies. The nested cause is `ERR_DLOPEN_FAILED`: `An Application Control policy has blocked this file.`

The existing file is `rollup.win32-x64-msvc.node`. Authenticode inspection reports it is not signed. SHA-256: `0ac58bc9544c233c23e3587483a391444157feca454b8830ec424c580a81a3da`.

Code Integrity events 3077 and 3033 confirm the blocked load by node.exe. CiTool identifies enforced policy `VerifiedAndReputableDesktop`, ID `0283ac0f-fff1-49ae-ada1-8a933130cad6`. This also occurs in ordinary user PowerShell.

The lockfile resolves to the official npm registry. Installed bytes have not been independently compared with the registry archive, and no separate minimal reproduction repository has been created. This report does not assert maliciousness.

### Modification Proposal

Please consider Authenticode signing the distributed Windows native modules, or document a supported trusted distribution. Also preserve a clear policy-denial diagnostic for ERR_DLOPEN_FAILED instead of recommending lockfile deletion as though the dependency were missing.

Microsoft recommends publisher signing for Smart App Control compatibility: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/threat-malware-protection/smart-app-control-frequently-asked-questions

No Windows security policy was disabled or modified during this investigation.

**Results:** EM 74.8 (+13.6 vs Naive), Faithfulness 0.94, 185ms latency.

body_text:
### Feature Description

Docs or a small example for AffixIO as host-side action proof around LlamaIndex tool calls (callback handler and/or tool wrapper / approval middleware).

AffixIO proves a host-side ACTION completed (signed yes/no). PII stays on the host. Not person/age/KYC.

Sit: before an agent runs a sensitive tool (spend, DB admin, destructive API), AffixIO can gate/prove the action on the host.

Natural fits:

1. `CallbackManager` / event handler on tool call events: require AffixIO proof, block or mark failed when unsigned
2. Thin wrapper around `FunctionTool` / agent tool dispatch that calls AffixIO before `fn(...)`

Not asking for a heavy first-party integration package. Example under docs or a community-style snippet is enough.

### Reason

Teams running LlamaIndex agents against privileged tools need a host-side yes/no proof that is not KYC and does not ship PII off-box. AffixIO is that gate. A canonical example would save people from reinventing fragile wrappers.

### Value of Feature

Clear pattern for tool lifecycle approval in LlamaIndex agents. Aligns with how other agent frameworks expose before-tool hooks.

### Install

```bash
npm i affixio
npm i @affixio/mcp@0.1.0
```

MCP is local stdio.

### Links

- https://www.affix-io.com/
- https://hub.affix-io.com/onboarding/

Happy to draft a minimal example PR if maintainers want that shape.

Kris / AffixIO

body_text:
I maintain [cognicore-env](https://github.com/cognicore-dev/cognicore-env) (open-source, MIT) — a memory layer for agents that speaks MCP and needs no vector database or embedding server (TF-IDF retrieval over pure stdlib).

LlamaIndex has a memory abstraction and a broad store ecosystem; what no store provides is portability with provenance. Memory written in one LlamaIndex deployment stays there, and when teams do move it, it travels as text — no verification state, no history, no expiry.

Proposal: a LlamaIndex memory integration where memories can be exported and imported as sealed bundles. Per memory: proof (command, result, exit code, output hash), chain of custody across agents, observed-until-reverified import semantics, trust decay across unverified hops, validity intervals (a fact verified in March is not evidence about April), and owner-per-concept for conflicts — the last two validated in a public design review with multi-team operators.

Use case: a LlamaIndex agent that spent a month indexing and querying a codebase exports its verified conventions; another deployment (or a non-LlamaIndex agent) imports them and starts from evidence instead of zero.

Happy to contribute the store integration plus a notebook example. The transfer machinery is implemented and tested across four platforms. Is this a fit for the integrations catalog?

Proposal: a LlamaIndex memory integration where memories can be exported and imported as sealed bundles. Per memory: proof (command, result, exit code, output hash), chain of custody across agents, observed-until-reverified import semantics, trust decay across unverified hops, validity intervals (a fact verified in March is not evidence about April), and owner-per-concept for conflicts — the last two validated in a public design review with multi-team operators.

Use case: a LlamaIndex agent that spent a month indexing and querying a codebase exports its verified conventions; another deployment (or a non-LlamaIndex agent) imports them and starts from evidence instead of zero.

body_text:
### Question

`CONTRIBUTING.md` and `close_new_integration_prs.yml` (#21139) say new integration packages are no longer accepted in-tree. Does that also apply when the package completes an existing in-tree provider family?

### Context

OCI Generative AI already has two first-party packages here: `llama-index-llms-oci-genai` and `llama-index-embeddings-oci-genai`. The one missing piece is rerank: OCI serves Cohere rerank models (`cohere.rerank-v4.0-fast`, `-v4.0-pro`, `-v3.5`) through its RerankText API, and Bedrock, Cohere and Google each have a `llama-index-postprocessor-*-rerank` package in-tree, so an OCI user today has LLM + embeddings from this repo and no rerank.

I have `llama-index-postprocessor-oci-genai-rerank` ready, mirroring `bedrock-rerank`/`google-rerank` and reusing the OCI LLM package's auth surface (API key, session token, instance/resource principal, dedicated endpoints): https://github.com/fede-kamel/llama_index/tree/feat-oci-genai-rerank/llama-index-integrations/postprocessor/llama-index-postprocessor-oci-genai-rerank. 20 mocked unit tests (95% coverage), pre-commit clean, verified live against the service including an end-to-end `VectorStoreIndex` + `OCIGenAIEmbeddings` + `OCIGenAIRerank` + `OCIGenAI` query.

### Ask

If the policy is firm, I'll publish it standalone and would appreciate a pointer to wherever external integrations get listed. If completing an existing provider family is an acceptable exception, I'll open the PR and you can wave it past the bot. Either answer is fine; I'd rather ask than have the bot close it.

LlamaIndex already provides MCP ToolSpec/agent tooling, so I am not proposing another agent runtime or a replacement for MCP integration.

I maintain SchemaRouter, which retrieves a query-dependent typed capability/field shortlist from large heterogeneous catalogs before execution. I am evaluating whether that retrieval step composes usefully with existing frameworks.

A narrow LlamaIndex example would discover a deliberately large MCP tool set through the existing MCP integration, use SchemaRouter only to select a bounded typed shortlist for the current query, expose that shortlist through the normal LlamaIndex tool path, and leave LlamaIndex authoritative for agent/RAG orchestration and tool execution.

The comparison would report required-tool recall, schema/context size, task success, latency, unsupported queries, and integration friction for full-catalog vs bounded exposure.

The aim is a reproducible integration/benchmark, not a core dependency. Would maintainers consider this useful, and if so should it live as an MCP integration example or elsewhere? I can prepare code after alignment.

## Request

Please list the external package `llama-index-tools-econdash` on LlamaHub.

`CONTRIBUTING.md` says this repository no longer accepts new integration packages (a PR that adds a `pyproject.toml` is closed automatically). New integrations stay in their own repo and are published to PyPI. This issue is the listing request, in the same spirit as #21413.

## Package

- Name: `llama-index-tools-econdash`
- Import: `llama_index.tools.econdash`
- Classes: `EconDashToolSpec` (`BaseToolSpec`, four tools) and `EconDashReader` (`BaseReader`)
- Source: https://github.com/econdash/econdash-python/tree/main/packages/llama-index-tools-econdash
- Tag: `llamaindex-v0.1.0` (commit `1c64786f04e2cdabe17aec3fb8456bd31258a154`)
- License: MIT
- Depends on: `llama-index-core>=0.12,<0.15` and `econdash>=0.2.3` (on PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/econdash/0.2.3/)
- PyPI project name is reserved for trusted publishing. The upload is waiting on a pending publisher for workflow `publish-llamaindex.yml`, environment `pypi`. I will comment the PyPI URL here as soon as that publish succeeds.

## What it does

`EconDashToolSpec.to_tool_list()` returns `search_indicators`, `get_series`, `get_metadata` and `compare_countries` for the EconDash API (time series across macro, markets, labor, demographics, real estate, energy, transport, health, education and tech). Descriptions are the tool docstrings. Output is a short text summary (last 20 points, citation, chart link). HTTP 402 and 429 become text for the model and do not include figures.

`EconDashReader.load_data(indicators=[...], countries=[...])` returns one `Document` per pair, with metadata `slug`, `iso3`, `source_url`, `data_changed_at` and `license`. A source licence that forbids redistribution is skipped and the series is not fetched.

`pyproject.toml` has the `[tool.llamahub]` block (`import_path = llama_index.tools.econdash`). Examples: `examples/llamaindex_agent.ipynb` and `examples/llamaindex_rag.ipynb`.

## Disclosure

The package was written with coding-agent assistance and checked with the package unit tests, a clean venv install of llama-index-core 0.14.25, and a live free-trial run of both notebooks.

### Bug Description

A run that is idle and waiting for human input is saved with `ctx.to_dict()` and restored into a fresh workflow instance with `Context.from_dict(...)`, as after a process restart. After a restore, the run can lose an event that a list join has already collected. The join then never fires, and the run never ends.

It happens with this shape:

- `start` fans out to `Left` and `Right`.
- `Left` fans out again, to `A` and `B`. Both wait for input.
- `Right` waits for input twice in a row.

The run is saved and restored each time it is idle, and then its pending inputs are answered:

1. First restore: `A` and `B` are answered. The inner join fires and produces `LeftDone`, which the outer join holds while `Right` waits again.
2. Second restore: `Right` is answered and produces `RightDone`. The outer join never fires; `LeftDone` is lost.

Without saving and restoring, the same run ends normally. The bug does not show if any one of these is removed:

- the nesting;
- `A` and `B` waiting for input;
- the second restore.


### Version

llama-index-workflows 2.26.0; also on main (5c55ee3). Python 3.13, macOS 15.

### Steps to Reproduce

Run this script. It runs the workflow once in place, then once with a save and restore at every idle point.

```python
import asyncio

from workflows import Context, Workflow, step
from workflows.events import Event, HumanResponseEvent, InputRequiredEvent, StartEvent, StopEvent, WorkflowIdleEvent


class Left(Event): pass
class Right(Event): n: int = 0
class A(Event): pass
class B(Event): pass
class ADone(Event): pass
class BDone(Event): pass
class LeftDone(Event): pass
class RightDone(Event): pass
class Ask(InputRequiredEvent): waiter: str
class Reply(HumanResponseEvent): waiter: str


async def wait(ctx: Context, waiter: str):
    await ctx.wait_for_event(Reply, waiter_event=Ask(waiter=waiter), waiter_id=waiter,
                             requirements={"waiter": waiter}, timeout=None)


class Nested(Workflow):
    @step
    async def start(self, ev: StartEvent) -> list[Left | Right]:
        return [Left(), Right()]

    @step
    async def left(self, ev: Left) -> list[A | B]:  # A fan-out nested in the first member.
        return [A(), B()]

    @step
    async def a(self, ctx: Context, ev: A) -> ADone:
        await wait(ctx, "a")
        return ADone()

    @step
    async def b(self, ctx: Context, ev: B) -> BDone:
        await wait(ctx, "b")
        return BDone()

    @step
    async def inner(self, events: list[ADone | BDone]) -> LeftDone:
        return LeftDone()

    @step
    async def right(self, ctx: Context, ev: Right) -> Right | RightDone:
        await wait(ctx, f"r{ev.n}")
        return Right(n=1) if ev.n == 0 else RightDone()  # The other member asks twice.

    @step
    async def outer(self, events: list[LeftDone | RightDone]) -> StopEvent:
        return StopEvent(result=sorted(type(item).__name__ for item in events))


async def run(restore: bool):
    workflow = Nested(timeout=None)
    handler = workflow.run()
    stream = handler.stream_events(expose_internal=True)
    while True:
        asks = []
        async for item in stream:  # Until the run is idle, waiting on its requests.
            if isinstance(item, Ask):
                asks.append(item.waiter)
            elif isinstance(item, WorkflowIdleEvent) and asks:
                break
        if not asks:
            return await handler
        print("   asked", asks)
        if restore:  # As after a restart: save the idle run and restore it into a fresh workflow.
            saved = handler.ctx.to_dict()
            await handler.cancel_run()
            try:
                await handler
            except BaseException:
                pass
            workflow = Nested(timeout=None)
            handler = workflow.run(ctx=Context.from_dict(workflow, saved))
            stream = handler.stream_events(expose_internal=True)
            async for item in stream:
                if isinstance(item, WorkflowIdleEvent):  # Restored and waiting again.
                    break
        for waiter in asks:
            handler.ctx.send_event(Reply(waiter=waiter))


for restore in (False, True):
    print("restored each time:" if restore else "in place:")
    try:
        print("  ", asyncio.run(asyncio.wait_for(run(restore), 10)))
    except TimeoutError:
        print("   no result within 10 s")
```

Expected: both runs print `['LeftDone', 'RightDone']`.
Actual: the restored run never ends.

### Relevant Logs/Tracebacks

```shell
in place:
   asked ['r0', 'b', 'a']
   asked ['r1']
   ['LeftDone', 'RightDone']
restored each time:
   asked ['r0', 'a', 'b']
   asked ['r1']
   no result within 10 s
```

body_text:
LlamaIndex users running bulk, non-latency-sensitive LLM workloads (evaluation sweeps, corpus extraction, synthetic data generation) currently pay full synchronous API pricing; OpenAI and Anthropic batch endpoints cost roughly half. Instructor demonstrates a complete implementation: BatchProcessor with per-provider request serialization, a CLI for job list/create/cancel/delete, and tests covering BytesIO in-memory submission to both providers. Julep's design notes add two useful constraints: custom_id should be globally unique ({run_id}:{cid}) because bare ids collide across runs, and OpenAI requires one model per input file, so a mixed batch must be sub-split by the adapter. Proposal: a small batch abstraction in llama-index-core (request + job handle types) with adapters in the existing OpenAI/Anthropic llm packages — no new integration package, per CONTRIBUTING.md. Scope: request serialization to each provider's format, submit/poll/cancel, per-entry result mapping by custom_id, and per-entry error fallback to the synchronous path. Static evidence only: in the supplied repository files the sole batch facility is BatchEvalRunner, so the gap claim is limited to the checked paths. Needs maintainer direction on where the abstraction lives before implementation.

## Research evidence (static; tests pending)

- https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/619d74664e8404612038bc15a1a40c686037277c/llama-index-core/tests/evaluation/test_batch_runner.py
  > from llama_index.core.evaluation.batch_runner import BatchEvalRunner
- https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/blob/619d74664e8404612038bc15a1a40c686037277c/CONTRIBUTING.md
  > we are no longer accepting new integration packages
- https://github.com/567-labs/instructor/blob/035c77b7b04dbbf70ae4457eb102038907b5a2a4/instructor/cli/batch.py
  > from instructor.batch import BatchProcessor, BatchJobInfo
- https://github.com/567-labs/instructor/blob/035c77b7b04dbbf70ae4457eb102038907b5a2a4/tests/test_batch_in_memory.py
  > provider.submit_batch(buffer)
- https://github.com/julep-ai/julep/blob/fc74d079a18c8124b2627ca4717f5a9c269267db/docs/plans/2026-06-21-cross-run-brain-batching.md
  > the provider async **Batch API** (Anthropic Message Batches, OpenAI
Batch), which trades latency for ~50% cost

### Users

Users running large offline workloads: bulk evaluation over datasets, batch ingestion/summarization, keyword or metadata extraction over corpora, and synthetic data generation. Today they pay full synchronous API prices or hand-roll batch submission outside the library.

### Expected Effect

Up to ~50% cost reduction on bulk LLM workloads via provider batch endpoints, with a uniform API to submit a set of prompts, poll job status, and map results back to each request.

### Scope

A small batch abstraction in llama-index-core (batch request + job handle types) plus adapters in the existing OpenAI (and Anthropic if present) llm integration packages. No new pyproject.toml — new integration packages are auto-closed. Exact files must be confirmed with maintainers since the llm package sources were not supplied.

### Validation

uv run -- pytest in each touched package. Mocked tests: serialize N requests to each provider's format (assert custom_id round-trip), submit via BytesIO and file, poll status transitions, parse results back to per-request responses, per-entry error promotion to a sync call. Expected: new tests pass; existing suites unchanged.

### Risks

Provider formats differ (OpenAI requires one model per input file; Anthropic mixes models inline); results are unordered so custom_id routing is mandatory; a wrong abstraction in core is hard to unship; maintainer design sign-off required before implementation.

### Effort

Multiple days: core request/job dataclasses, two provider adapters, submit/poll/cancel, error promotion, mocked test suites, and docs.

### Acceptance

Moderate. CONTRIBUTING.md welcomes extensions to core and main integrations, and a cost-saving provider feature fits the project direction. But it is a new API surface, needs design approval, and no maintainer requested it in the supplied evidence.

### Comparison

instructor: implemented — BatchProcessor plus provider adapters plus CLI plus in-memory submission tests. julep: plan only — BATCH QoS design with custom_id routing, no code in supplied files. llama_index target: in checked paths only BatchEvalRunner (concurrent eval), no provider batch endpoint path observed.

Maintainer direction requested before implementation.

AI-assisted contribution.

### Feature Description

Hey team 👋

When autonomous AI agents execute shell commands or code loops, prompt injections and hallucinations can accidentally run destructive commands (e.g., `rm -rf`, environment secret exfiltration, or unauthorized process spawns).

We built a lightweight, pre-execution security engine in Python & FastAPI that intercepts command strings at the execution boundary and blocks threats in **~1.3ms to 3ms** before they hit the terminal.

### 🛡️ Key Features:
* **Sub-3ms Overhead:** Zero noticeable delay in agent execution loops.
* **48/48 Integration Tests:** Benchmark-verified on live terminal agent workflows.
* **Zero-Network Privacy Option:** Runs 100% offline via local Python import or through a hosted API endpoint.

Would you be open to an opt-in pre-execution security hook for your repo, or trying a free test API key for your core maintainer team this week?

cc @epage @joshtriplett @ehuss @weihanglo @Byron

This asks the Cargo team to settle four related parts of `-Z bindeps` (currently unstable): how features are shared, whether versions remain shared, whether `lib = true` remains, and how artifact dependencies appear in `cargo metadata`. An artifact dependency asks Cargo to build a binary, static library, or dynamic library from another package and provide the resulting path to a crate or build script.

I propose:

1. Features requested by one artifact dependency do not affect any other use of that package, including its transitive dependencies.
2. Several outputs requested by one dependency continue to share features.
3. Versions remain shared across the entire Cargo dependency tree.
4. `lib = true` is retired for new manifests.
5. Metadata reports one structured record per artifact dependency rather than one record per output.

Here, a dependency declaration means one named entry in `[dependencies]`, `[build-dependencies]`, or `[dev-dependencies]`. This proposal does not change feature sharing between ordinary dependencies outside an artifact dependency's tree, or stabilize any part of `-Z bindeps`.

## Current behavior and the problem

Suppose `schema` contains a code generator binary and the runtime library used by its generated code:

```toml
[dependencies]
schema-runtime = { package = "schema", version = "1", features = ["runtime"] }

[build-dependencies]
schema-codegen = { package = "schema", version = "1", artifact = "bin:schema-codegen", features = ["cli"] }
```

Cargo builds `schema-codegen` before the build script runs and exposes its path through a `CARGO_BIN_FILE_...` environment variable. The parent crate links the `schema` library as `schema_runtime`. Resolver v2 already keeps their features separate because one is a normal dependency and the other is a build dependency. Cargo selects one version of `schema` for both.

[RFC 3176](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3176) permits several names for the same package. Cargo still rejects that case today; [#17067](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/pull/17067) implements it without changing feature behavior. It can land before this design is settled. With that PR applied, this becomes valid:

```toml
[build-dependencies]
schema-json = { package = "schema", version = "1", artifact = "bin:schema-codegen", features = ["json"] }
schema-protobuf = { package = "schema", version = "1", artifact = "bin:schema-codegen", features = ["protobuf"] }
```

#17067 keeps Cargo's current rule of selecting features by package and artifact target. Because these declarations have the same package and target, both generator builds receive `json` and `protobuf`. The features need not conflict for this to be surprising: an optional parser, backend, or logging stack requested for one generator also changes the other.

I propose that `schema-json` receive `json` and `schema-protobuf` receive `protobuf`. The separation follows their normal and build dependencies as well. The same rule applies when an artifact and an ordinary library dependency use the same package and dependency kind: features requested through the artifact do not move in either direction between the two declarations.

All outputs listed by one declaration still share features. They describe products of one requested build. Users who need different feature sets can write separate declarations.

This change can compile the same package and its transitive dependencies more than once. That increases build time and target-directory size. Nightly users whose builds rely on a feature being enabled indirectly through another declaration may also stop compiling, and `cargo tree` and `--unit-graph` will show separate builds. No stable behavior, lockfile, or stable metadata changes, so this remains inexpensive to reverse before stabilization.

## How we arrived here

[RFC 3028](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3028) introduced artifact dependencies and `lib = true`; [#9992](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/pull/9992) implemented them. It kept version selection unified and separated features when an artifact was built for a different target.

RFC 3176 added same-package aliases. It says Cargo combines declarations for a given artifact target and separates features only across different targets. Declaration-private features reverse that part of the accepted design, so they require an RFC amendment and explicit Cargo team agreement.

## Why keep version selection shared?

Independent versions have a real benefit. For example, a generator might require `helper >=1,<1.5` while the runtime requires `helper >=1.8,<2`. Cargo treats those versions as compatible and tries to select one, so the build cannot resolve. Independent artifact resolution could select both.

I do not think that benefit currently justifies the implementation cost. Cargo identifies resolved packages by name, version, and source throughout the resolver, lockfile, metadata, and package-selection commands. Independent resolution would require another identity for each occurrence, a new lockfile format, new `cargo update` and `[patch]` rules, and cycle handling for nested artifacts. It would also increase duplicate downloads and builds. Users encountering the conflict must currently align the requirements, patch a dependency, fork one side, or build the tool separately.

We do not have evidence that this problem is common enough to warrant that system-wide change. Shared versions also help keep a code generator and runtime on compatible releases. This proposal therefore retains the behavior required by RFCs 3028 and 3176. Version isolation can return as a separate proposal if real use cases justify its cost.

## Why retire `lib = true`?

The original syntax can ask one declaration for both an artifact and the package's Rust library:

```toml
[dependencies]
schema = { version = "1", artifact = "bin:schema-codegen", lib = true, features = ["json"] }
```

The one `features` list then controls two relationships with different sharing rules: an artifact with private features and a library using Cargo's ordinary feature behavior. Separate declarations state those roles directly, as in the first example. This is not a mechanical rewrite: each new declaration must list the features its role needs. The split becomes possible once #17067 permits two names for one package.

`lib = true` should become an error in new manifests, and `cargo publish` should stop writing it. Cargo should continue parsing the field in registry entries published by older nightly versions, but apply the new feature rule. Already-published nightly packages that relied on features being shared between the library and artifact may therefore need an update. Preserving the old behavior would require a permanent second sharing model in the resolver, which does not seem worthwhile for an unstable feature. This is another change to RFC 3028 and belongs in the same amendment.

## Alternative: opt-in feature isolation

@epage [suggested](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/pull/17067#issuecomment-5136584239) preserving today's sharing rule and using a future “opaque dependency” feature for isolation. In behavioral terms, users would add a separate option when they want one declaration's features not to combine with another use of the package.

A general option may be useful, but artifact dependencies already name separately built products and select their targets and outputs. Requiring another option would make sharing the default even though it is not visible from these declarations. I prefer private features as the artifact default; a general mechanism could later reuse the implementation.

## Implementation

2. Several outputs requested by one dependency continue to share features.
3. Versions remain shared across the entire Cargo dependency tree.

Suppose `schema` contains a code generator binary and the runtime library used by its generated code:

```

Cargo builds `schema-codegen` before the build script runs and exposes its path through a `CARGO_BIN_FILE_...` environment variable. The parent crate links the `schema` library as `schema_runtime`. Resolver v2 already keeps their features separate because one is a normal dependency and the other is a build dependency. Cargo selects one version of `schema` for both.

### Problem

This has been requested here: https://users.rust-lang.org/t/suppress-clippy-autofix-for-certain-rules/91483

Right now, if a user wishes to disable autofixes for certain lints, they can either a) disable autofix entirely or b) silence the lints in question, not only preventing their autofixes from being applied, but disabling them from being surfaced entirely. Neither is satisfactory.

A common use case is a fix-on-save workflow where you want to apply fixes for some lints while still surfacing others (so you don't miss them), but not autofixing those other ones, such as the `unused_` lints whose autofixes can be intrusive while typing.

### Proposed Solution

The goal is to decouple "I want a lint shown" from "I want a lint fix applied" in a `--fix` setup.
For that, I propose a new, repeatable flag (`--no-fix`) to cargo fix (and therefore also to cargo clippy --fix) such that:
1. selected lints get autofixed (as usual)
2. using the flag, you can specify certain lints which are excluded from the set of autofixed lints
3. the specified lints still have their lints surfaced.

### Notes

The implementation works for clippy and rustc lints. The flag is repeated for every lint to exclude from autofixing, and clippy lints are namespaced (rustc ones aren't). e.g. `cargo fix --allow-no-vcs --no-fix clippy::clone_on_copy --no-fix unused_imports`

#### discussion and alternatives explored
- "just silence the lints": `-A lint` (e.g. via `env RUSTFLAGS="-Aunused_variables" cargo fix --allow-dirty` or the equivalent `cargo clippy --fix --allow-dirty -- -A unused_variables`) is not an alternative. It doesn't surface the `unused_variables` lint. The goal of this change is to allow "warning, but not autofixing", not "disabling both the warning and autofixing".
- "just change/fix the lints if they're disruptive": boils down to user preference, and this shouldn't be up to the tooling to decide. This incledes situations where refactoring or fixing is done in an automated fashion, such as during interactions with CI, where users might want to exclude some fixes but still have all of them surfaced in logs. Tooling itself should be maximally composable.
- "you shouldnt enable autofix in your ide" / "use `ctrl + .` on every lint": is just an opinion of equal value as "you should enable autofix in your ide"
- r-a could expose some kind of "fix" layer: currently, `cargo fix` is driven via  `"rust-analyzer.check.command": "clippy"` with `"extraArgs"` to enable `--fix` in user configurations (e.g. VS Code, Zed). Rust-analyzer does not support this, aand as far as I can tell, neither do modern editors (even if r-a had it). @ChayimFriedman2 has suggested the proposed approach would currently work well.

#### (tangentially) related issues
- https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/13029 - the workaround proposed therein doesn't interact well with configuring lints in Cargo.toml, while this does
- https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/11125

#### implementation plan
I have already implemented this and plan to submit a PR if this this feature is accepted without requiring an RFC.
`cargo fix` architecture is a bit odd, but flexible enough to make adding this functionality (in the same "json serializing  and passing to cargo in proxy mode" style already in use for other features) trivial.

#### open questions and future work
1) This should probably be configurable in the `.toml` file
2) There's possibly a missing interaction with range diffs: format on save supports them, this does not. Seems out of scope for cargo
3) related to 1) and 2): modern editors have integration for only formatting changed lines when a project does not enforce rustfmt formatting. How would this work for fixes being applied across the entire codebase? Probably out of scope too.
4) flag name. I chose `--no-fix` but haven't given this much thought.

My project does contain submodules which are not initialized in the job in which `cargo publish` runs in.
While I don't directly see a dependency to my submodules for `cargo publish`, it should not fail in the way it does regardless, since it's not really obvious what's wrong or that it tries to access the submodules.

In the official [GitLab CI template for Rust](https://gitlab.com/to-be-continuous/rust/) I also don't see any mention in regards to the submodule strategy.
The default Gitlab CI `GIT_SUBMODULE_STRATEGY` is `none`, meaning no submodules are initialized.

What I expect to happen is at least some kind of error message that it detected uninitialized submodules or that it ignores the fact that the submodules are not initialized.

### Steps

1. Setup a cargo project which includes a submodule
2. Create a GitLab CI pipeline which uses `cargo publish` and uses the default `GIT_SUBMODULE_STRATEGY: none`
3. Run the pipeline and the `cargo publish` should fail with `error: No such file or directory (os error 2)`

My project does contain submodules which are not initialized in the job in which `cargo publish` runs in.
While I don't directly see a dependency to my submodules for `cargo publish`, it should not fail in the way it does regardless, since it's not really obvious what's wrong or that it tries to access the submodules.

In the official [GitLab CI template for Rust](https://gitlab.com/to-be-continuous/rust/) I also don't see any mention in regards to the submodule strategy.
The default Gitlab CI `GIT_SUBMODULE_STRATEGY` is `none`, meaning no submodules are initialized.

What I expect to happen is at least some kind of error message that it detected uninitialized submodules or that it ignores the fact that the submodules are not initialized.

### Steps

1. Setup a cargo project which includes a submodule
2. Create a GitLab CI pipeline which uses `cargo publish` and uses the default `GIT_SUBMODULE_STRATEGY: none`
3. Run the pipeline and the `cargo publish` should fail with `error: No such file or directory (os error 2)`

### Problem

I sometimes struggle with using lints (in general) because of outdated or missing documentation. I've had lints be completely absent from documentation and had documentation listing only the old name of a renamed lint, for example. It can also be tricky to keep track of when new lints are available.

I've found that it is much more reliable to trust the tool providing the lints to tell me what lints are available. This also allows tools to parse this output and use it, and improves access to information when developers are offline. For example, [the lints crate], which parses the output of `rustc -Whelp`, or the [similar tool] I started working on recently for myself, which parses the output of `clippy-driver -Whelp`. I also plan to parse the output of `rustdoc -Whelp` in the future (I don't need to parse `rustc -Whelp` because both `clippy-driver -Whelp` and `rustdoc -Whelp` currently include the same information). I have found no way to get similar information about the lints recently added to Cargo, which it seems I can only learn about by encountering them or reading the online documentation.

[the lints crate]: https://crates.io/crates/lints
[similar tool]: https://github.com/hashcatHitman/lint-wizard

### Proposed Solution

I would like there to be some way to get:
- All lint groups defined by Cargo
- Which lints are in those groups
- All lints defined by Cargo
- The default level of those lints

From the command line. Sticking to the `-Whelp` convention might be nice, something like `cargo -Whelp` or `cargo lint -Whelp`, perhaps.

Ideally, this should be done in a way that derives this information directly from the lints available in that particular version of Cargo. That is, if Cargo `x.y.z` has `lint_i`, and Cargo `a.b.c` adds `lint_j`, where `a.b.c` is some version greater than `x.y.z`, I would expect Cargo `x.y.z` to report `lint_i`, and I would expect Cargo `a.b.c` to report both `lint_i` and `lint_j`. The addition of `lint_j` should automatically make it part of this output; it should not need to be something people remember to do, like updating documentation. Going back to Cargo `x.y.z` should report only `lint_i` as before, as `lint_j` isn't available.

body_text:
### Problem


I maintain a monorepo containing several Rust projects as subtrees. During development, I use `[patch]` entries to make those projects compile against local versions of shared dependencies. The same patches are also needed when building the system with Nix.

This works for compilation, but Cargo writes patch information into `Cargo.lock`. That creates unwanted changes from normal editor activity, including rust-analyzer or even just from running cargo normally, and makes the lockfile describe the local development setup instead of the dependency declared by the package, which adds unwanted changes in git and makes the packages impossible to be compiled separately without modifying the lock file all the time.

For example, a dependency declared from crates.io or GitHub should continue to point to that source in `Cargo.lock`, even when a local path patch is used during development. Unused patch entries should not be added either.


### Proposed Solution


Add a boolean configuration option:

```toml
[resolver]
write-patches-to-lockfile = false
```

When disabled, Cargo should:

- Continue applying patches during dependency resolution and compilation.
- Avoid writing `[[patch.unused]]` entries.
- Ignore existing `[[patch.unused]]` entries when reading the lockfile.
- Preserve the original dependency source in `Cargo.lock`, including crates.io or GitHub sources.
- Preserve the existing lockfile contents when applying a patch does not otherwise change the dependency graph.

The default should remain `true` for compatibility with current Cargo behavior.


### Notes

I have vibecoded an ad-hoc patch to borrow myself some time to develop the main project while this feature is not in standard cargo. It's available at https://github.com/ardos-os/cargo/tree/codex/lockfile-patch-sources
If you're fine upstreaming that exact code I can submit a pull request or if you want to change something in the implementation, i'm available to make those adjustments.

### What it does

Checks that all `include[_*]?`d files are within the `cargo` workspace.

### Advantage

No release with missing files.

### Drawbacks

I'm not sure if `cargo` can have this information and `rustc` doesn't have enough information either.

### Example

```rust
fn main() {
    let x = include_str!("/etc/passwd");
}
```

### Problem

Two concurrent `cargo check`s of the same workspace with `-Zfine-grain-locking` often deadlock from a clean state. Both processes stop using CPU, and each waits on a build unit lock the other holds. We first hit it with two cross builds that used separate `--target-dir`s and one shared `build.build-dir`.

### Steps

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
dir=$(mktemp -d) && cd "$dir"
printf '[workspace]\nmembers = ["app", "dep*"]\nresolver = "3"\n' > Cargo.toml
for i in $(seq 1 16); do
  mkdir -p dep$i/src
  printf '[package]\nname = "dep%s"\nversion = "0.1.0"\nedition = "2024"\n' $i > dep$i/Cargo.toml
  for k in $(seq 1 400); do echo "pub fn f$k(x: u64) -> u64 { (0..$((k % 40 + 1))).fold(x, |a, b| a.wrapping_mul(31).rotate_left(b) ^ $k) }"; done > dep$i/src/lib.rs
done
mkdir -p app/src
{ printf '[package]\nname = "app"\nversion = "0.1.0"\nedition = "2024"\n\n[dependencies]\n'
  for i in $(seq 1 16); do echo "dep$i = { path = \"../dep$i\" }"; done; } > app/Cargo.toml
echo 'fn main() { println!("{}", dep1::f1(1) ^ dep8::f1(8)); }' > app/src/main.rs

for attempt in $(seq 1 8); do
  rm -rf target
  timeout 60 cargo +nightly -Zfine-grain-locking check -p app >/dev/null 2>&1 & a=$!
  timeout 60 cargo +nightly -Zfine-grain-locking check -p app >/dev/null 2>&1 & b=$!
  wait $a; ra=$?; wait $b; rb=$?
  echo "attempt $attempt: exit $ra / $rb"  # 124 = hung until the timeout
done
```

7 of 8 attempts hang here. Without `-Zfine-grain-locking`, none do.

`/proc/locks` during a hang, from a run with 8 dependency crates:

```
debug/build/dep1/6634f7d28328c938/.lock: held shared by B, exclusive wanted by A
debug/build/dep2/0df4cbf1d5349301/.lock: held shared by A, exclusive wanted by B
debug/build/dep3/70818309f13b4c2a/.lock: held shared by A, exclusive wanted by B
debug/build/dep4/403e3d501cf46364/.lock: held shared by B, exclusive wanted by A
...
```

### Cause

Both processes find all units dirty. [`compile`](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/blob/98a09e7e7d62850f14e5b6132101fc1edd19a16f/src/compiler/mod.rs#L255-L270) wraps each dirty job in a blocking exclusive lock, then downgrades to a shared lock that it keeps for the rest of the build. A builds `dep2` while B builds `dep1`. Each then keeps a shared lock on its own unit and waits for an exclusive lock on the other's.

The failures in #16657's Windows CI may have been this. The known issue in #4282 about a shared dirty unit blocking is a permanent deadlock once there are two such units.

### Version

```
cargo 1.100.0-nightly (98a09e7e7 2026-09-21)
Linux x86_64
```

{"repository": "rust-lang/cargo", "task_candidate_id": 22573, "repository_id": 255, "issue_number": 17508, "github_issue_id": 5565682435, "html_url": "https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/17508", "created_at": "2026-09-24T08:45:25+00:00", "author_association": "NONE", "title": "`-Zfine-grain-locking`: concurrent builds deadlock when both compile the same units", "body_text": "### Problem

Two concurrent `cargo check`s of the same workspace with `-Zfine-grain-locking` often deadlock from a clean state. Both processes stop using CPU, and each waits on a build unit lock the other holds. We first hit it with two cross builds that used separate `--target-dir`s and one shared `build.build-dir`.

### Steps

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -u
dir=$(mktemp -d) && cd "$dir"
printf '[workspace]\nmembers = ["app", "dep*"]\nresolver = "3"\n' > Cargo.toml
for i in $(seq 1 16); do
  mkdir -p dep$i/src
  printf '[package]\nname = "dep%s"\nversion = "0.1.0"\nedition = "2024"\n' $i > dep$i/Cargo.toml
  for k in $(seq 1 400); do echo "pub fn f$k(x: u64) -> u64 { (0..$((k % 40 + 1))).fold(x, |a, b| a.wrapping_mul(31).rotate_left(b) ^ $k) }"; done > dep$i/src/lib.rs
done
mkdir -p app/src
{ printf '[package]\nname = "app"\nversion = "0.1.0"\nedition = "2024"\n\n[dependencies]\n'
  for i in $(seq 1 16); do echo "dep$i = { path = \"../dep$i\" }"; done; } > app/Cargo.toml
echo 'fn main() { println!("{}", dep1::f1(1) ^ dep8::f1(8)); }' > app/src/main.rs

for attempt in $(seq 1 8); do
  rm -rf target
  timeout 60 cargo +nightly -Zfine-grain-locking check -p app >/dev/null 2>&1 & a=$!
  timeout 60 cargo +nightly -Zfine-grain-locking check -p app >/dev/null 2>&1 & b=$!
  wait $a; ra=$?; wait $b; rb=$?
  echo "attempt $attempt: exit $ra / $rb"  # 124 = hung until the timeout
done
```

7 of 8 attempts hang here. Without `-Zfine-grain-locking`, none do.

`/proc/locks` during a hang, from a run with 8 dependency crates:

```
debug/build/dep1/6634f7d28328c938/.lock: held shared by B, exclusive wanted by A
debug/build/dep2/0df4cbf1d5349301/.lock: held shared by A, exclusive wanted by B
debug/build/dep3/70818309f13b4c2a/.lock: held shared by A, exclusive wanted by B
debug/build/dep4/403e3d501cf46364/.lock: held shared by B, exclusive wanted by A
...
```

### Cause

Both processes find all units dirty. [`compile`](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/blob/98a09e7e7d62850f14e5b6132101fc1edd19a16f/src/compiler/mod.rs#L255-L270) wraps each dirty job in a blocking exclusive lock, then downgrades to a shared lock that it keeps for the rest of the build. A builds `dep2` while B builds `dep1`. Each then keeps a shared lock on its own unit and waits for an exclusive lock on the other's.

The failures in #16657's Windows CI may have been this. The known issue in #4282 about a shared dirty unit blocking is a permanent deadlock once there are two such units.

### Version

cargo 1.100.0-nightly (98a09e7e7 2026-09-21)

body_text:
### Problem

So, the specific use case I'm running into here is `allocator-api2` for the `hashbrown` crate, which is enabled by default for MSRV reasons: even though `allocator_api` was *just* stabilised on nightly, we still need it for most users.

However, *with* the `nightly` feature, we explicitly do not use this dependency at all, and thus it gets reported as unused. The only way to fix this would be to use `--no-default-features` alongside the `nightly` feature, plus every feature *except* `allocator-api2`, to avoid the unused dependency.

It would be nice if, in this case, we could simply mark this one case as being acceptable as an unused dependency, rather than completely disabling the lint. Or even `expect(...)` the lint somehow and acknowledge it.

### Steps

_No response_

### Possible Solution(s)

Since the resolver is additive, we should not have some way to disable certain feature combinations, but we could have a way to accept unused dependencies when certain features are enabled. For example, in this case, specifically configure the lint to state that, whenever the `nightly` feature is enabled, `allocator-api2` will be unused. In this case, cargo should be able to determine that, since `allocator-api2` is an optional dependency, it will only be unused if it's explicitly enabled.

### Notes

_No response_

body_text:
### Problem

`cargo::unused_dependencies` misfires when a build-dependency is only used by `package.metabuild`.

### Steps

Create crates at `./` and `metabuild-helper/`. Use `metabuild-helper` in the former crate's `Cargo.toml`:

```toml
cargo-features = ["metabuild"]

[package]
name = "unused-deps-repro"
edition = "2024"
metabuild = ["metabuild-helper"]

[build-dependencies]
metabuild-helper = { path = "metabuild-helper" }
```

This produces warning:

```console
$ cargo +nightly check
warning: unused build dependency `metabuild-helper`
  --> Cargo.toml:10:1
   |
10 | metabuild-helper = { path = "metabuild-helper" }
   | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
   |
   = note: `cargo::unused_dependencies` is set to `warn` by default
help: consider removing the dependency on `metabuild-helper`
warning: `unused-deps-repro` (manifest) generated 1 warning
   Compiling unused-deps-repro v0.1.0 (/tmp/20260925)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.06s
```

Removing it following the suggestion breaks the build:

```console
$ cargo +nightly check
error: failed to parse manifest at `/tmp/unused-deps-repro/Cargo.toml`

Caused by:
  metabuild package `metabuild-helper` must be specified in `build-dependencies`
```

_No response_

### Problem

There is currently no convenient way to remove lint acknowledgements from a project.

During development, it can be useful to suppress warnings temporarily with `#[allow(...)]` or `#[expect(...)]`, either manually or with `cargo fix`. Once the code has settled, however, you may want to see those warnings again and reassess them.

At the moment, this requires finding and removing the acknowledgements manually, or disabling acknowledgements.

### Proposed Solution

Add a `cargo unfix` command.

By default, `cargo unfix` would remove outer `#[allow(...)]` attributes from the project.

Additional options could extend its scope:

> `cargo unfix --expect`

Also remove `#[expect(...)]` attributes.

> `cargo unfix --inner`

Also remove inner lint attributes (`#![allow(...)]`, and `#![expect(...)]` when `--expect` is used).

> `cargo unfix --manifest`

Also handle lint configuration in `Cargo.toml` (potentially with comments, see notes).

The options would be composable:

> `cargo unfix --expect --inner --manifest`

Remove `#[allow(...)]` and `#[expect(...)]` attributes, including inner lint attributes from the project, and handle lint configuration in `Cargo.toml`.

### Notes

`cargo unfix` would not attempt to reverse the source changes made by `cargo fix`. It would specifically remove lint acknowledgements so that the compiler can report those lints again.

For `Cargo.toml`, lint configuration could be commented out rather than deleted, preserving the previous configuration, as lingering comments would likely be convenient in the future, and cause little headache compared to commented acknowledgements in code:

```
[lints.rust]
# dead_code = "allow"
# unused_variables = "allow"
```

A `--lint <lint>` option could also allow removing acknowledgements for only a particular lint:

`cargo unfix --lint dead_code`

The intended workflow would be:

```
cargo fix
# work on the project
cargo unfix
# see the warnings again
```

### Problem

The Makefile-style dependency file generated by cargo doesn't escape backslashes in filenames properly.

Create the following source tree in an empty cargo project:

`src/main.rs`

```rust
include!("a\\ b.rs"); // file name: `a\ b.rs` (backslash, then a space)
include!("c\\"); // file name: `c\` (ends in a backslash)
include!("d.rs");

fn main() {
    println!("{}", A + C + D);
}
```

`src/a\ b.rs`

```rust
const A: u8 = 1;
```

`src/d.rs`

```rust
const D: u8 = 3;
```

`src/c\`

```rust
const C: u8 = 2;
```

This generates a `.d` file as follows:

```
.../target/debug/depinfo-repro: .../src/a\\ b.rs .../src/c\ src/d.rs .../src/main.rs
```

`make` parses this as a file named `a`, another file named `b.rs`, and another file named `c src/d.rs`. Perhaps there are two separate bugs, because I think a full path should've been printed for `d.rs`.

The correct escaping (as interpreted by `make`) is that every backslash and space in a filename should be escaped with a backslash. This way the escaping is unambiguous.

_No response_

_No response_

### Problem

`profile.trim-paths` was stabilized in #17488, but Cargo passes no remap flags to `rustdoc --test` at all.

rustdoc is stabilizing `--remap-path-scope` and the new `documentation` scope in rust-lang/rust#163895 (and rust-lang/rust#163896 for rustc).

We should figure out a way to integrate trim-paths to doctest.

### Proposed Solution

* Pass the same remap rules from `trim_paths_remap` to `rustdoc --test` when `trim-paths` is not `"none"`, for both consistency and cases where a source path isn't within workspace.
* Which scope to pass for `"object"` is unclear.
  rustdoc seems to gate `file!` (and everything) behind `documentation` rather than `macro`, which is a bit weird.
  Cargo may either
  1. map `"object"` to `object,documentation` for doctests, or
  2. ask rustdoc to honor `macro` for doctest paths (so that `documentation` scope remains for real docs stuff not doctest)
  3. expose `documentation` scope.

### Note

This is best discussed with t-rustdoc and @Urgau, especially before the stabilization on rustdoc/rustc side.

rustdoc is stabilizing `--remap-path-scope` and the new `documentation` scope in rust-lang/rust#163895 (and rust-lang/rust#163896 for rustc).

We should figure out the difference between `documentation` and `all` scope, and when should we pass what.

### Proposed Solution

Not until we figure out what rustdoc does.

### Notes

This is best discussed with t-rustdoc and @Urgau, especially before the stabilization on rustdoc/rustc side.

### Problem

This is a weird issue, though I feel like this will become an issue hurting <https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/pull/17512> and <https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/17453>.

Some background, Cargo generates two (actually more) kinds of dep-info files during a rustc compilation

* rustc's dep-info
  * This is from `rustc --emit=dep-info` along with the rlib/rmeta compilation
  * source dependency paths are absolute in this dep-info
  * Once this is translated to the Cargo ad-hoc one, this is no longer used.
* Cargo's ad-hoc dep-info file (fingerprint)
  * The purpose of this is a relocatable when the package location or the target directory is moved

  * This is derived from the rustc dep-info file.

I was using a patched sccache that support cache reuse from different workspace path (with different CARGO_HOME). The bug is like this:

1. Workspace FOO compiles `hex`. rustc writes `hex-*.d` depinfo listing `<CARGO_HOME_FOO>/registry/src/.../hex-0.4.3/src/lib.rs`. Under sccache (or any tool that caches rustc outputs) that dep-info file is cached.
2. Now delete workspace FOO as we are in a different machine/host.
3. Workspace BAR compiles `hex` at a different path and a different `CARGO_HOME_BAR`. sccache hits and restores FOO's `.d`. However, when translating FOO's rustc dep-info, given the path is not under BAR's pkg root or the build dir, the translated dep-info now contains absolute path (based on [the logic in `translate_dep_info`](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/blob/8d91d31c70c6c32b60e5e55562a022ec51b857ff/src/compiler/fingerprint/dep_info.rs#L355-L367)). 
4. 💥 If you build BAR again, it would look at the translated dep-info file's `<CARGO_HOME_FOO>/.../hex-0.4.3/src/lib.rs`, and found nothing. Then it consider recompilation is needed `hex`, so scache request for cache again, and restore the same bad dep-info file, (and Cargo translated that to Cargo dep-info file that still contain `<CARGO_HOME_FOO>/.../lib.rs`)

This is stuck forever in BAR, even it is a cache hit, it still go through the roundtrip of cache request.

This happens to git and registry dependencies, which is extremely weird and unnecessary, as we expect they are immutable, but because CARGO_HOME changes they are not skipped anymore. See: 

https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/blob/784be26fd122c9d181def7d5241c2f5adcc042f1/src/compiler/fingerprint/mod.rs#L2136-L2144









### Steps

I can share some LLM reproducible scripts, but I don't think they are pleasant to review. Let me know if you want some.

### Possible Solution(s)

Looks like absolute path support in Cargo dep-info was added to addresss rustc bootstrap's issue (see rust-lang/cargo#7030), along with `-Zbinary-dep-depinfo`. I wonder if we should special case git and registry dependencies not to track their source file paths at all in Cargo dep-info, given we already aussme they are immutable. That said, it would fall short if people has absolute path like `include_bytes!("/usr/lib/openssl.so")` (which is also rare, machine-dependent, and a anti-pattern).

For keeping the support of `-Zbinary-dep-depinfo`, given it is a special case if the dep path is from sysroot then track it. I don't know if this covers every scenario though.

I am actually not sure though, it is a bit messy.

### Notes

Some other relevant issues:

* mozilla/sccache#984 — this is a similar the issue, though just a different way describing it.
* rust-lang/rust#63329 — this was also a similar issue (can't found path so always rebuild), though got fixed by not applying `--remap-path-prefix` to dep-info files in rust-lang/rust#63342.
* If per shared build cache store becomes a thing, Cargo then is both consumer and producer of the dep-info, and we'll be bitten by this issue. Of course if it were per-user store it is fine as we don't expect one user has different CARGO_HOME across workspaces. That said, it makes sharing artifact store across hosts/users hard to happen (rust-lang/cargo#17453)

body_text:
### What it does

It is possible to create a workspace with a member that is not in the workspace directory:
```toml
[workspace]
members = ["foo", "../external-package"]
resolver = "3"
```

This lead to problems like missing members once its committed to version control.

### Advantage

* Avoids a missing member not being added to version control
* Keeps all workspace crates within a single directory

### Drawbacks

Could be a bit annoying for users with niche setups where a workspace is purposefully creating members in other directories. (though I can't think of any usecases to do this off the top of my head)

### Example

```toml
members = ["../external-package"]
```

Could be written as:

```toml
members = ["relative-package"]
```

## Problem

Found in rust-lang/rust#164086.

Cargo accepts `crate-type = ["lib"]` together with `proc-macro = true` and compiles an ordinary library while treating it as a proc-macro internally for some logic.
The behavior is pretty inconsistent.

This became visible after rust-lang/cargo#17410

A binary using that library now fails with some error like:

```text
error[E0463]: can't find crate for `dep` which `foo` depends on
```

## Steps

See rust-lang/rust#164086

## Possible Solution(s)

For the short term, maybe we should treat this as an ordinary rlib consistently, including the internal `proc_macro` and `for_host` flags. Explicit `crate-type` takes precedence when invoking rustc, so our internal flags should follow I feel like.

Later, we may want to warn on this combination and eventually reject it during manifest validation.

## Notes

The inconsistency already existed before #17410, see some evidence below

* explicit crate type takes precedence: https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/blob/e8cb624d5701824f46a2ec5873cfd59ee3d2f66c/src/workspace/parser/targets.rs#L242-L264
* however, `configure` still sets `proc_macro` and `for_host` from the manifest: https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/blob/e8cb624d5701824f46a2ec5873cfd59ee3d2f66c/src/workspace/parser/targets.rs#L939-L952
* then later [#17410](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/pull/17410) removes direct dependencies' `-L` paths, while dependency walk stops at target that set as `proc-macro=true`: https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/blob/3167045fceb698d70e0de548779088178e2bc10a/src/compiler/mod.rs#L1827-L1858
## Version

```
cargo 1.100.0-beta.4 (7552a885e 2026-09-29)
```

### Problem

The build script for jl-sys uses `cargo::metadata` to expose information like the detected version of Julia to dependent crates. Crates that need this information must specify jl-sys as a dependency. The jlrs-macros crate, a proc-macro crate, only needs the metadata, so it triggers this warning.

If I add `use jl_sys as _` to jlrs-macros lib.rs, compiling on macos fails with the following error:
> dyld[11780]: Library not loaded: @rpath/libunwind.1.dylib 

### Steps

1. Build jlrs. The warning always appears.

### Possible Solution(s)

Allow disabling the lint for specific dependencies.

### Notes

I have tried to refactor the metadata into a separate crate to avoid depending on jl-sys directly, but this leads to the same library loading issues as adding `use jl_sys as _` does.

### Problem

Here is the repo to reproduce this:
https://github.com/VEY-OSS/crt-static-host-config

When build with env var:
```
RUSTFLAGS=-Ctarget-feature=+crt-static
```

and with this in cargo.toml config:
```toml
[host]
rustflags = [
    "-C", "target-feature=-crt-static",
]

[unstable]
host-config = true
target-applies-to-host = true
```

```
CARGO_CFG_TARGET_FEATURE=fxsr,sse,sse2,x87
CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS=-Ctarget-feature=+crt-static
```

while without host config, `crt-static` will be contained in `CARGO_CFG_TARGET_FEATURE`.

body_text:
### Problem

Profile `trim-paths` is stabilized in 1.101 <https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/pull/17488>. We haven't yet changed the default value for any built-in profiles.

The `"object"` scope is actually a saner default that

* enhances privacy when distributing binaries
* helps byte-idential reproducibility, which may help build artifact deduplication and caching (see <https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/17453> and <https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/5931>)

Changing the default profile values is not an impossible thing.

* We have done that for split debuginfo: https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/pull/9298
* We plan to do that for debug: https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/15931
* In 1.101, users will have `build.profile` to pin the dev profile to avoid impact on default changing: https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/pull/17215

We should have a plan transitioning the default trim-path value to `"object"` as well.

[^1]: With limitations. See <https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/cargo/reference/profiles.html#limitations>

#### Reasons not to do this

* Debuggers and other debuginfo consumers cannot find  sources
  * Assuming that rust-lang/rust#163910 got merged, but plain debuggers like gdb/lldb/WinDbg, crash reporters like sentry, profilers like samply still haven't yet supported the unremap files.
  * Some may even rely on absolute path in `DW_AT_comp_dir` for loading current working directory, but we remap it to `"."` (current dir). If the tool doesn't understand it or not invoked from working dir, it doesn't work.
  * Expected to be improved over time by the community. 
* Coverage tools may be impacted as well
  * haven't yet checked how much but the `"object"` scope includes coverage remaps.
  * Expected to be improved over time by the community. 
* Backtrace and panic messages from non-workspace dependencies now show virtual paths under the `"object"` scope.
  * If under `"all"`, compiler diagnostics show virtual paths as well.
* Reading expanded `file!` value at runtime, if the `file!` macro is from generated rust file, git/registry deps, or deps outside the cargo workspace. https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/17586#issuecomment-6177635423

### Proposed Solution

Given the benefits of trim-paths are not only about artifact distribution privacy but also reproducibility and cacheability, I'd like to propose that we change `trim-paths` in both `dev` and `release` profiles to `"object"`. We might want to change it after a couple of releases when trim-paths is more widely used and adopted, in case there are bugs.

We could also wait for next edition, though I don't think it is necessary as we have precedent of changing profile values and has a way to override.

We also need to have crater run before changing any default.

### Problem

In a workspace, cargo tries to query all git repositories, even if they are not required for a build. This causes builds to fail if a git repository is not accessible, even if it isn't required.


### Steps

Imagine a workspace with two main crates `with-git-dependecy` and `without-git-dependecy`. `with-git-dependecy` depends on a other crate via git. If this crate is not accessible or not present, it becomes impossible to build `without-git-dependecy`.

### Possible Solution(s)

Build tree first, then query required git repositories, then only build required crates 

### Notes

`cargo tree -p without-git-dependency` fails as well.

body_text:
### Problem

Tools that build Rust code outside of Cargo still need to agree with Cargo about which versions get selected. The case I have in hand is rules_rust (cargo-bazel), which shells out to `cargo` for resolution today and would rather call the resolver directly.

From Rust code there are currently two ways to get Cargo's answer. One is to shell out to `cargo` (`cargo metadata`, `cargo generate-lockfile`, `cargo tree`). That works, but it ties a pure computation to a cargo binary of the right version, a real workspace on disk, cargo's own registry and network handling, and a process boundary, and it can't run anywhere cargo itself can't run. The other is to depend on the `cargo` crate. It's published, but it's all of Cargo, including git2, curl, OpenSSL, SQLite and jobserver. It's slow to build and doesn't compile for `wasm32`.

I don't want to reimplement resolution. Between feature unification, version preferences, yanked and offline handling, `min-publish-age` and lockfile encoding, any reimplementation drifts from Cargo, and users end up getting different answers from different tools. What I need is to compute the same answer Cargo computes, in-process, as a function from a set of summaries and a registry to a `Resolve`.

The resolver itself is already that function. It performs no I/O; everything it needs from its environment is a handful of flags and a clock.

### Proposed Solution

Move `src/resolver` and the types it operates on into `crates/cargo-resolver`, a workspace member published the same way as `cargo-platform` and `cargo-util-schemas`, with the same disclaimer (maintained by the Cargo team, primarily for use by Cargo, not intended for external use, may make major changes without warning). Version bumps and publishing go through the existing `xtask-bump-check` / `publish.py` flow. I'm not asking for a stability promise; consumers pin to the version matching their Cargo release.

Some findings from the prototype I put together for this proposal:

- **Contents:** `src/resolver` (~6.3k lines) plus the value types it operates on (~4k lines): `Summary`, `PackageId`, `PackageIdSpec` queries, `Dependency`, `SourceId`, `InternedString`, `Graph`, the semver extensions, and the `Registry` trait with `IndexSummary` and `QueryKind`.
- **Dependencies:** anyhow, cargo-platform, cargo-util-schemas, futures (executor only), im-rc, jiff, rustc-hash, semver, serde, serde-untagged, tracing, url. No native code.
- **Stays in Cargo:** `PackageRegistry`, all sources, lockfile I/O and version policy, config reading, `Workspace`.
- **One design change:** the resolver reaches its environment through a five-method `ResolverHost` trait (direct-minimal-versions flag, elapsed time, slow-resolution notice, offline flag, directory scan for path dependency hints) instead of `&GlobalContext`. Cargo implements it on top of `GlobalContext`; `resolve()` keeps its current signature, so no call site changes. Everything else is file moves.
- **Tests:** `resolver-tests` passes unchanged against the crate, and no longer needs to construct a `GlobalContext`.
- **Portability:** builds for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, given a 20-line `cfg` fallback in `cargo-util-schemas` where `Url::from_file_path` does not exist.

The cost is one more published crate and a version bump per release, plus a couple of trait impls that have to move because of the orphan rule (the `rusqlite` impls for `InternedString` end up in `util::sqlite`, which is arguably where they belong anyway). API churn between releases is expected and fine.

I would do the extraction PR and the ongoing maintenance. To make it reviewable I've split the preparatory work into small, independent PRs that each stand on their own and can land in any order:

1. `cargo-util-schemas`: build on targets without `Url::from_file_path`
2. `Dependency::serialized` takes the public-dependency flag
3. `extern_crate_name_and_dep_name` takes a crate name instead of `&Target`
4. Move `ArtifactTarget` compile-kind resolution to the compiler
5. Separate reading `min-publish-age` config from `PublishAgePolicy`
6. Decode lockfiles without a `Workspace`
7. Define `IndexSummary` and `QueryKind` next to the `Registry` trait
8. Reach the environment through a `ResolverHost` trait

After those, the extraction itself is almost entirely `git mv`.

Two things I'm less sure about and would like input on. The `ResolverHost` trait is a first cut; five methods was the smallest surface that covered what the resolver actually reads, but I'm open to a different shape, or to passing some of it as plain arguments. And `InternedString` is in the crate because `Summary` and `Dependency` are built on it, but a global interner is an odd thing for a library to export, so if people would rather it stayed in Cargo I'd want to work out what replaces it at the boundary.

### Notes

Alternatives I've looked at. `cargo metadata` is the status quo, described above. The `cargo` crate has the native-dependency, wasm and build-time problems above. pubgrub is a different algorithm and so gives different answers, and the whole point here is to match Cargo. What I actually run today is an out-of-tree extraction, a patch series re-applied to every nightly. It works, but every upstream refactor of the resolver turns into a merge conflict for me when it could have been a file move for everyone.

If publishing is the sticking point, an unpublished in-tree `crates/cargo-resolver` member would still get me most of the way there. I can depend on it by git path, and the boundary stops the resolver from getting tangled back up with the rest of Cargo. It would also give `resolver-tests` a target that makes future resolver work, such as the PubGrub experiments, easier to evaluate in isolation.

- **Dependencies:** anyhow, cargo-platform, cargo-util-schemas, futures (executor only), im-rc, jiff, rustc-hash, semver, serde, serde-untagged, tracing, url. No native code.
- **Stays in Cargo:** `PackageRegistry`, all sources, lockfile I/O and version policy, config reading, `Workspace`.
- **One design change:** the resolver reaches its environment through a five-method `ResolverHost` trait (direct-minimal-versions flag, elapsed time, slow-resolution notice, offline flag, directory scan for path dependency hints) instead of `&GlobalContext`. Cargo implements it on top of `GlobalContext`; `resolve()` keeps its current signature, so no call site changes. Everything else is file moves.
- **Tests:** `resolver-tests` passes unchanged against the crate, and no longer needs to construct a `GlobalContext`.
- **Portability:** builds for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, given a 20-line `cfg` fallback in `cargo-util-schemas` where `Url::from_file_path` does not exist.

The cost is one more published crate and a version bump per release, plus a couple of trait impls that have to move because of the orphan rule (the `rusqlite` impls for `InternedString` end up in `util::sqlite`, which is arguably where they belong anyway). API churn between releases is expected and fine.

I would do the extraction PR and the ongoing maintenance. To make it reviewable I've split the preparatory work into small, independent PRs that each stand on their own and can land in any order:

1. `cargo-util-schemas`: build on targets without `Url::from_file_path`
2. `Dependency::serialized` takes the public-dependency flag
3. `extern_crate_name_and_dep_name` takes a crate name instead of `&Target`
4. Move `ArtifactTarget` compile-kind resolution to the compiler
5. Separate reading `min-publish-age` config from `PublishAgePolicy`
6. Decode lockfiles without a `Workspace`
7. Define `IndexSummary` and `QueryKind` next to the `Registry` trait
8. Reach the environment through a `ResolverHost` trait

After those, the extraction itself is almost entirely `git mv`.

Two things I'm less sure about and would like input on. The `ResolverHost` trait is a first cut; five methods was the smallest surface that covered what the resolver actually reads, but I'm open to a different shape, or to passing some of it as plain arguments. And `InternedString` is in the crate because `Summary` and `Dependency` are built on it, but a global interner is an odd thing for a library to export, so if people would rather it stayed in Cargo I'd want to work out what replaces it at the boundary.

### Notes

Alternatives I've looked at. `cargo metadata` is the status quo, described above. The `cargo` crate has the native-dependency, wasm and build-time problems above. pubgrub is a different algorithm and so gives different answers, and the whole point here is to match Cargo. What I actually run today is an out-of-tree extraction, a patch series re-applied to every nightly. It works, but every upstream refactor of the resolver turns into a merge conflict for me when it could have been a file move for everyone.

If publishing is the sticking point, an unpublished in-tree `crates/cargo-resolver` member would still get me most of the way there. body_text:
### Problem

As the maintainer of the `zip` crate, I unfortunately caused some disruption by following my own long-established rule that versions of the crate with known security vulnerabilities would be yanked once a fix was released; so I've unyanked the last release of each major version and will wait 14 days to yank them again.

I'm still expecting this to cause some disruption when I finally do re-yank these versions, but right now the alternative is not having any barriers at all to continuing to use a vulnerable version indefinitely. It would be nice if there was a way to sunset such versions incrementally.

### Proposed Solution

One way to do it might be:

1. As soon as a "soft yank" is issued, when `cargo` is run from an interactive terminal, it raises a warning and prints the date when the "hard yank" is scheduled. The user must type `yes` to continue using the deprecated version.
2. After 7 days, crates that depend directly on the bad version can no longer be published to crates.io.
3. After 14 days, crates that depend on it *transitively* can no longer be published to crates.io.
4. After 21 days, Cargo refuses to download the bad version except for `--locked` builds or when a command-line option such as `--allow-yanked=zip@7.0.0` is passed.
5. After 35 days, the `--allow-yanked` option no longer works.
